Intended status: Standards Track                        Proofpoint, Inc.
Expires: 24 April 2027                                   21 October 2026


              The Agent Mediated Messaging Protocol (AMMP)
                           draft-rapp-ammp-00

Abstract

   The Agent Mediated Messaging Protocol (AMMP) is a wire contract,
   carried over a filesystem namespace, between an untrusted per-agent
   connector and a trusted, credentialed, store-and-forward messaging
   runtime.  It gives a sandboxed AI agent the ability to send and
   receive messages (email, and under an optional profile, messages to
   other agents) through a runtime that does not trust it: every
   outbound message begins as an inert request file that the runtime
   copies into private staging, validates independently, and applies
   policy to before anything is transmitted, and every inbound message
   is authenticated and screened by the runtime before a notice
   describing it appears in the agent's namespace.

   This document specifies the directory layout and its filesystem
   obligations — ownership, write and delete rights, and the path,
   symlink, and concurrency discipline a runtime observes; the JSON
   message shapes for submit requests, results, deliver notices, spooled
   message bodies, and an optional binding record; the correlation and
   versioning rules, including a direction-aware unknown-member
   tolerance rule; and two conformance classes.  An optional profile
   gives agent-to-agent traffic within one principal its own tree, and
   specifies how a Runtime signs and verifies that traffic when it
   travels between hosts as mail.

   AMMP is deliberately not a mail protocol: it neither defines nor
   replaces SMTP, IMAP, or provider-side infrastructure, and composes
   with them rather than displacing them.  Its single design center is
   that no security property depends on the agent — or on the connector
   speaking for it — behaving correctly.

1.  Introduction — Motivation and Problem Statement

   AI agents increasingly need to correspond, by email above all.  They
   are tasked over it, they return results over it, and they correspond
   over it with people and with systems that speak no other protocol.
   An agent is nonetheless an untrusted process: it can be prompt-
   injected by the very content it is asked to read, it can be
   defective, and it can be compromised outright.  Granting such a
   process email capability directly is dangerous along three concrete
   axes.

   *Inbound.* Delivered mail is untrusted content routed directly into
   the agent's reasoning.  A message body, a subject line, a sender
   display name, or an attachment filename can carry instructions the
   agent was never meant to follow.  The delivery path is therefore an
   injection vector by construction, and no amount of care inside the
   agent removes that property.

   *Outbound.* An agent that can send mail can exfiltrate anything it
   has read, to any address it chooses, and can do so under an identity
   that recipients associate with its operator.  Outbound mail is
   simultaneously a data-loss channel and an impersonation channel.

   *Credentials and identity.* Any mailbox credential, API token, or
   send endpoint held inside the agent's sandbox can be read, copied, or
   abused by whatever compromises the agent.  Worse, an agent holding a
   credential has no identity of its own that a recipient — or its own
   operator — can verify independently of that credential.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                 [Page 5]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


1.1.  Why the existing options are insufficient

   Handing the agent mailbox credentials, or a mail-send API, makes the
   agent a _trusted_ participant in the mail system.  That is precisely
   the wrong posture for a component whose defining risk is that it may
   be compromised: the trust must be withdrawn exactly when it is least
   possible to detect that it should be.  Wrapping the credential in a
   helper process that the agent calls does not change the analysis by
   itself, because a callable send capability is still a capability the
   agent holds; what matters is whether the capability crosses the
   boundary at all.

   The common alternative is per-deployment glue: a bespoke script or
   service wired between one agent harness and one mail system.  Such
   glue may even be correct, but it produces no reviewable contract, no
   interoperability, and no shared conformance bar.  Nothing tells a
   second implementer what the first one guarantees, and nothing tells
   either of them what a third-party reviewer should check.

   Adjacent agent protocols do not fill the gap, because they are
   solving a different problem: integration and interoperation _among
   credentialed participants_, rather than isolation of an _untrusted_
   one.  Section 3.4 positions AMMP against that landscape in detail.

1.2.  The approach

   The premise is isolation.  The agent runs in a sandbox, and the only
   path from that sandbox to its correspondence is the one this document
   specifies.  Isolation is what makes an agent safe to connect, and it
   is also what makes it operable: a process that is contained can be
   replaced, replayed and audited as a unit.  This document specifies
   what crosses the boundary, not the sandbox itself.

   AMMP interposes a *trusted runtime* between the agent and the systems
   that carry its messages, holding each message before forwarding it.
   The runtime holds every credential, owns the agent's sending
   identity, and makes every policy decision.  The agent interacts with
   the runtime only through a channel that carries *no capability*: it
   writes an inert request file into a directory, and the runtime —
   independently, on its own schedule, over its own private copy of
   those bytes — decides what, if anything, happens next.  In the other
   direction the runtime authenticates and screens each message before
   writing a notice describing it into the agent's namespace, and
   withholds the bytes of anything it will not vouch for.

   The payoff, which the rest of this document formalizes, is the load-
   bearing invariant:




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                 [Page 6]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      No security property depends on the agent — or on the connector
      speaking for it — behaving correctly.  Enforcement is entirely
      runtime-side.  A compromised agent or connector can at most write
      a well-formed request that the runtime then refuses.

   AMMP is the wire contract at exactly that trust boundary, and is
   owned by neither side of it.  That ownership choice is what allows a
   runtime and a connector built by different parties, on different
   schedules, to interoperate and to co-evolve against a versioned
   contract with an offline conformance suite.

1.3.  Why a filesystem namespace rather than an API, RPC, or queue

   The medium _is_ the boundary.  An API, an RPC endpoint, or a message
   queue is a live capability: something the agent invokes, whose
   invocation is itself the grant.  Its security therefore rests on
   authenticating and authorizing each call, on the client library
   behaving, and on the transport being what it claims to be.  A file
   written into a directory grants nothing at all.  It has no callee, no
   session, and no side effect until a separate, trusted process chooses
   to read it — at a time of that process's choosing, into memory of its
   own, under validation of its own.  The runtime is free to ignore the
   file, to refuse it, to hold it for human review, or to consume it and
   answer with a verdict.  Section 3.3 develops this point, along with
   the obligations it puts on the runtime in exchange.

1.4.  Design goals

   *  *Capability-free isolation.* The channel available to an untrusted
      agent grants no send capability, no credential, and no reach
      outside its own namespace.

   *  *Vendor-neutral interoperability.* A runtime and a connector built
      independently interoperate because both are built against this
      contract rather than against each other.

   *  *Versioned co-evolution with offline conformance.* Either side
      proves conformance against a fixture suite with no counterpart
      present, and version changes are deliberate, legible, and fail
      closed rather than silent.

   *  *Composition with real email.* Interactions remain federated, of-
      record, and human-inclusive, rather than confined to a closed
      agent-only channel.

   *  *Portability across agent runtimes.* Nothing in the contract
      presumes a particular agent harness, language, or tool interface.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                 [Page 7]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


1.5.  Non-goals

   *  *AMMP is not a mail transport.* It neither defines nor replaces
      SMTP, IMAP, or any provider-side mail infrastructure.  It
      describes what a runtime and a connector exchange _locally_;
      whatever the runtime does with a mail provider is out of scope.

   *  *AMMP is not agent-to-agent RPC.* The core contract is local to
      one deployment's filesystem, between two components on either side
      of a single trust boundary.  The optional peer-origin profile
      (Section 12) lets Agents of one principal write to one another,
      but as messages: between hosts they travel as ordinary mail,
      signed by the sending Runtime.  The profile defines no call or
      return semantics, no discovery mechanism, and no transport of its
      own.

   *  *AMMP is not a policy language.* What a runtime's policy decides —
      which recipients are permitted, which content is held for review,
      how a sender's standing is computed — is deliberately out of
      scope.  The wire defines only the shapes of requests and verdicts,
      never the computation that produces them.

   Every obligation in this document is grounded in what the contract
   actually provides.  Where a capability is sketched but not in force,
   it is marked as such (Appendix K), and where a property is a runtime
   obligation rather than a wire-verifiable fact, this document says so
   (Section 14.14).

1.6.  Why This Work Is Brought to the IETF

   This section is to be removed before publishing as an RFC.

   AMMP began as an implementation: a Runtime and Connectors built
   separately against a shared contract, with an offline conformance
   suite so that each side could be tested without the other.  It has
   been exercised in deployments of several cooperating Agents from more
   than one vendor, but every deployment so far has run under a single
   operator.  The authors bring it to the IETF for the things that
   implementation alone cannot supply:

   *  *Review.* The design rests on a security argument (Section 3.2),
      and that argument needs review by people who did not make it,
      particularly from the mail, security and identity communities.

   *  *Interoperation.* A contract owned by neither side is useful only
      if independent implementers build both sides.  The authors are
      looking for implementers and for interoperation testing across
      organizations.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                 [Page 8]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Collaborators.* The work should be shaped by more than one
      organization, and by the people who operate mail at scale.

   *  *Alignment with related work.* AMMP deliberately adds no new
      transport and no new identity scheme: email stays SMTP, and how an
      Agent's identity is established is left to work designed for that
      purpose.  Where AMMP touches such work, it should follow it rather
      than invent its own.

   Much of this document records why a rule is the way it is, because
   the reasoning is what a reviewer needs in order to disagree with it.
   None of it is offered as settled.  The questions below are ones the
   authors already know are open; others will surely be raised, and
   every one of them deserves a fresh look now that more people are
   reading the work.

   *  *The wire version.* The wire version starts at "2" rather than
      "1", because implementations already emit and check "2"
      (Section 13.1).  Whether to reset it is a fair question.

   *  *Registries.* Whether the wire version, the Result reason_code
      vocabulary, or the Control Notice's outcome and cause vocabularies
      should be governed by IANA (Section 15).

   *  *The name of the attestation member.* In this document it is the
      identity stamp a Runtime applied to an outbound message
      (Section 6.1).  In IETF usage, attestation usually means remote
      attestation of platform state, and the member may need another
      name.

   *  *Identity between Runtimes.* The peer-origin profile signs traffic
      between hosts with Ed25519 keys configured per Runtime
      (Section 12.6.7).  Whether that identity should instead be carried
      by an existing mechanism is open, and the candidates differ in
      what they would replace: a workload-identity system such as SPIFFE
      would replace the configured keys (distribution and attestation),
      while a standard signed envelope such as JWS with EdDSA (RFC 7515,
      RFC 8037) or COSE (RFC 9052) would replace the statement's own
      encoding, which is close to a detached JWS already.  DKIM and ARC
      sign on behalf of a mail domain rather than a Runtime, so they
      neither bind a message to the issuing Runtime nor carry the
      statement's members.

   *  *Document structure.* Whether the peer-origin profile belongs in
      this document or in a companion document.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                 [Page 9]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Internationalized addresses.* Addresses are restricted to a
      narrow ASCII addr-spec (Section 5.1), and internationalized
      addresses are out of scope for now.

   *  *A consumption signal.* Whether a Connector should be able to tell
      its Runtime that a Notice has been handled (Appendix K).

2.  Conventions and Terminology

   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP
   14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.

   Every message defined by this document is a JSON text as defined by
   [RFC8259], encoded in UTF-8 [RFC3629].  The schemas in Appendix A
   through Appendix H are written in the JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect
   [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12].

   Long lines in the JSON examples and schemas in this document are
   folded using the single-backslash strategy of [RFC8792].  Each folded
   block begins with that strategy's header line, which is part of the
   folded content: it is what allows the original to be reconstituted
   mechanically, so it is kept inside the block.

   Sections and subsections explicitly marked _(informative)_ or _(non-
   normative)_ carry no requirements; Section 3.4, Section 3.5,
   Appendix K, and Appendix L are the only such parts of this document.

2.1.  Terminology

   *  *Admitting Component* — in the peer-origin profile, a Runtime
      component that admits messages from a transport not restricted to
      authorized peer senders; a mail deliverer is the usual example.
      It does not hold write authority over the peer tree
      (Section 12.3).

   *  *Agent* — the untrusted process whose messaging capability this
      protocol mediates: email, and under the peer-origin profile,
      messages to other Agents.  It holds no credential, has no send
      path of its own, and reaches the protocol only through its
      Connector.  Nothing in this document places a requirement on the
      Agent, because no security property may depend on it.

   *  *Binding Record* — the optional, informational artifact at the
      Volume root naming which mailbox the Volume is bound to
      (Section 9).



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 10]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Connector* — the per-Agent component that speaks the Agent-side
      half of this contract: it writes Submit Requests, reads Results
      and Notices, and surfaces them to its Agent in whatever form its
      harness uses.  It is semi-trusted at best; for the purpose of
      every security property in this document it is treated as
      untrusted, and the requirements placed on it are well-formedness
      and non-crashing obligations, never obligations another party's
      safety rests on.

   *  *Control Notice* — in the peer-origin profile, the signed report a
      receiving Runtime sends to a configured sending Runtime about a
      Peer Statement it did not place (Section 12.6.8).

   *  *Descriptor* — one entry in an attachments[] array, describing an
      attachment (its display filename, media type, size, and —
      depending on direction — digest, Disposition, or content
      reference).  A Descriptor is metadata, not a path.

   *  *Disposition* — the Runtime's assertion about an inbound
      attachment's handling: clean, stripped, quarantined, or unscanned
      (Section 7.2).

   *  *Drop* — to discard an artifact without surfacing it.  Where this
      document says a consumer drops an artifact, the consumer MUST NOT
      surface the artifact to its Agent and MUST NOT act on it.  A drop
      is a consumer's decision about one artifact; it is unrelated to
      the outbound tree, into which a Connector writes requests.

   *  *Fail Closed* — to refuse to process an artifact rather than
      proceed on a partial or guessed interpretation of it.

   *  *Inbound Message* — the Runtime-authored artifact carrying a
      delivered message's body text and headers, spooled under a
      Notice's identifier and fetched on demand (Section 7.3).

   *  *Lane* — one class of traffic between an Agent and its Runtime, or
      between two Agents: the mail lane (inbound/ and outbound mail)
      and, under the peer-origin profile, the peer lane (peer/).  The
      Peer Directory states, per peer, which lanes are open.

   *  *Namespace* — the per-Agent subtree <volume-root>/<agent-id>/,
      mounted into that Agent's sandbox.  It is the unit of isolation
      and the sole authority for attributing an artifact to an Agent.

   *  *Notice* (Deliver Notice) — the Runtime-authored artifact
      announcing that a message was delivered to the Agent's mailbox
      (Section 7).  It is a pointer and summary, not the message.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 11]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Ordinal* — the integer naming a Sidecar blob.  It equals the
      index of the corresponding Descriptor in its array, and is the
      sole binding authority between a Descriptor and its bytes.

   *  *Origin Class* — the class of origin a consumer assigns to an
      inbound document, derived only from the Tree it was read from:
      mail for inbound/, and same-principal peer origin for peer/
      (Section 4.1, Section 12.3).

   *  *Peer Notice* — the Runtime-authored artifact, in the peer-origin
      profile, announcing a message from a same-principal Agent; the
      Deliver Notice shape with kind "peer", placed under peer/notices/
      (Section 12.2).

   *  *Peer Statement* — the signed JSON object a sending Runtime
      attaches, in an AMAP-Peer-Statement header field, to peer traffic
      it sends to another host (Section 12.6.1).

   *  *Result* — the Runtime-authored verdict for one consumed Submit
      Request (Section 6).

   *  *Runtime* — the trusted, credentialed, Agent-agnostic, store-and-
      forward messaging component that speaks the other half: it holds
      the messaging credentials, owns each Agent's identity, makes every
      policy decision, and is the only party that transmits or receives
      messages.  It holds each message before forwarding it: an outbound
      message is copied into private staging and checked before anything
      is transmitted, and an inbound message is screened before a Notice
      describing it appears.

   *  *Sandbox* — the isolation boundary within which an Agent and its
      Connector run.  The Runtime mounts the Agent's Namespace into it
      and nothing else of the Volume; no credential, send path or other
      messaging capability exists inside it.  This document does not
      specify the sandbox mechanism: it presumes one, and every property
      it states holds only as well as the Sandbox holds.

   *  *Sidecar* — attachment bytes stored beside a Submit Request or a
      Notice, in a directory named after that artifact, with each blob
      named by a 0-based ordinal.

   *  *Staging* — Runtime-private storage outside the Volume,
      unreachable from any Agent's mount, into which the Runtime copies
      Agent-authored bytes before acting on them (Section 4.1).

   *  *Submit Request* — the Connector-authored artifact requesting that
      a message be sent (Section 5).  It is inert: it carries no
      capability and effects nothing by existing.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 12]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Tree* — one of the Runtime-owned inbound-class subtrees of a
      Namespace: inbound/, and, under the peer-origin profile, peer/.
      Each Tree is an Origin Class.

   *  *Volume* — the runtime-owned filesystem tree carrying this
      protocol, containing one Namespace per Agent plus an optional
      Binding Record at its root.  Its mount path is a deployment
      choice; this document writes <volume-root>/ for it and nothing in
      the protocol derives from its name.  No implementation may depend
      on that name or any other.

3.  Architecture and Trust Model

3.1.  Actors

    +=============+===============+====================+==============+
    | Actor       | Trust         | Holds              | Reaches      |
    +=============+===============+====================+==============+
    | *Runtime*   | trusted       | messaging          | the mail     |
    | (host-side) |               | credentials, Agent | provider,    |
    |             |               | identity, policy,  | the Volume   |
    |             |               | the record of what |              |
    |             |               | was sent           |              |
    +-------------+---------------+--------------------+--------------+
    | *Connector* | semi-trusted, | nothing            | its own      |
    | (per Agent) | Agent-side    | credentialed       | Namespace on |
    |             |               |                    | the Volume;  |
    |             |               |                    | its Agent's  |
    |             |               |                    | input and    |
    |             |               |                    | output       |
    +-------------+---------------+--------------------+--------------+
    | *Agent*     | *untrusted*   | only what the      | the          |
    |             |               | Connector surfaces | Connector;   |
    |             |               |                    | its sandbox  |
    +-------------+---------------+--------------------+--------------+

                                  Table 1

   The Runtime is trusted by construction: it is the party holding the
   credentials, and a compromise of it is a compromise of the messaging
   capability itself.  The Connector is the interesting case.  It runs
   Agent-side, is reachable by whatever compromises the Agent, and is
   therefore treated as untrusted for every property that protects the
   Runtime, other Agents, or the outside world.  Requirements this
   document places on a Connector fall into two distinct classes, and
   the difference matters when reading them:





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 13]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Well-formedness and liveness obligations* — emit valid documents,
      tolerate a missing artifact, do not crash on hostile input.  A
      Connector that violates one harms itself and its own Agent, not
      any other party.

   *  *Obligations that protect an Agent from its own inbox* — the
      untrusted-content posture of Section 7.  These are necessarily
      Connector-implemented, because the Connector is the only component
      on the Agent's side of the boundary, and they are stated as such
      rather than as properties the Runtime relies on.

   No requirement in this document places a Runtime-side, other-Agent-
   side, or outside-world safety property in a Connector's hands.  The
   Connector's obligation not to rewrite a published Submit Request
   might appear to be one; Section 4.1's ingest-by-copy rule removes
   that dependency, leaving the obligation as pure well-formedness.

3.2.  The load-bearing invariant

      *Invariant.* No security property may depend on the Agent or the
      Connector behaving.  Enforcement is entirely Runtime-side.  A
      compromised Agent or Connector can at most write a well-formed
      request that the Runtime then refuses.

   Everything else in this document is downstream of that sentence.  It
   is why the Agent's declared identity is a cross-check rather than an
   attribution source (Section 4.1); why the Runtime re-derives every
   path from data it controls rather than from a file's contents
   (Section 4.1); why recipient policy is evaluated Runtime-side over
   the exact recipient set that will be transmitted to (Section 5.1);
   why the digest an Agent supplies for its own attachment bytes is an
   integrity aid and not a trust boundary (Section 5.1); and why the
   absence of bytes, rather than a flag inside a document, is the access
   gate on inbound attachments (Section 7.2).

   The invariant also bounds what this document can promise.  A wire
   contract cannot make a Runtime honest, and a fixture suite cannot
   observe a filesystem.  Section 14.14 states which properties are
   wire-verifiable and which are Runtime obligations that a green
   conformance run does not prove.

3.3.  Why a filesystem namespace

   The Runtime mounts each Agent's Namespace into that Agent's sandbox,
   and the Agent's entire protocol surface is that directory.  This is a
   deliberate choice of medium, with three consequences.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 14]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Writing a file carries no capability.* It invokes nothing.  There is
   no callee to authenticate, no session to hijack, no method whose mere
   reachability is a grant.  The request exists as bytes until a trusted
   process elects to look at them.  Compare an API or queue, where the
   act of enqueuing is itself the privileged act and every security
   property depends on the authorization check in front of it being
   correct and unbypassable.

   *Isolation is structural rather than enforced by policy.* A Connector
   scoped to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/ cannot name another Agent's
   Namespace at all.  Attribution follows from _where a file appeared_,
   not from what the file says about itself, so spoofing attribution
   requires defeating the mount rather than lying in a JSON member.

   *The medium's costs are real and are paid explicitly.* A shared
   filesystem between a trusted and an untrusted party is itself an
   attack surface: symlinks, directory swaps, special files, hard links,
   and unbounded sizes are all available to the untrusted side, and
   every path-based check the trusted side performs is racy against a
   concurrent rename.  This document therefore does not treat "it is
   just a directory" as a simplification.  Section 4.1 states the path,
   open, copy, and concurrency discipline a Runtime observes in exchange
   for the medium's advantages, and Section 14 revisits each as a
   threat.

3.4.  Relationship to Other Agent Protocols (Informative)

   _This subsection is informative.  It contains no requirements and
   creates no dependency on any external protocol.  Nothing here claims
   that AMMP replaces, subsumes, or competes with any protocol named
   below._

   AMMP occupies a narrow position: it is the local seam at a single
   trust boundary, where one side holds every credential and the other
   holds none.  The adjacent protocols in the agent ecosystem sit at
   different layers, and the common question of "why not use one of them
   here" has a specific answer in each case.

   *Model Context Protocol (MCP)* [MCP] connects an agent host to tools
   and context through JSON-RPC servers.  It is an integration
   interface: live capabilities are exposed across it and exercised by
   the agent through it.  That makes MCP complementary to AMMP rather
   than an alternative.  A Connector often surfaces AMMP's operations to
   its Agent through MCP, or through whatever tool interface its harness
   uses natively; AMMP is the capability-free seam sitting behind that
   surface.  The contrast worth stating is exactly the one that
   motivates the two coexisting: an MCP-style interface grants live
   capability across the boundary it spans, while AMMP's channel



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 15]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   deliberately grants none — the Agent-side surface can be as rich as
   the harness likes, because what crosses the trust boundary underneath
   it is an inert file.  MCP originated at Anthropic.

   *Agent2Agent (A2A)* [A2A] is networked agent-to-agent RPC between
   mutually authenticated services, with agent cards, tasks, and
   HTTP/SSE/JSON-RPC transport.  It presumes both endpoints are
   credentialed participants that can authenticate to each other.
   AMMP's design center is the opposite: an untrusted agent that holds
   no credentials at all, with enforcement placed entirely on the
   trusted side of a local boundary.  The two are orthogonal, and
   compose without friction — an agent that speaks A2A to its peers can
   use AMMP for its mail capability, and neither protocol needs to know
   about the other.  A2A originated at Google and is hosted by the Linux
   Foundation.

   *The two protocols abbreviated "ACP" are not the same protocol*, and
   the collision is worth disambiguating in a document a reviewer may
   arrive at with one of them in mind.

   *  The *Agent Communication Protocol* (IBM/BeeAI) is of historical
      interest here: it merged into A2A under the Linux Foundation,
      announced in August 2025, with its repository archived
      [ACP-MERGER].

   *  The *Agent Client Protocol* [ACP-CLIENT] is a distinct and
      currently active protocol at a different layer — an interface
      between a host or editor and an agent — originated by Zed
      Industries.  It is unrelated to the merged Agent Communication
      Protocol and unrelated to AMMP.

3.5.  Runtimes Built from Several Components (Informative)

   _This subsection is informative.  It contains no requirements._

   The Runtime is defined by its role, not as a single process.  A
   Runtime may be built from several trusted components: for example,
   one that drains Agent Namespaces and applies policy, and another that
   holds the mail credentials and talks to the provider.  Every
   obligation this document places on the Runtime binds the composite as
   seen from the Agent's Namespace.  How the components divide the work,
   and how they communicate, is Runtime mechanism and out of scope.
   They may communicate by any means, for example SMTP [RFC5321] between
   hosts or LMTP [RFC2033] within one; this document specifies only the
   Agent boundary.

   Some existing obligations are easy to lose when the work is divided:




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 16]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  exactly one Result per consumed request, including when an inner
      component fails or never answers (Section 6.1);

   *  accepted only once the provider has accepted the message for relay
      (Section 6.1);

   *  the recipient set handed to the provider is exactly the set on
      which recipient policy was evaluated (Section 5);

   *  nothing quarantined or unverified becomes a Notice (Section 7),
      and clean is asserted only for bytes the publishing component has
      verified, with every content_ref bound to the Notice it sits in
      (Section 7.2);

   *  attribution is carried between components by Runtime
      configuration, never by anything the Agent wrote (Section 4.1);
      and

   *  only the component facing the Agent's Namespace writes the Agent's
      lanes.

4.  Volume Layout

   The Runtime owns the Volume and mounts each Agent's Namespace into
   that Agent's sandbox.  A Connector has access *only* within its own
   <agent-id>/, and only to the paths below.  Within that Namespace,
   write access may be narrower still: the inbound/ subtree is Runtime-
   owned and MAY be mounted read-only.

   The Volume root's own name is a *deployment choice and is not part of
   this protocol* — nothing derives from it, and no implementation may
   depend on it. <volume-root>/ below stands for whatever a deployment
   calls it.


















Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 17]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   <volume-root>/
     identity.json           # runtime/provisioner: Binding Record (S9)
     <agent-id>/
       outbound/
         req-<id>.json          # agent -> runtime: Submit Request
         req-<id>.attachments/  # agent -> runtime: Sidecar bytes,
                                #   ordinals 0 1 2 ...
         results/<id>.json      # runtime -> agent: verdict for req <id>
         processed/req-<id>.json  # runtime: consumed requests
         ext/<name>/            # connector-owned side channel a
                                #   runtime MAY read by out-of-band
                                #   agreement; <name> is a STABLE,
                                #   opaque connector id
       inbound/
         notices/notice-<id>.json  # runtime -> agent: delivered event
         notices/<notice-id>.attachments/  # bytes asserted clean,
                                           #   ordinals 0 1 2 ... (S7.2)
         notices/processed/     # OPTIONAL - connector archive,
                                #   writable-inbound deployments only
         messages/notice-<id>.json  # runtime -> agent: full message
         cursor.json            # runtime: inbound poll cursor
       peer/                    # OPTIONAL - peer-origin profile:
                                #   same layout as inbound/
       directory.json           # OPTIONAL - runtime: Peer Directory
       audit/
         log.jsonl              # runtime: append-only action log

           Figure 1: Volume layout (illustrative — not a fixture)

   There is exactly one inbound Sidecar directory — inbound/
   notices/<notice-id>.attachments/ — and both a Deliver Notice's and an
   Inbound Message's content_ref resolve there.  No second, message-
   specific Sidecar directory exists.

4.1.  Obligations

   *Attribution by Namespace.* <agent-id> is assigned by the Runtime,
   not declared by the Agent.  Attribution is _the Namespace a file
   arrived in_; an agent_id member inside the file is a cross-check
   only.  A Runtime MUST reject a Submit Request whose agent_id, when
   present, does not match the Namespace it was found in, and MUST NOT
   use that member to attribute the request.  A Runtime MUST know the
   <agent-id> of every Namespace it serves: from its own configuration
   or, where its own layout carries it, from the Namespace's path, and
   MUST NOT take it from anything the Agent writes.  A Runtime that
   cannot name the Namespace in which it found a Submit Request MUST
   reject that request rather than accept its agent_id unchecked.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 18]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Isolation is structural.* A Connector scoped to <agent-id>/ cannot
   read another Agent's drafts or Notices.

   *All writes are atomic.* Every artifact in the tree above is
   published by writing a .tmp sibling and then renaming it into place
   (os.replace or the equivalent).  Readers MUST ignore *.tmp entries.

   *Single writer, single drainer.* At any moment a Namespace has
   exactly one Connector instance writing outbound/ and exactly one
   Runtime instance draining it.  Every concurrency-sensitive rule in
   this document — the atomic .tmp-then-rename discipline above, the
   commit sentinel below, and the derivation of req_id from max(pending,
   processed, results) + 1 (Section 5.1) — is sound only under that
   assumption and provides no mutual exclusion of its own.  Each side
   MUST ensure single-instance operation over a Namespace by a mechanism
   outside this protocol, such as an OS-level lock held for the process
   lifetime.  A Runtime MUST NOT run two concurrent drains of one
   Namespace, and a Connector MUST NOT run two concurrent writers into
   one.  Behavior under violation is unspecified: duplicated delivery,
   clobbered published requests, and false verdicts are all reachable.

   *Filename identifiers are the authority for paths.* An identifier
   taken from a file's _contents_ — a req_id member in a request body,
   for instance — MUST NOT determine a write path.  The Runtime derives
   identifiers from the validated filename, on a restricted character
   set.

   *Write-side path discipline.* Every write, rename, directory
   creation, or archive move into or within a Namespace MUST satisfy all
   three of the following *conjunctively*. Each closes a distinct gap
   the other two leave open, and none is sufficient alone.

   *  *(a) Full parent-chain pinning.* The write resolves its full
      parent chain through pinned directory descriptors from the
      Namespace root — openat, mkdirat, renameat off a descriptor the
      Runtime opened once per Namespace — and MUST NOT re-resolve a path
      string for the act itself.  A path-based containment check
      followed by a path-based act is a race, not a check: the parent
      directory the check inspected and the parent directory the act
      touches are not guaranteed to be the same object, because the
      Agent can swap a parent directory for a symlink in between.
      Applying a no-follow flag to the _final_ path component alone does
      not close this gap — it constrains only the last component, not a
      swapped parent — and rename and directory-creation calls have no
      no-follow equivalent at all, so a bare "writes do not follow
      symlinks" requirement is not sufficient on its own.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 19]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *(b) No-follow while building the chain.* Each directory component
      that goes into that parent chain MUST itself have been opened with
      O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY at the moment it was added to the pinned
      chain.  A descriptor counts as pinned only if the open that
      produced it refused to follow a symlink at that step.  Requirement
      (a) without this is equally insufficient, and the gap is the
      symmetric one: nothing otherwise stops the Runtime from
      _acquiring_ a "pinned" descriptor by following an Agent-planted
      symlink in the first place — the Agent replaces a Namespace
      subdirectory with a symlink before the Runtime's once-per-
      Namespace open, or before a later re-open after a restart — and a
      descriptor obtained that way is pinned to the wrong object, so
      every write built off it inherits the redirection no matter how
      faithfully (a) is followed from there.

   *  *(c) Non-following final component.* The final path component MUST
      NOT be followed if a symlink exists at that name: the open MUST
      carry O_NOFOLLOW and MUST fail closed on ELOOP rather than writing
      through whatever the name currently resolves to.  Two cases differ
      in what else they require, and both are covered:

      -  *A newly created file* — the .tmp sibling the atomicity rule
         above already requires, and any Sidecar blob — MUST
         additionally be created with O_EXCL (O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL,
         never O_TRUNC in place of O_EXCL), failing closed on EEXIST.

      -  *An append-mode or directory-creating write that has no .tmp
         sibling* — audit/log.jsonl is the case this document names —
         cannot use O_EXCL, because the target legitimately already
         exists.  It MUST instead open with
         O_NOFOLLOW|O_APPEND|O_NONBLOCK (or use mkdirat with the parent
         pinned per (b)), MUST NOT block on a special file, and MUST
         verify through the resulting descriptor (fstat, never a pre-
         open stat) that the object is a regular file it may append to;
         it SHOULD refuse a target whose link count exceeds 1.  The non-
         blocking open is load-bearing and is not a performance concern:
         O_NOFOLLOW does not apply to a FIFO — a FIFO is not a symlink —
         and opening one for writing blocks until a reader appears, so
         without O_NONBLOCK the fstat is never reached and an Agent that
         plants a FIFO at this name stalls the drain indefinitely.  The
         first branch's O_EXCL refuses that case on its own; the second
         branch has no O_EXCL to lean on and states it explicitly.
         Requiring O_EXCL in the second branch would forbid appending to
         an existing log at all; requiring nothing there would leave the
         one write this document names that has no .tmp sibling
         unprotected.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 20]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      Requirement (c) is needed in both of its branches because an Agent
      can pre-plant a symlink at a filename the Runtime is about to
      write. req_id is Agent-chosen, and every Runtime-written filename
      in the layout tree above — results/<id>.json, the .tmp sibling of
      processed/req-<id>.json, inbound/notices/notice-<id>.json,
      inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json, audit/log.jsonl — is reachable
      to an Agent that can predict or observe it.  Absent (c), such a
      name gets its bytes written through the planted symlink with the
      Runtime's own privileges, even though the parent chain that
      reached the containing directory was itself correctly pinned under
      (a) and (b).

      This discipline governs every Runtime-side write named in the
      layout tree, not only the initial consumption of an Agent-authored
      artifact.

   *Read-side discipline.* The same rule applied to reads.  When the
   Runtime opens any path the Agent can influence — every req-<id>.json,
   every Sidecar ordinal, and, in a deployment that leaves inbound/
   writable, anything it later reads back from there — it MUST open
   without following symbolic links at any component (per-component
   O_NOFOLLOW, or an equivalently pinned directory-descriptor walk from
   the Namespace root, matching the write-side rule above), MUST NOT
   block on a special file (a non-blocking open), MUST verify that the
   opened object is a regular file through the open descriptor (fstat
   and an S_ISREG test — never a pre-open stat, which is a race), SHOULD
   refuse a file whose link count exceeds 1, and MUST enforce a
   deployment-configured per-file size cap (a bounded read) and a per-
   request Sidecar count cap.  The too_large value in the Result
   vocabulary (Section 6.1) presumes that cap: enforcing one is an
   obligation, not an option.

   A Connector's one Agent-influenceable read path — resolving a
   notice_id to inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json — MUST be built only
   from a pattern-validated notice_id (the schemas pin the pattern) and
   MUST confine resolution to the Connector's own inbound/ tree
   (Section 7.3).

   *Sidecar ordinal binding.* Sidecar blobs are named by Runtime-
   assigned 0-based ordinals equal to the Descriptor's array index,
   which is the sole binding authority.  Nothing else names a blob; a
   Descriptor's filename is display-only, and MUST NOT be used as a
   path.








Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 21]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Commit sentinel.* All Sidecar bytes are written — .tmp sibling, then
   rename — *before* req-<id>.json; the JSON file's presence is the only
   publish signal.  The Runtime MUST verify that every referenced
   ordinal exists and MUST re-verify size and digest before acting on
   the request, against the snapshot it took at ingest (below), never
   against the live path.

   *Inbound Sidecar directories are keyed on the Runtime-minted notice
   identifier.* A Runtime MUST NOT name one after the provider
   message.id.  The provider identifier is external and is not
   character-set-safe, so using one as a path component would let a
   sender influence where the Runtime writes.  The same rule extends to
   the body artifact: inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json MUST be keyed on
   the notice identifier, and MUST NOT be keyed on message.id.  Inbound
   bytes are published only at inbound/notices/<notice-
   id>.attachments/<index>, the single Sidecar directory named in the
   layout tree.

   *Runtime-private Staging lives outside the mounted Volume* — at a
   path the Agent's mount cannot reach at all.

   *Ingest by copy.* Before validating, evaluating policy on, or
   composing from any Agent-authored artifact — req-<id>.json and every
   Sidecar ordinal — the Runtime MUST copy the bytes into Runtime-
   private Staging and MUST act only on that private copy.  All checks —
   schema validation, recipient policy, size and sha256 verification —
   and all message composition MUST run over that snapshot, and the
   Runtime MUST NOT re-read any Agent-writable path after a decision
   that depends on its content.  Verify-then-use against a live Agent-
   writable path is a race, not a check.

   This obligation is what makes the Connector's "MUST NOT delete or
   rewrite a published request" (Section 4.2) a pure well-formedness
   rule: a Runtime MAY treat an observed post-publish change as
   malformed, but no safety property depends on the Connector honoring
   immutability — which is what the invariant of Section 3.2 requires.
   (This governs the properties that protect the Runtime, other Agents,
   and the outside world.  Obligations that protect an Agent from its
   own inbox are necessarily Connector-implemented and are stated as
   such, not as properties the Runtime relies on a Connector for.)

   *Byte-absence is the gate.* The Runtime MUST NOT place non-clean
   bytes in an Agent's Namespace. content_ref is the Runtime's access
   grant, present only for bytes it has published as clean
   (Section 7.2).






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 22]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Tree rules.* Every Runtime-owned inbound-class tree is an *origin
   class*: a consumer MUST derive the class of a document from the tree
   it was read from, and MUST NOT derive it from any member of the
   document. notice_id uniqueness is per tree, and where a tree has more
   than one writer each MUST mint so that cross-writer collision is
   negligible — at least 128 bits of entropy under the identifier
   character set, or a writer-specific prefix — and a consumer keying
   state across trees MUST include the tree in that key. content_ref
   resolves only within the notices/ directory of the tree the enclosing
   document was read from.  Write authority per tree is distinct and
   MUST be structurally enforced; it MUST NOT depend on configuration
   the writer itself reads. inbound/ is the one tree the core protocol
   defines; a profile, such as the peer-origin profile of Section 12,
   MAY define others.

   *Inbound is Runtime-owned, and read-only is a valid posture.* The
   inbound/ tree is Runtime-owned end to end.  A Runtime MAY expose it
   to the sandbox read-only — for instance as a read-only mount, which
   is the mechanism that actually makes a delivered Notice unforgeable,
   since file permission bits do not bind a same-uid Agent, which can
   change a mode it owns.  A Connector MUST NOT require write access
   anywhere under inbound/: it MUST start, relay Notices, and resolve
   bodies when every write, rename, and directory creation under
   inbound/ fails. inbound/notices/processed/ is OPTIONAL — a
   conventional archive location a Connector MAY use only where a
   deployment leaves inbound writable; nothing on either side may depend
   on its existence or its contents.

   *Consumption tracking is Connector-private.* How a Connector records
   which Notices it has already relayed to its Agent is Connector-
   private state, outside this protocol.  Such state lives in the
   Connector's own storage outside the Volume, or in Connector-owned
   paths under outbound/ not enumerated in the layout tree — which MUST
   NOT use the req- prefix, reserved for Submit Requests and their
   Sidecars, so that a Runtime's scan of outbound/ never encounters
   Connector-private state.  Either way, the Runtime neither reads nor
   relies on it.  A seam-visible consumption signal is deliberately not
   specified by this document; Appendix K records the reasoning.

   *Outbound extension space.* outbound/ext/<name>/ is a Connector-owned
   side channel, one directory per <name>, that a Runtime MAY read by
   out-of-band agreement. *<name> is a stable Connector id: the
   Connector chooses it once, and it MUST NOT change when the
   Connector's repository, package, or deployment is renamed or moved.
   A Runtime that reads the directory MUST treat <name> as opaque — it
   is an identifier, never a name to be parsed, resolved, or matched
   against a repository or path.* Because it is also a path segment in
   an Agent-writable tree, <name> MUST be a single path segment of 1 to



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 23]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   64 characters drawn from lowercase ASCII letters, digits, hyphen and
   underscore, beginning with a letter or digit, so that it names the
   same directory on case-sensitive and case-insensitive filesystems
   alike.  This document specifies no shape for anything under it; it
   lies outside the req- prefix the Runtime scans, and nothing security-
   relevant may be built on it.  Its first use is a Connector's per-
   Notice *outcome* file, written by the receiving Agent's own uid and
   therefore forgeable by construction.  An outcome is a statement by
   the receiving side about what it did with a Notice; a party MUST NOT
   treat an outcome as proof of delivery or of non-delivery, and the
   Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it
   (Section 14.15).  There is deliberately no inbound extension space:
   an inbound tree is a Runtime assertion about origin, and a Connector
   cannot know what a vendor-named assertion means.

5.  Outbound: Submit Request

   An Agent's only outbound action is writing an inert request file into
   its Namespace.  The file carries no send capability; the Runtime
   enforces policy before anything leaves.

   A Submit Request is written to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/outbound/
   req-<id>.json as a JSON text [RFC8259].  Its Sidecar bytes, if any,
   are written first, into req-<id>.attachments/, one blob per
   Descriptor, named by that Descriptor's 0-based array index
   (Section 4.1, commit sentinel).

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "req_id": "00000001",
     "agent_id": "agent.research",
     "ts": "2026-07-20T04:10:56Z",
     "in_reply_to": "1721457600000000000-4242",
     "draft": {
       "to": ["owner@example.com"],
       "cc": [],
       "subject": "Run report",
       "body_text": "The run finished; details below.",
       "reply_to_message_id": null,
       "attachments": [
         {
           "filename": "report.pdf",
           "media_type": "application/pdf",
           "size_bytes": 48213,
           "sha256": "970e441b6c4ecd37abf2541e1276c680bdec8481cef9368ff\
       1d010fd6b784b07"
         }
       ]
     }
   }

      Figure 2: draft/examples/submit-request.json (illustrative — not
                                 a fixture)

   The normative shape is Appendix A.  The Submit Request envelope is
   *closed*: additionalProperties is false at every level, and a Runtime
   MUST reject a request carrying any unrecognized member.  Section 13.1
   explains why this direction is closed while the Runtime-authored
   artifacts are open.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 27]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


5.1.  Field semantics and obligations

   *  *contract_version* (REQUIRED) is the wire major version, the
      string "2".  A Runtime MUST check it before schema validation and
      MUST fail closed on an absent, lower, or higher major
      (Section 13.1).

   *  *req_id* (REQUIRED) is *monotonic per Namespace* and MUST NOT be
      reused for the life of the Namespace's outbound/ tree; derive it
      from max(pending, processed, results) + 1.  Reuse collides message
      identifiers and triggers provider-side idempotency deduplication.
      req_id is pinned to a filename-safe character set by the schema,
      but it is not the path authority: the Runtime derives the path
      identifier from the validated filename (Section 4.1).

   *  *agent_id* (OPTIONAL), if present, MUST match the Namespace the
      request was found in, and a Runtime MUST reject a mismatch.  A
      Runtime MUST NOT use it as the attribution source (Section 4.1).

   *  *ts* (OPTIONAL) is the Connector's timestamp for the request.  It
      is Agent-authored and therefore advisory.

   *  *in_reply_to* (OPTIONAL) correlates this request with prior
      inbound work.  It carries either a Runtime-minted notice_id or a
      mail message identifier [RFC5322].  It is a *hint from an
      untrusted party* and MUST NOT by itself widen what the request is
      permitted to do — the same posture Section 8 fixes for task_id.

   *  The Runtime derives the message identity and the From/Reply-To of
      the composed message itself; identity is Runtime-owned, and the
      Agent does *not* choose its sending identity.

   *  *draft.to* is REQUIRED and carries at least one recipient;
      *draft.cc* is OPTIONAL and MAY be empty. *draft.subject* and
      *draft.body_text* are REQUIRED and MAY be empty strings. body_text
      is *plain text*; this document defines no alternative body
      representation.

   *  *draft.reply_to_message_id* (OPTIONAL, nullable) names the message
      this draft replies to, as an [RFC5322] message identifier.  It is
      composed directly into an In-Reply-To: header, which is why it
      carries a control-character pattern in the schema (below).









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 28]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Recipient policy is a Runtime decision.* The Agent's chosen
      draft.to and draft.cc are *not* inherently trusted.  Allowlisting,
      task-counterpart binding, and any other recipient rule are
      evaluated Runtime-side.  A populated allowlist plus a fresh
      recipient is an exfiltration surface that the Runtime, not the
      Connector, must close.

   *  *Recipient syntax and header-injection discipline.* Each draft.to
      and draft.cc element is exactly one bare addr-spec: no display
      name, address list, quoted local part, comment, IP literal, or
      folding whitespace.  The schema pins the pattern.  This profile is
      deliberately narrower than [RFC5322], because those excluded forms
      are exactly what makes allowlist evaluation non-mechanical;
      internationalized (EAI/SMTPUTF8) addresses are out of scope for
      now and may be added later.  A Runtime MUST reject — with a top-
      level rejected Result — a request whose recipient entries do not
      parse under this profile, MUST evaluate recipient policy over
      exactly the recipient set it will transmit to, and MUST NOT
      transmit to any address not present in draft.to or draft.cc.

      Separately, a Runtime MUST NOT allow any Agent-authored string —
      subject, a recipient entry, an attachment filename, an attachment
      media_type, draft.reply_to_message_id, in_reply_to, agent_id, ts,
      or body_text where it abuts headers — to introduce a header
      boundary in the composed message.  CR, LF, and NUL MUST be
      rejected or stripped before composition *even where schema
      validation was bypassed upstream*: the schema-level control-
      character patterns on subject, filename, media_type,
      reply_to_message_id, in_reply_to, agent_id, and ts are the first
      line of defense, not the only one.  Two of those fields are easily
      overlooked: reply_to_message_id and media_type are composed
      _directly into headers_ — In-Reply-To: and a MIME part's Content-
      Type: [RFC2045] respectively — rather than into a body or a
      display field.

   *  *draft.attachments[]* (OPTIONAL) is an array of Descriptors, each
      carrying filename, media_type, size_bytes, and sha256. *size_bytes
      and sha256 are REQUIRED on every Descriptor*, computed by the
      Connector over the *decoded* bytes it wrote, with sha256 in
      lowercase hexadecimal.

      There is *no outbound content_ref*. The Runtime re-derives each
      Sidecar's path from req-<id> plus the Descriptor's array index,
      which is the sole binding authority; an Agent-supplied path string
      would be pure disagreement and attack surface, so it is absent
      from the schema entirely and additionalProperties: false rejects
      it. attachments: [] is valid and is equivalent to the member being
      absent; the Sidecar directory MUST then be absent.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 29]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      sha256 here is an integrity and deduplication aid, *not an
      outbound trust boundary*: the Agent controls both the bytes and
      the hash, so a mismatch catches corruption, never a hostile Agent.
      Its value to the Runtime is that it detects an inconsistent
      request, not that it authenticates one.

6.  Outbound: Result

   A Result is the Runtime's verdict for one consumed Submit Request,
   written to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/outbound/results/<id>.json.

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "req_id": "00000001",
     "outcome": "accepted",
     "detail": null,
     "reason_code": "allowlisted",
     "ts": "2026-08-09T19:14:00Z",
     "recipients": ["owner@example.com"],
     "message_id": "<20260809191400.1@example.org>",
     "job_id": null,
     "attestation": {
       "form": "self-stamp",
       "token": "selfstamp.v1.abcdef",
       "claims": {
         "agent": "agent.research",
         "acts_for": "owner@example.com",
         "issued_at": "2026-08-09T19:14:00Z"
       }
     },
     "attachments": [
       { "index": 0, "outcome": "accepted", "detail": null }
     ]
   }

    Figure 3: draft/examples/result.json (illustrative — not a fixture)

   The normative shape is Appendix B.  The Result envelope is *open*: a
   consumer MUST tolerate members it does not recognize, at every level
   (Section 13.1).

6.1.  Field semantics and obligations

   *  *The Runtime writes exactly one Result per Submit Request it
      consumes.* A request the Runtime never consumes gets no Result,
      and no signal in this protocol distinguishes "not yet" from
      "never."




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 30]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *outcome* (REQUIRED) is one of accepted, queued_for_human, or
      rejected.  This is a *closed vocabulary*: it gates which
      processing path a document takes, so a consumer cannot safely
      treat an unrecognized value as opaque, and introducing a new value
      is a major change (Section 13.1).

   *  *Any policy miss — allowlist, rate limit, DLP hold, halt — MUST
      produce queued_for_human.* A Runtime MUST NOT send such a request,
      and MUST NOT drop it without a Result.

   *  *accepted* means the provider accepted the message for relay.
      Downstream delivery or quarantine is out of the Runtime's hands
      and is surfaced later via an inbound delivery-status notification,
      if any.

   *  *detail* (OPTIONAL, nullable) is human-readable text.  It carries
      no machine semantics.

   *  *reason_code* (OPTIONAL) records _which policy path_ authorized or
      refused the request; human text stays in detail.  A Runtime
      *SHOULD* set a reason on every Result, successes included.  The
      suggested vocabulary — recipient_bound, allowlisted,
      no_verified_counterparty, recipient_not_allowlisted, dlp_hold,
      no_screener, halted, rate_limited, unsupported_contract_version —
      is *extensible and not enum-locked in the schema*. Two consumer
      obligations follow: a consumer MUST tolerate a reason_code it does
      not recognize, treating it as opaque and never as an error, and a
      consumer MUST NOT infer the outcome from it. outcome is the sole
      authoritative verdict; reason_code only explains which path
      produced it, and a Runtime may add codes at any time without a
      protocol change. unsupported_contract_version is the code a
      Runtime sets on the rejected Result it writes for a version-
      refused Submit Request (Section 13.1).

   *  *ts* (OPTIONAL) is the Runtime-set, of-record time of the verdict,
      in ISO-8601 form.

   *  *recipients* (OPTIONAL) records the recipient set the Runtime
      actually transmitted to.

   *  *message_id* (OPTIONAL, nullable) is the [RFC5322] message
      identifier the Runtime assigned to the composed message.

   *  *job_id* (OPTIONAL, nullable) is a provider-side job identifier,
      opaque to this protocol.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 31]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *attestation* (OPTIONAL) is the identity stamp the Runtime applied
      to the outbound message.  Its form is self-stamp or verifiable,
      distinguishing a stamp a stranger cannot verify from one that can
      be verified independently.  A Connector _surfaces_ an attestation,
      and does not verify it; verification is a Runtime concern.

   *  *attachments[]* (OPTIONAL) carries one diagnostic entry per
      submitted attachment: index, an outcome of accepted, dlp_held,
      rejected_type, or too_large, and an optional detail. *index MUST
      equal the entry's own position in the array* — contiguous, unique,
      and covering 0 through n-1 exactly once.  Array position is the
      binding authority for attachments in both directions
      (Section 4.1).  This constraint is not expressible in JSON Schema
      and is enforced by the conformance gate as a named post-check
      rather than by the schema (Appendix J).

      *Two paths, kept apart.* A _malformed_ attachment — a size or
      digest mismatch, a missing or extra Sidecar, a duplicate index —
      is not a policy decision: it fails the whole request with a top-
      level rejected.  A _policy hold_ — DLP, a disallowed type, a size
      cap, including a fail-closed hold when no screener is available —
      is queued_for_human.  Per-attachment outcomes are diagnostic
      detail under *one* governing top-level outcome, and a Runtime MUST
      NOT send part of a request on their strength.

7.  Inbound: Deliver Notice and Inbound Message

   The Runtime writes one Deliver Notice per *delivered* message.
   Quarantined or unverified mail produces *no Notice*: a Runtime MUST
   NOT write a Notice for it, and logs it on its own side instead.  The
   Notice is a _pointer and summary_; the body is fetched on demand from
   a separate spooled artifact (Section 7.3) and is *untrusted content*.



















Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 32]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "notice_id": "1721457600000000000-4242",
     "ts": "2026-07-20T04:00:00Z",
     "kind": "deliver",
     "message": {
       "id": "42",
       "from": "Alex Doe <owner@example.com>",
       "subject": "status?",
       "preview": "hey, how is the run going",
       "mailbox": "inbox",
       "task_id": "0f1e2d3c4b5a6978",
       "thread_id": "T-9182",
       "in_reply_to": "<20260719120000.7@example.com>",
       "references": ["<20260718090000.3@example.com>"],
       "sender_standing": "known",
       "provenance": "external",
       "verdict": {
         "auth": "dmarc-pass",
         "screen": "clean",
         "entitlement": "task-counterparty"
       },
       "attachments": [
         {
           "filename": "invoice.pdf",
           "media_type": "application/pdf",
           "size_bytes": 12345,
           "disposition": "unscanned"
         }
       ]
     }
   }

      Figure 4: draft/examples/deliver-notice.json (illustrative — not
                                 a fixture)

   The normative shape is Appendix C.  The Deliver Notice envelope is
   *open*: a consumer MUST tolerate members it does not recognize, at
   every level (Section 13.1).

7.1.  Field semantics and obligations

   *The drop rule.* A Connector relays only deliver Notices.  It MUST
   drop — not surface — a Notice that fails *either* of two independent
   checks, treating a failure of either one alone as sufficient grounds
   to drop:





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 33]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   1.  *Schema failure.* The Notice fails validation against the
       deliver-notice schema (Appendix C) for *any reason other than an
       unrecognized member*. That single formulation covers a kind other
       than deliver, a missing required member, an enum violation on a
       closed vocabulary, a pattern violation (including a traversal or
       character-set violation in notice_id, or a shape violation in
       content_ref's own pattern), a conditional (allOf / if-then)
       violation, and a type violation alike, with no need to enumerate
       schema-failure categories separately. *A Connector MUST NOT drop
       a Notice because it carries an unrecognized member*
       (Section 13.1); that is the one carve-out from "fails schema
       validation."

   2.  *The content_ref index and prefix binding.* A Notice can pass
       check 1 — every member individually well-shaped — and still carry
       an attachment Descriptor whose content_ref does not equal
       <notice_id>.attachments/<i> for its own 0-based array position i
       (Section 7.2): a mismatched trailing index, or a leading
       notice_id prefix pointing into a _different_ Notice's Sidecar
       directory.  A Connector MUST run this check independently of
       schema validation and MUST drop the Notice on failure exactly as
       it would a schema failure.

   *This is not a closure over schema validation.* Check 2 binds two
   members of the same document — a Descriptor's content_ref against the
   enclosing document's own notice_id and against the Descriptor's own
   array position — against each other, which is not expressible in the
   JSON Schema vocabulary these schemas use [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12].  It
   therefore cannot be folded into "fails schema validation" no matter
   how the schema is phrased: it is a second, independent condition, not
   a special case of the first.  The conformance suite enforces it as a
   named post-check and pins it with a fixture that is schema-valid on
   its own and fails only this check (Appendix J).

   A *version refusal* — an absent or non-matching contract_version
   major — is explicitly *not* part of this drop path.  It is handled
   first and separately (Section 13.1) as a distinct, logged outcome: a
   Connector checks the version before it ever reaches schema
   validation, so a version-refused Notice never falls into the drop
   rule at all.

   A document with kind: "peer" found under inbound/notices/ fails check
   1 against this schema, and is dropped the same way (Appendix F, the
   peer-origin profile's cross-lock).

   *Field obligations.*





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 34]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *contract_version*, *notice_id*, *ts*, *kind*, and *message* are
      REQUIRED. notice_id is Runtime-minted and is pinned by the schema
      to a character set that is safe as a path component and as a
      content_ref prefix.

   *  Required members of message are id, from, subject, preview, and
      mailbox.  The rest is enrichment (Section 13.2).

   *  *message.id* is the provider's message identifier.  It is
      *external and not character-set-safe*, and MUST NOT be used as a
      path component anywhere (Section 4.1).  It is the mail store's
      identifier for the message (an IMAP UID, for example), not the
      [RFC5322] Message-ID; an Agent replies to a delivered message by
      naming its notice identifier in in_reply_to (Section 5).

   *  *message.from is attacker-controlled display data.* Its display-
      name half is chosen freely by the sender —
      "security@yourbank.example <attacker@evil.example>" is a legal
      value — and it MUST NOT be used for any trust decision, nor
      rendered to a human or to an Agent as verified identity.  Verified
      sender identity is only ever what the Runtime summarizes into
      sender_standing and verdict; it is not the from string itself.
      The one exception in this protocol is the message.from of a Peer
      Notice, which the Runtime asserts (Section 12.4).

   *  *Presentation obligations.* A Connector that presents a message
      body to its Agent MUST convey two things, whatever words it uses:
      quoted or forwarded material inside the body carries no authority
      of its own — a message's authority extends to what its author
      wrote, never to what they relayed — and that an attachment's
      disposition is the Runtime's assertion about handling and not a
      scanner verdict, so a Connector MUST NOT imply that bytes have
      been screened and MUST NOT contradict the per-attachment status
      the Runtime published.  A Connector MUST also convey that an
      attachment's filename and media_type are sender-chosen display
      strings on the mail tree; on a tree whose sender the Runtime
      authenticated it SHOULD.  On the mail tree a Connector MUST
      additionally convey that the sender is not authenticated beyond
      whatever standing the Runtime has already summarized — carried in
      sender_standing and verdict, named here as the locus and not as
      vocabulary to repeat to a reader — and that message.from is
      sender-chosen text.  These are obligations about substance, not
      vocabulary: a Connector satisfies them with any wording its reader
      can act on without consulting this document, and they MUST be
      satisfiable by a literal string the Connector carries, requiring
      no lookup or computation when a body is presented.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 35]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *The untrusted-content posture covers every sender-originated
      string* in the Notice and in the spooled Inbound Message:
      message.from, subject, preview, body_text, references, attachment
      filename and media_type, and the Inbound Message's from, to, cc,
      and subject.  This is not limited to the members called out
      individually here.

   *  *message.sender_standing* (OPTIONAL) is an *open, advisory
      vocabulary* — known, agent-tier, first-contact, read-only, and
      others.  How the values are computed is Runtime policy and out of
      scope; the wire fixes only today's known vocabulary, so that a
      Connector can tell its Agent "stranger," "agent," or "needs sign-
      off."  A Connector MUST tolerate a value outside this list,
      treating it as opaque — never as grounds to drop the Notice — and
      a Runtime MAY add a value as a minor change (Section 13.1).

   *  *message.provenance* (OPTIONAL) classifies the message source —
      external, internal, and others — so that a Runtime can route
      provenance-labelled screening.  It is advisory metadata, like
      verdict, and a Connector MUST NOT present it as license for an
      Agent to obey body content.  It is likewise an *open, advisory
      vocabulary*: a Connector MUST tolerate a value outside this list,
      treating it as opaque, and MUST NOT drop the Notice on its
      account; a Runtime MAY add a value as a minor change.

   *  *message.verdict* (OPTIONAL) carries the upstream authentication,
      screening, and entitlement results the Runtime consumed.  A
      Connector treats it as advisory metadata, and MUST NOT present it
      as license for an Agent to obey body content.  The object is open:
      unrecognized members inside it are tolerated, as they are
      everywhere else in this artifact.

   *  *message.thread_id*, *message.in_reply_to*, and
      *message.references* (all OPTIONAL) carry provider and [RFC5322]
      threading identity.  They grant correlation, and a consumer MUST
      NOT treat them as grounds for trust (Section 8).

   *  *message.task_id* (OPTIONAL) is Runtime-minted; Section 8 states
      the obligations on it.

   *Direction and openness.* This artifact is Runtime-authored, and its
   envelope is open at every level: a Connector MUST tolerate a member
   it does not recognize, in message or at the top level, and MUST NOT
   drop the Notice on that account.  Emitting an unrecognized member
   remains Runtime non-conformance (Section 13.1).






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 36]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


7.2.  Inbound attachment Descriptors

   *message.attachments[]* (OPTIONAL) is an array of Descriptors
   carrying filename, media_type, and size_bytes — all REQUIRED — plus a
   REQUIRED disposition, and OPTIONAL sha256 and content_ref members
   gated on it.

   *disposition is the Runtime's assertion, not a scanner verdict.* Its
   values are clean, stripped, quarantined, and unscanned, and the
   vocabulary is *closed*: it gates byte publication, so a new value
   would be a behavioral fork a consumer cannot treat as opaque, and
   introducing one is a major change (Section 13.1).  On what basis a
   Runtime asserts clean is deliberately unspecified — a screening
   pipeline's pass in one deployment, a closed operator-supervised
   topology in another.  That is Runtime policy and out of scope for the
   wire, the same posture sender_standing takes: the wire fixes the
   vocabulary, never the computation.  The Runtime is trusted by
   construction (Section 3.1); the load-bearing invariant is that the
   _Agent_ is not.

   The counterpart obligation is equally plain: *a Runtime that cannot
   make the determination MUST NOT assert clean.* It emits unscanned —
   or stripped or quarantined where it made that decision — and
   publishes no bytes.

   *Byte publication and the access grant.* A Runtime MAY publish an
   attachment's bytes at inbound/notices/<notice-id>.attachments/<index>
   *only* for a Descriptor it asserts disposition == "clean", and only
   then MAY it emit content_ref (a path of the form <notice-
   id>.attachments/<index>) and sha256.  Byte-absence remains the gate
   (Section 4.1) for anything not asserted clean.  Exposing sha256 on a
   withheld item would be a confirmation oracle for no integrity value,
   which is why it is clean-gated too.  Both conditionals are expressed
   in the schema.

   *The content_ref binding.* content_ref's leading notice_id prefix
   MUST equal the enclosing document's own notice_id, and its trailing
   <index> MUST equal the Descriptor's own 0-based array index.  The
   array index remains the sole binding authority (Section 4.1), and a
   consumer that resolves bytes MUST derive the path from the enclosing
   notice_id and the index, and MUST NOT use the content_ref string's
   own text as the path, since a Descriptor could otherwise point into
   another Notice's Sidecar directory.  This is a wire-shaped, document-
   level obligation, enforced by the conformance gate as a named post-
   check (Appendix J) in the same way the Result-side
   attachments[i].index == i binding is.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 37]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *A grant, not a directive.* A consumer MUST tolerate a Descriptor
   whose bytes it does not resolve — relaying the Notice as usual — and
   MUST NOT treat the presence of content_ref as a requirement to fetch.
   A Connector that never dereferences content_ref remains fully
   conformant.  A Connector MUST resolve published bytes only within its
   own Namespace's inbound/notices/ tree and MUST reject any content_ref
   that does not match the pinned pattern — the same confinement
   Section 4.1's read-side discipline requires generally.

   *filename and media_type here are attacker-controlled, untrusted
   display strings.* The untrusted-content posture extends to attachment
   Descriptors: a quarantined file named to look like an instruction is
   still an injection payload even with its bytes withheld.  A clean
   assertion covers the bytes' screening disposition, never the
   truthfulness of these strings.

   *Inbound size_bytes is provider-declared and therefore advisory and
   untrusted* — it comes from the provider's structure report, and is
   not Runtime-verified the way outbound size_bytes is.

   *MIME edges.* filename is the [RFC2047] / [RFC2231]-*decoded*,
   Runtime-sanitized display string.  An "attachment" is any part
