   carrying Content-Disposition: attachment [RFC2183], or any named or
   non-inline text part — inline images and multipart/related parts
   count, which is the conservative reading of [RFC2045] and [RFC2046].
   The declared media_type is display-only: the Runtime sniffs the
   bytes, and the sniffed type governs policy on the outbound gate.

7.3.  The Inbound Message (body spool)

   The Runtime spools the delivered body at <volume-root>/<agent-
   id>/inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json, keyed on the Runtime-minted
   notice identifier — never on the provider message.id, for the reason
   given in Section 4.1.

















Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 38]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "notice_id": "1721457600000000000-4242",
     "id": "42",
     "date": "Mon, 20 Jul 2026 04:00:00 +0000",
     "from": "Alex Doe <owner@example.com>",
     "to": "agent@example.org",
     "subject": "status?",
     "body_text": "hey, how is the run going",
     "attachments": [
       {
         "filename": "report.pdf",
         "media_type": "application/pdf",
         "size_bytes": 48213,
         "disposition": "unscanned"
       }
     ]
   }

     Figure 5: draft/examples/inbound-message.json (illustrative — not
                                 a fixture)

   The normative shape is Appendix D.  Required members are
   contract_version, notice_id, and body_text; the rest — id, date,
   from, to, cc, subject, and attachments[] — is enrichment
   (Section 13.2).  Descriptors here follow exactly the rules of
   Section 7.2, including the content_ref binding and the clean gating.
   This artifact's envelope is *open*, like the other Runtime-authored
   artifacts.

   *Resolution.* A Connector MUST resolve a notice identifier to a body
   from this artifact only, and MUST NOT fetch the body from the
   provider.  The body is *untrusted content*, the same posture as the
   rest of message.

   *Enforcement by absence.* A body the Runtime withholds — because of
   screening or quarantine, or because the message was never delivered —
   is simply not spooled, and a read against a missing artifact returns
   "not resolved."  There is no other signal and no fallback fetch.  The
   same "not resolved" response also covers an artifact the Runtime
   later removes under its own retention policy (Section 4.2): from the
   Connector's side, retired and never-spooled are indistinguishable,
   and both are already-specified behavior.








Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 39]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


8.  Task Correlation

   The Runtime mints and owns task_id; a Connector only reads it, to
   correlate a Notice with prior work.  The minting and thread-
   resolution _algorithm_ is Runtime policy and out of scope.  This
   protocol fixes three security obligations on it.

   *  *task_id MUST be unguessable and Runtime-minted* — an HMAC over
      the thread root, for instance.  It MUST NOT be a sequential or
      otherwise guessable value, and it MUST NOT be a capability an
      inbound sender can assert: a guessable task_id lets a sender who
      has seen one predict others.

   *  *Matching a task_id, by itself, MUST NOT grant a message entry
      into that task.* Authoritative correlation is header threading
      *plus* per-message verified sender identity.  A subaddress or
      header token supplied by an inbound sender is a _hint_ only, and a
      Runtime MUST NOT treat it as authoritative: it is attacker-
      controllable, and it is stripped by many gateways.

   *  *Threading grants correlation, not trust.* A message that threads
      onto a known task is still identity-verified per message; it does
      not inherit the task's standing.

9.  Binding Record

   The Binding Record is written by the Runtime or provisioner at the
   *Volume root* — <volume-root>/identity.json, a sibling of <agent-
   id>/, not inside it — and names which mailbox this Volume is bound
   to.  Its normative shape is Appendix E.

   The Binding Record names which mailbox a Volume is bound to; it is
   informational and not consulted for enforcement.

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "agent_id": "agent-research",
     "address": "agent@example.org",
     "provisioned_ts": "2026-07-20T04:10:56Z"
   }

                Figure 6: fixtures/valid/identity-basic.json









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 40]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


9.1.  Field semantics and obligations

   *  *Informational, not authoritative.* The Volume is an Agent-
      writable filesystem, so a compromised Agent can edit or delete
      this file at will.  Attribution and policy stay keyed on Runtime-
      side configuration (Section 4.1).  This record grants nothing, and
      a Runtime MUST NOT consult it for enforcement.

   *  *Consumers MUST tolerate its absence*, and *MUST treat its
      contents as untrusted data*: a reader MUST NOT crash, or change
      its protocol behavior, because of a malformed, oversized, or
      hostile file.

   *  Its jobs are narrow by design: operator sanity — a human
      confirming which mailbox a Volume is bound to — a pre-start
      conflict check for whatever wrote it, catching for instance one
      Agent's credentials pointed at another Agent's Volume, and letting
      a Connector surface the Agent's own address back to its Agent.

   *  *The file is OPTIONAL* (Section 13.2): nothing in this protocol
      requires a Runtime to write it or a Connector to read it, and both
      sides MUST work correctly with it absent.

   *  Required members, if the file is present, are agent_id, address,
      and provisioned_ts. label is OPTIONAL. contract_version is
      OPTIONAL here, as it is on the Peer Directory (Section 10),
      because the file is not a protocol artifact a consumer must parse
      to function; if present it is pinned to "2".

   *  This artifact's envelope is *closed* (additionalProperties:
      false), for a different reason than the Submit Request's is:
      closure here is an anti-secret-leak lint, catching a provisioner
      that writes credential material into a file living on an Agent-
      readable Volume.  It is not a compatibility surface.

10.  The Peer Directory

   A Runtime MAY publish, at the Agent's Namespace root (<agent-
   id>/directory.json, beside the lanes rather than inside one), a per-
   instance projection of the authorisation graph naming which peers
   that Agent may address.










Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 41]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "router": "amap.router@fleet.example",
     "written_at": "2026-09-18T12:00:00Z",
     "delegate_to": [
       "bravo@fleet.example",
       "charlie@fleet.example"
     ],
     "mail_to": []
   }

       Figure 7: draft/examples/directory.json (illustrative — not a
                                  fixture)

   *  *Advisory, not authoritative.* The directory is the Runtime's most
      recent word about the graph, and grants nothing.  A Connector MUST
      NOT treat an address's presence as a prediction that a submission
      to it will be accepted, nor its absence as a prediction of
      refusal: authorisation is evaluated by the Runtime at submission
      time, and the Result (Section 6) is the only thing that reports
      what happened.  A consumer that reads the directory as a
      prediction is wrong even when the file is current.

   *  *A Runtime MUST NOT read directory.json back, for any purpose.* It
      is write-only from the Runtime's side: the graph is derived from
      policy, the file is a projection of the graph, and nothing derives
      the graph from the file.  Enforcement remains the Runtime's own
      check against its graph, on every message.  The prohibition is on
      the direction rather than the purpose, because the ways this
      decays — as an optimisation, a cache, a recovery source, or a
      cross-check — all have innocent intent, and the last two turn a
      projection into a source.  A projection that can be read back
      becomes a cache; a cache becomes a record; a record that disagrees
      with policy wins by accident.

   *  *Per-instance projection.* Each Agent's directory carries only the
      edges that Agent is party to.  It MUST NOT carry the set of peers
      who may address that Agent, which is an allowlist in all but name,
      and MUST NOT carry the Agent's own address — attribution is the
      Namespace a file arrived in (Section 4), so an address an Agent
      reads is a claim rather than an identity.

   *  router is the publishing Runtime's own address and MUST NOT appear
      in either list.  Every address is one bare addr-spec (Section 5).

   *  *Both lists are always present*, and empty when that lane is
      closed for this Agent; mail_to is empty in a delegation-only
      deployment.  Absent and empty MUST NOT be conflated.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 42]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Written whole and atomically.* A Runtime MUST NOT publish a newly
      adopted instance's address to others before it has adopted that
      instance itself.

   *  *A Runtime that publishes the directory MUST ensure the Agent can
      read it*, and SHOULD expose it read-only.  Publishing to a path
      the Agent's Namespace does not expose is not conformant: the write
      succeeds, the file is correct, and no Agent can read it — a
      failure that reports nothing on either side.  Publishing is
      optional, so a Runtime that cannot make the file readable MUST NOT
      publish it; an unreadable directory is indistinguishable from an
      absent one to a consumer, and worse than an absent one to an
      operator, who has a file on disk that looks like it is working.
      The trap follows from the location: the file deliberately belongs
      to no lane, which is what keeps a delegation-only deployment from
      materialising a mail tree, and is exactly what places it outside
      an exposure built lane by lane.

   *  *written_at* is the only staleness signal a consumer gets: an
      honest marker, not a freshness guarantee.

   *  *Where the consumer is an Agent rather than a parser, these become
      obligations to convey.* A Connector that surfaces the directory to
      its Agent instead of interpreting it satisfies the obligations
      above by stating them, under the presentation rule in Section 7:
      the Agent is the party forming a belief, so the Connector MUST
      convey that an address's presence is not a prediction of
      acceptance, that the file may be absent, that an empty list and an
      absent list differ, and that written_at is the only staleness
      signal there is.  A Connector with no directory parser does not
      thereby satisfy them vacuously.

   *  *The file MAY be absent* — before first adoption, on a Runtime
      that does not implement this section, or after a failed write —
      and a consumer MUST tolerate absence exactly as it tolerates a
      missing Binding Record (Section 9).

   *  *A Runtime that cannot write it keeps routing.* The directory is
      advisory, so a failed write loses a convenience, not the ability
      to enforce; failing closed would convert an advisory artifact into
      a dependency.  The Runtime MUST log the failure.  The Agent's only
      signal remains written_at going stale.









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 43]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


11.  The Fleet Roster

   A Runtime MAY publish a fleet roster: a single file, written for the
   whole fleet rather than per instance, naming the instances the
   Runtime has admitted.  The Peer Directory (Section 10) answers which
   peers an Agent may address; the roster answers only which instances
   exist.  It is a separate artifact, and no obligation of Section 10
   applies to it except where this section states one.

   *  *Existence is not authorisation.* A member's presence says the
      instance exists.  It does not say this Agent may address it, and
      it is not a prediction that a submission to it will be accepted:
      authorisation is evaluated by the Runtime at submission time, and
      the Result (Section 6) is the only thing that reports what
      happened.  A Connector MUST NOT treat membership as authorisation
      or as a prediction of acceptance.

   *  *Not a source of identity.* The roster is fleet-wide, so the
      reader's own address MAY appear in it.  A consumer MUST NOT derive
      its own identity from the roster and MUST NOT treat its own entry
      as a peer: attribution is the Namespace a file arrived in
      (Section 4), and an address read from a file is a claim rather
      than an identity.

   *  *Write-only from the Runtime's side.* A Runtime MUST NOT read the
      roster back, for any purpose, for the reasons given for the
      directory in Section 10.

   *  *Written whole and atomically.* A Runtime MUST NOT list a newly
      admitted instance before it has adopted that instance itself.
      router is the publishing Runtime's own address and MUST NOT appear
      in members.  Every address is one bare addr-spec.

   *  *Unknown is not empty.* members is always present.  When the
      Runtime cannot determine membership, it MUST NOT write an empty
      members list; it leaves the previous file in place to age.
      written_at is the only staleness signal a consumer gets, and
      interval_s, when present, is the Runtime's nominal rewrite
      interval to judge it against.  A consumer MUST treat an absent
      roster, or one it judges stale, as unknown, and MUST NOT treat it
      as an empty fleet.  Unknown is not unusable: an Agent may still
      address a member of a stale roster, and the Runtime decides; what
      it must not do is conclude that an instance is absent from the
      fleet.  This section fixes no freshness bound; how stale is stale
      is the consumer's judgement, made against interval_s where it is
      present.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 44]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Readability is split between the parties that can observe it.* A
      Runtime cannot observe a mount.  It MUST publish the roster only
      into a location the deployment designates for it, and MUST NOT
      create that location.  The deployment MUST expose that location
      read-only to each Agent it points at the roster, and SHOULD stop
      pointing Agents at the roster before, or together with, ceasing to
      expose it.  A roster written where nothing is exposed is inert,
      not a violation: an Agent is only ever pointed at a roster its
      deployment exposes.

   *  *Conveyed, where the consumer is an Agent.* Whatever points an
      Agent at the roster, whether a Connector that surfaces it or a
      deployment that tells the Agent where to read it, MUST convey that
      membership is neither authorisation nor a prediction of
      acceptance, that the roster is not the Agent's identity and its
      own entry is not a peer, and that an absent or stale roster means
      unknown.  Stating these in text the Agent receives whenever it is
      pointed at the roster satisfies this; no tool is required.

   The roster's shape is pinned by its schema (Appendix H) and by the
   roster-* fixtures (Appendix J).  The envelope is Runtime-authored and
   therefore open (Section 13.1): a consumer ignores members it does not
   recognize, and emitting one remains producer non-conformance.

12.  The Peer-Origin Profile (Optional)

   This section is an optional profile.  It gives agent-to-agent traffic
   between Agents of the same principal its own inbound tree, peer/, and
   states what that tree asserts, who may write it, how peers are
   addressed, how a reply is correlated with the message it answers, and
   how peer traffic is carried and verified between hosts.  A deployment
   that implements the profile is bound by every requirement in this
   section; a deployment that does not is unaffected.  No schema or
   fixture outside the profile depends on it, and the wire
   contract_version is the same for both.

12.1.  Scope

   The profile is optional because peer origin is needed by deployments
   in which Agents task one another, and by no deployment that only
   handles mail.










Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 45]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   The tree is named for what it asserts, not for what it is used for:
   peer/ asserts authenticated, same-principal peer origin, and the
   document kind is peer.  What a Connector does with a peer message
   (delegation, review, notification) is the Connector's business.
   Because the kind and the tree share a name, the rule that a
   document's kind equals the name of the tree it was read from is
   mechanical.

   The profile adds an origin class and reuses mail threading for
   correlation.  It defines no call or return semantics, no method or
   operation member, and no status vocabulary for the work itself: a
   reply is prose authored by an Agent, with the posture of any other
   peer content.  This keeps the profile on the mail side of the line
   drawn in Section 1.5.

   The profile relies on two generic rules in Section 4.1: the _tree
   rules_ (every Runtime-owned inbound-class tree is an origin class,
   derived from the tree and never from a member, with notice_id
   uniqueness, content_ref confinement and write authority all per
   tree), and the _outbound extension space_ outbound/ext/<name>/, where
   delivery outcomes are kept (Section 12.8).  There is deliberately no
   inbound extension space.

12.2.  The Peer Tree

   <agent-id>/
     outbound/                   # as in the Volume Layout
     inbound/                    # mail
       notices/  messages/
     peer/                       # PROFILE: same layout, conventions
       notices/notice-<id>.json  #   and Sidecar rules as inbound/
       notices/<notice-id>.attachments/<i>
       messages/notice-<id>.json
     audit/

     Figure 8: Namespace layout with the peer tree (illustrative — not
                                 a fixture)

   *A sibling of inbound/, never a child.* Nesting the peer tree inside
   the mail tree would put the tree the mail deliverer must not write
   inside the tree it must write, so the write-authority partition
   (Section 12.3) would have to be carved out of a mount instead of
   being one.  As a sibling, the partition coincides with mount
   granularity.  Every obligation on inbound/ in Section 4 applies to
   peer/ unchanged: it is Runtime-owned; it MAY be mounted read-only; a
   Connector MUST NOT require write access to it; only the Runtime
   deletes from it; and its retention is conservative and age-based.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 46]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Its own schema.* A Peer Notice is pinned by the peer-notice schema
   (Appendix F): the Deliver Notice shape with kind fixed to "peer" and
   message.mailbox fixed to "peer", message.from pinned to a bare addr-
   spec (Section 12.4), message.id, message.in_reply_to and
   message.references[] pinned to the notice_id character set
   (Section 12.5), and the optional Runtime-asserted
   message.sender_exposure (Section 12.7).  Attachment Descriptors are
   exactly those of Section 7.2.  The body spool uses the Inbound
   Message schema (Appendix D) unchanged.  Because a Peer Notice appears
   only in a tree that a mail-only consumer never reads, the closed kind
   vocabulary of the Deliver Notice is untouched.

   *The cross-lock.* A deliver document under peer/notices/ fails the
   peer-notice schema, and a peer document under inbound/notices/ fails
   the Deliver Notice schema.  Both are dropped under the rule of
   Section 7.1.

   *The placer mints notice_id.* The component that places a notice into
   a tree mints its notice_id.  Where a tree has more than one writer,
   each MUST mint so that a collision between writers is negligible: at
   least 128 bits of entropy under the notice_id character set, or a
   writer-specific prefix.  A consumer that keys state across trees MUST
   include the tree in the key.  On a single host, a Runtime MAY make
   the notice_id equal to the peer message id (Section 12.5).  Between
   hosts they differ, because the receiving Runtime mints the notice_id
   and the message id is the sender's.  A consumer MUST NOT assume that
   they coincide.

   *content_ref is confined to its tree.* Bytes resolve only within the
   notices/ directory of the tree the enclosing document was read from,
   recomputed from that document's notice_id and the Descriptor's index.
   A Peer Notice cannot point into the mail Sidecar directory, or the
   reverse.

   *Advisory members.* provenance on a Peer Notice is redundant with the
   tree and MAY be omitted; if present, it is advisory, and a consumer
   MUST NOT derive or override the origin class from it.
   sender_standing, if present, SHOULD be the existing agent-tier value.

12.3.  Origin Class Follows the Tree

   Write authority per tree is a behavioral obligation of the same kind
   as read-only inbound tolerance, single-writer and single-drainer
   operation, and ingest by copy (Section 4.1): invisible to a document
   validator, and checked operationally.  If it were left to
   deployments, the separate tree would be decorative, because one
   writer that chose the tree by inspecting a member would be routing on
   a member with one level of indirection.  The mechanism that enforces



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 47]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   it (user identities, mount sets, a host boundary) is out of scope;
   the property is not, and this section prescribes a check for it.

   *Connector obligations.* The tree a notice is read from is the
   Runtime's sole assertion of its origin class: inbound/ is mail, and
   peer/ is same-principal peer origin.  A Connector MUST derive the
   class from the tree, and MUST NOT derive or override it from any
   member of the document.  A document whose kind does not equal the
   name of the tree it was read from is dropped under the rule of
   Section 7.1.  A Connector that cannot establish which tree a document
   came from MUST treat it as mail.

   The peer tree asserts authenticated origin: a same-principal Agent,
   reaching this Namespace through a path restricted to authorized peer
   senders.  It asserts nothing about content.  Peer content is authored
   by a peer and unscreened, and may paraphrase external mail
   (Section 12.7).  How a Connector treats each class is out of scope;
   that it distinguishes the classes only by tree is not.  Like the
   untrusted-content posture of Section 7, this obligation protects an
   Agent from its own inbox, and is stated as a Connector obligation
   rather than as a property the Runtime relies on.  The invariant of
   Section 3.2 is unaffected.

   *Write-authority partition (Runtime).* Write authority over peer/
   MUST be distinct from write authority over inbound/. A component that
   admits messages from a transport not restricted to authorized peer
   senders (the _admitting component_, of which a mail deliverer is the
   usual example) MUST NOT hold write authority over peer/. The
   restriction MUST be structural, and MUST NOT be configuration that
   the component reads.  The prescribed operational check is a write
   attempt against peer/ from inside the admitting component, which MUST
   fail.  The rule is one-directional: a component holding peer write
   authority MAY write inbound/, as the delivery failure notice of
   Section 12.5 requires.

   A Runtime MUST NOT write a notice into peer/ on the basis of any
   claim the message makes about itself.  It MAY write there only when
   the message arrived through a path whose write authority is already
   restricted to authorized peer senders, or when the message carries a
   signature that verifies against a configured peer key (Section 12.6).











Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 48]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Verification placement (Runtime).* Verification MUST be performed by
   a component holding peer write authority, which receives candidates
   through a location that is neither tree (Section 12.6.10).  The
   admitting component MUST NOT perform verification.  A verdict
   computed by one component and acted on by another would cross a trust
   boundary as data, which is what this rule keeps out of the decision;
   and the verifier processes hostile input, so it needs to be the
   component whose write authority the outcome concerns, not one that
   parses raw mail.

12.4.  Addressing

   *A peer address is a bare addr-spec*, under the same pattern and
   exclusions that Section 5.1 fixes for draft.to, with no display name.
   Its local part is the Agent's name within its Runtime, and its domain
   is the Runtime's authority.  A deployment confined to one host, with
   no mail, MAY use a non-routable domain.  Traffic between hosts
   requires a routable domain, because it travels as mail
   (Section 12.6).  "Routable" means deliverable by the mail system that
   carries the deployment's peer traffic; the domain need not resolve in
   the public DNS, because peer keys are configured rather than looked
   up (Section 12.6.7).  A peer domain MUST belong to exactly one
   Runtime among those configured as peers, so a deployment that may
   peer across organizations should use domains it controls.  Where an
   Agent has a bound mailbox (the Binding Record's address, Section 9),
   the deployment SHOULD use it, so that the Agent has one identity on
   both lanes.

   An addr-spec is used rather than an opaque identifier with a
   directory, or a URI scheme, because between hosts the transport
   address is an email address.  Any other scheme would need a mapping
   onto one, and someone to run the mapping.  With an addr-spec, the
   domain names the authority, the peer-key table is keyed by domain,
   and a signature has something to bind.  The grammar, the schema
   pattern and the header-injection discipline already exist.

   *Sending needs no new wire shape.* A sending Agent writes an ordinary
   Submit Request (Section 5) whose draft.to names the peer.  The
   Runtime's recipient policy recognizes a declared edge and routes the
   request to the peer tree rather than to mail.  The Result vocabulary,
   outbound Sidecars and reply key are the existing ones.  Whether a
   recipient is a peer is Runtime policy, and out of scope, like an
   allowlist.

   *message.from on a Peer Notice is authenticated.* It is the one from
   in this protocol that a consumer may treat as authenticated origin: a
   bare addr-spec, pinned by the schema, and asserted by the Runtime
   from the restricted write path or from a verified statement



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 49]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   (Section 12.6).  A Runtime MUST NOT copy it from text the sender
   supplied.  This is the opposite of the rule for mail from
   (Section 7.1).  A Connector's sender check may key on it, because the
   Runtime asserted it.

   *A configured peer key vouches only for its own Runtime's domains*
   (Section 12.6.7).  Without this, one Runtime's key could sign a
   message claiming an address in another Runtime's domain.

   *One address, one Namespace.* A peer address resolves to exactly one
   Namespace, as every address does in this protocol: one Namespace, one
   Connector instance, one Agent.  Sessions are below the Connector, and
   this document does not define them.

   A peer message is a single unit addressed to one Agent.  A Connector
   MUST NOT cause it to be acted on more than once.  A Connector that
   cannot identify a single target MUST hold the notice rather than fan
   it out, and SHOULD report the condition through its own side channel
   (Section 12.8).

   "One Agent, one live session; refuse when there are several" is one
   conformant implementation, not the only one.  A finer target (a named
   session) is out of scope.  A coarser one (a pool) is a Runtime alias
   that expands to several addresses, each resolving to one Namespace,
   and is not a change to addressing.

12.5.  Correlation and Replies

   *The peer message id.* The sending Runtime mints the peer message id
   when it accepts the submit.  The id MUST be globally unique and
   unguessable, with at least 128 bits of entropy, and MUST be spelled
   under the notice_id character set (^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$).
   It has exactly one spelling inside every AMMP document: message.id,
   message.in_reply_to and message.references[] on a Peer Notice,
   message_id on a peer-routed Result, and the reply key a sender
   submits all carry the bare id.  When the id is carried in a mail
   header, it is encoded as <id@domain>, where domain is the domain of
   the sender's address (Section 12.6.3).  The encoding is applied on
   the way into the header and removed on the way out, and MUST NOT
   appear in an AMMP document.

   The reverse edge and every ledger depend on two properties of the id:
   that it is unguessable, and that it has one spelling end to end.
   Bare 32-character hexadecimal satisfies both, and so does unpadded
   base64url (subject, between hosts, to Section 12.6.1).  A mail
   notice's in_reply_to remains an [RFC5322] identifier; the Deliver
   Notice schema is unchanged.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 50]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *A reply is a Peer Notice in the reverse direction*, on the same
   tree, correlated with the message it answers.  It is not a third kind
   or a third tree: the tree grants the class, and a reply deserves the
   class of the message it answers.  There is no correlation member;
   mail threading already provides one, and between hosts it is
   [RFC5322] threading.

    +===========================+====================================+
    | Member                    | On the peer lane                   |
    +===========================+====================================+
    | message.id (Peer Notice)  | The peer message id.               |
    +---------------------------+------------------------------------+
    | message_id (the sender's  | MUST equal the peer message id, so |
    | Result)                   | that the sender learns it from its |
    |                           | own Result. reason_code SHOULD be  |
    |                           | peer_routed, so that the sender    |
    |                           | can tell the lanes apart (an open  |
    |                           | vocabulary, Section 6.1).          |
    +---------------------------+------------------------------------+
    | message.in_reply_to (Peer | REQUIRED on a reply, and equal to  |
    | Notice)                   | the id being answered.  A new task |
    |                           | omits it.                          |
    +---------------------------+------------------------------------+
    | message.references[]      | Multi-step threads, as in mail.    |
    | (Peer Notice)             |                                    |
    +---------------------------+------------------------------------+
    | in_reply_to or            | How a responder names the message  |
    | draft.reply_to_message_id | it answers.                        |
    | (Submit Request)          |                                    |
    +---------------------------+------------------------------------+

              Table 3: Correlation members on the peer lane

   task_id remains an optional, Runtime-minted thread handle
   (Section 8).
















Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 51]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Reverse edges.* The authorization graph is directed, yet a reply
   must be able to flow from B to A when only A to B is declared.  A
   Runtime permits a reverse message when its reply key names a peer
   message in the opposite direction that the Runtime itself issued or
   placed (at submission, one it placed for the submitting Agent; at
   reception, one it issued to the replying Agent), within a configured
   window.  This consults a member, but checks it against state the
   Runtime minted, which is the posture Section 8 takes for threading:
   correlation, not trust.  Because ids are unguessable, the key is not
   a forgeable capability.  Several replies to one id within the window,
   and a reply to a reply under the id the Runtime issued for it, are
   conformant.  This document does not fix the window's length; it
   requires only that the window exists and is configured.

   *An unresolved reply key is refused, not stripped.* A reply key
   (in_reply_to, or else draft.reply_to_message_id) that the Runtime
   cannot resolve from its own ledger MUST produce a rejected Result
   with reason_code unresolved_reply.  A Runtime MUST NOT strip the key
   and route the message on draft.to as a new peer message.  A key that
   resolves but whose reverse edge is not permitted (no declared edge,
   or an expired window) MUST likewise produce a rejected Result
   (reason_code peer_reply_window_expired, or the Runtime's own code),
   and MUST NOT be re-routed.  A Peer Notice MUST carry in_reply_to if
   and only if the placing Runtime resolved it from its own ledger to a
   peer message id that it issued or placed.

   The reason is the reason this profile exists.  On the peer lane, a
   message the sender meant as a reply, which the Runtime quietly turned
   into a new task, arrives as a new instruction.  That is worse than a
   rejection the sender can act on by resubmitting without the key.  The
   rule is a requirement rather than a permission because a Connector
   may build policy on it (for example, admitting a replier it would not
   otherwise accept), and that is sound across a deployment only if
   every conformant Runtime upholds it.  Such a policy MUST NOT widen
   anything else about the notice's treatment.

   Between hosts, the sending Runtime has already rejected an
   unresolvable key at submission.  A verified statement whose
   in_reply_to the _receiving_ Runtime cannot resolve therefore
   indicates a stale or forged capability from a configured peer.  The
   receiver MUST NOT place it in peer/ with the key, MUST NOT place it
   as a new peer task, and MUST log the cause, and it SHOULD tell the
   sending Runtime with a signed Control Notice (Section 12.6.8).  The
   ledger binds the participants as well as the id (Section 12.6.6).
   The statement is not demoted to mail either: its origin was verified,
   only its correlation claim failed, and routing it as mail would be a
   third silent transformation.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 52]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Two things called a result.* A _work result_ is the responder's
   content for the requester, described above.  A _delivery outcome_ is
   mechanical feedback from a Connector to its Runtime (delivered, held,
   and so on).  A delivery outcome is not a peer message; it is kept in
   outbound/ext/<name>/ (Section 12.8).

   *Delivery failure notices.* A Runtime that reports a terminal
   delivery failure to the sending Agent SHOULD do so as a deliver
   Notice in the sender's inbound/ tree, with message.from set to the
   Runtime's own address (amap.router@<domain> or equivalent),
   in_reply_to set to the peer message id, and a body authored by the
   Runtime alone.  Such a notice MUST NOT be placed in peer/, and MUST
   NOT quote or forward any text from the receiving Connector's outcome
   file.

   The Runtime is never an allowed peer sender, so this keeps it out of
   every Connector's peer policy.  The mail tree's untrusted-content
   posture is the right one for "your message did not arrive".  And the
   outcome file is text written by the receiver, so forwarding it would
   let one Agent put prose in front of another under the Runtime's name.
   A component holding peer write authority that writes inbound/ is the
   one direction Section 12.3 permits.  The peer message id appears in a
   mail-tree notice, but only to the sender, who already holds it from
   its own Result, so no capability is disclosed.

12.6.  Peer Traffic Between Hosts

   Peer traffic between hosts is mail.  The sending Runtime signs it
   with its own key; there are no per-Agent keys.  Traffic on one host
   needs no signature, because local write permission is a stronger
   guarantee, although a Runtime MAY sign it too, for a uniform code
   path, without changing its treatment.  A receiving Runtime places a
   message from another host in peer/ only when every rule in this
   section holds.  Otherwise it hands the message to mail admission,
   drops it, or refuses it, as Section 12.6.4 specifies.

12.6.1.  The Statement

   The sending Runtime builds a _statement_, a small JSON object, signs
   its exact bytes with Ed25519 (Section 5.1 of [RFC8032]), and carries
   the bytes and the signature in one header field (Section 12.6.2).
   The receiver verifies the signature over the bytes it received
   _before_ parsing them.  Nothing is re-serialized: no canonicalization
   is defined, and whatever serialization the sender chose is the one
   that is signed.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 53]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   The peer-statement schema (Appendix F) pins the statement: version v
   1, closed at every level, with the members v, key_id, kind ("peer"),
   id, in_reply_to (optional), from, to, ts, subject, body_sha256 (the
   digest of the body the receiver will publish), attachments (each with
   sha256, size_bytes, filename and media_type, in leaf order),
   sender_exposure (optional, Section 12.7) and sender_since (optional,
   Section 12.6.9).

   Unlike the Runtime-authored notices (Section 13.1), the statement is
   closed, because it is signed bytes that another Runtime acts on.  A
   member the receiver does not know is a member it cannot bind to what
   it publishes, and v is the path for evolution.  The schema states the
   shapes.  The following rules, which JSON Schema cannot express, are
   also part of the statement:

   *  *Formats.* ts, sender_since and the timestamps in sender_exposure
      are [RFC3339] date-times in UTC, in whole seconds, with the Z
      designator, and each MUST denote a real instant.  Digests are
      SHA-256 [FIPS180-4], in lowercase hexadecimal.  Every number is a
      lexical integer, with no fraction and no exponent, so 1.0 is not
      1.  No string contains an unpaired surrogate (Section 8.2 of
      [RFC8259]).

   *  *Ids.* A sending Runtime MUST mint the ids it sends between hosts
      under ^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$, which is the notice_id
      character set (Section 12.5) without ".", with at least 128 bits
      of entropy, so that <id@domain> is a valid msg-id (Section 3.6.4
      of [RFC5322]).  Hexadecimal satisfies this; a base64url id whose
      first character is "-" MUST be minted again.  The statement schema
      enforces the pattern for id and in_reply_to.  An id used only on
      one host MAY also contain ".", as the notice_id character set
      allows; an id sent between hosts MUST NOT.

   *  *to* is one address: a peer message is addressed to one Agent
      (Section 12.4).

   *  *sender_exposure* obeys Section 12.7: window_start is not later
      than window_end; last_external_delivery_ts is present if and only
      if external_mail_delivered is true, and then lies within the
      window; and asserted_by is the signing Runtime's configured
      Runtime address (Section 12.6.7).

   *  *sender_since*, when present, is not later than ts.

12.6.2.  Carriage, and the Candidate the Verifier Sees

   *The header field.*




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 54]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   AMAP-Peer-Statement: k=<key_id>; s=<statement>; b=<signature>

   *  s is the statement's bytes, and b is the 64-byte signature over
      exactly those bytes.  Each is base64url without padding (Section 5
      of [RFC4648]).

   *  k is the statement's key_id, in the clear: the receiver verifies
      before it parses, so it must choose the key before it can read the
      statement.  The signed key_id MUST equal k.

   *  The field name is matched case-insensitively.  The sending Runtime
      MUST emit exactly one such field.

   *  The sender MUST fold the field so that no line exceeds 998 octets
      (Section 2.1.1 of [RFC5322]), and SHOULD fold at 78.  It may
      insert folding whitespace anywhere, because the receiver removes
      all of it.

   *  A statement MUST NOT exceed 8192 bytes.  A sending Runtime that
      would otherwise emit a larger one SHOULD refuse the submit
      instead, with a rejected Result whose reason_code is
      peer_statement_too_large.

   *  The sending Runtime MUST also set Message-ID to <id@domain>, where
      domain is the domain of from, and SHOULD set In-Reply-To and
      References to the encoded forms (Section 12.5), so that mail
      threads coherently and a demoted message still threads as mail.

   *The message shape.* A sending Runtime SHOULD send either a single
   text/plain part, or multipart/mixed holding one text/plain part
   followed by the attachments.  The text part SHOULD be charset=utf-8
   with base64 transfer encoding, so that transport cannot rewrite it.
   The sender hashes the UTF-8 encoding of the body after replacing
   every CRLF pair with LF.  Nothing else is normalized: a bare CR, a
   bare LF, trailing whitespace and a leading dot are all content.

   *The selection rule.* The admitting component reduces a message to a
   candidate, and the rule is the same at every receiver:

   *  *Leaves.* Walk the MIME tree [RFC2046] depth-first, descending
      only into multipart/*. Every other part is a leaf, including
      message/rfc822, whose octets are its part body as transmitted.

   *  *Body.* The first leaf of type text/plain whose Content-
      Disposition [RFC2183] is not attachment is the body.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 55]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Attachments.* Every other leaf, in walk order, is an attachment:
      a text/html alternative, an inline image, or a second text/plain
      part.

   *  *No body leaf* means the empty body.

   A different structure is not forbidden; it is simply likely to fail
   the attachment count or the body digest, and so to be demoted.

   *The candidate.* The intake location (Section 12.6.10) MUST hold the
   following, in a layout this document does not prescribe:

   *  *Field bodies.* The body of each AMAP-Peer-Statement, AMAP-Peer-
      Control and Message-ID field, in message order.  The admitting
      component MAY unfold a field body or trim its surrounding
      whitespace, and MUST NOT otherwise alter it.  A field body over
      12288 octets MUST be carried as an _oversize_ marker, and MUST NOT
      be truncated.  The 12288-octet limit applies to the field body as
      transmitted, before unfolding or trimming.  A field body the
      admitting component cannot carry as ASCII text (a non-ASCII octet,
      or an undecodable value) MUST be carried as an _invalid_ marker in
      the field's position.  A marker keeps the field's identity and
      multiplicity: the admitting component MUST NOT omit a field,
      because omitting a second, malformed statement field would leave
      one well-formed field, and the verifier would select it.

   *  *The body leaf*, if there is one: its octets after transfer
      decoding, and the value of its charset parameter, if any.

   *  *Each attachment leaf:* its octets after transfer decoding, in
      order.

   The verifier, not the admitting component, decodes the body octets
   strictly.  The charset label, compared case-insensitively, MUST be
   utf-8 or us-ascii; an absent label means us-ascii.  Any other label,
   or octets that are invalid in the labelled charset, fail check 9
   (Section 12.6.3).  The verifier then replaces CRLF pairs with LF and
   hashes the result, and that same text is what it publishes as
   body_text.

   *What is published.* On placement, the receiver takes all of the
   following from the verified statement, and MUST NOT take them from
   headers: message.id, in_reply_to and from; subject; sender_exposure;
   and the attachment Descriptors' filename, media_type, size_bytes and
   sha256. to selects the Namespace.  The receiver MUST NOT publish
   references from headers; it MAY derive them from its own ledger
   (Section 12.6.6).  The byte sniffing, caps and disposition rules of
   Section 7.2 still apply to the attachment bytes.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 56]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Comparisons.* Addresses (from, to, the edge graph, the ledger and
   Runtime addresses) compare the local part exactly and the domain
   case-insensitively in ASCII.  Ids compare exactly, because they are
   opaque.  After unfolding and trimming, Message-ID MUST be exactly
   "<", the id, "@", the domain and ">", with the id equal to the
   statement's id and the domain equal to the domain of from.

   *Logging.* A receiver MUST NOT log a raw header field value
   unescaped.  Fields are supplied by the attacker, and k is validated
   against the key_id pattern before it is used for anything.

12.6.3.  Verification

   The receiver applies these checks in this order.  The first one that
   fails decides the outcome (Section 12.6.4).  Only a candidate that
   passes every check is eligible for peer/.

   1.   *The field.* There is exactly one AMAP-Peer-Statement field;
        with none, the message is not a peer candidate, and is ordinary
        mail.  A message that also carries an AMAP-Peer-Control field is
        dropped (Section 12.6.8).  The field body is ASCII and is not
        oversize.  With every SP, HTAB, CR and LF removed, it consists
        of exactly the tags k, s and b, each once, in any order,
        separated by ";". k matches the key_id pattern. s and b are
        unpadded base64url; b decodes to 64 bytes, and s to at most
        8192.

   2.   *Known statement.* If the SHA-256 digest of the statement bytes
        equals that of a statement the receiver has recorded and still
        retains (Section 12.6.5), the candidate is a duplicate.  This
        check needs no key, and holds whatever else has changed since: a
        timestamp now outside the window, a key since expired or
        removed, or a body modified in transit.

   3.   *Key.* k names exactly one configured key, valid at the
        receiver's clock (not-before ≤ now ≤ not-after, inclusive).

   4.   *Signature.* The signature is valid for that key over the
        received bytes, under the verification policy of Section 12.6.7.

   5.   *Statement.* (a) The bytes are UTF-8 without a byte-order mark,
        and parse as JSON with no repeated member name and no non-JSON
        constant.  They validate against the schema, and key_id equals
        k. (b) Every rule of Section 12.6.1 that the schema cannot
        express holds.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 57]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   6.   *Key domain.* The domain of from is one of the domains
        configured for the Runtime that owns the key.  A key vouches
        only for its own Runtime's domains (Section 12.4).

   7.   *Freshness.* ts lies within the window of Section 12.6.5.  While
        peer admission is closed (no trustworthy bound, Section 12.6.5),
        the window is undefined: the candidate is _held_ in intake,
        undisposed, until admission reopens.

   8.   *Exposure asserter.* If sender_exposure is present, asserted_by
        is the configured Runtime address of the Runtime that owns the
        key.

   9.   *Body.* The body decodes under the charset rule of
        Section 12.6.2, and its digest equals body_sha256.  The verifier
        MUST hash bytes it holds itself, and MUST NOT use a digest that
        the admitting component computed.

   10.  *Attachments.* The count matches; then, for each attachment in
        order, sha256 and size_bytes match the octets.

   11.  *Message-ID.* There is exactly one such field, matching
        Section 12.6.2.

   12.  *Reservation.* No record exists for the pair (the configured
        Runtime that owns the key, id) (Section 12.6.5).  The candidate
        is reserved, atomically.

   A reserved candidate is then _decided_, and the following are not
   verification failures:

   *  if to is not hosted here, the candidate is misrouted;

   *  if in_reply_to is present, it must resolve and be permitted
      (Section 12.6.6);

   *  otherwise, the receiver's own graph must have the edge from from
      to to (Section 12.6.6);

   *  any deployment admission policy is applied (Section 12.6.9);

   *  otherwise, the decision is placement.

   The decision MUST be persisted on the record before it has any effect
   (Section 12.6.5).  Only a persisted placement decision is ever
   published; a persisted refusal or drop MUST NOT be published,
   whatever happens afterwards.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 58]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


12.6.4.  Outcomes

   +============+========================================+=============+
   | Outcome    | When                                   | Control     |
   |            |                                        | Notice      |
   +============+========================================+=============+
   | peer       | Every check passes, and the            | none        |
   |            | message is routed and permitted.       |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | held       | Check 7 while peer admission is        | none        |
   |            | closed (Section 12.6.5); not yet       |             |
   |            | disposed of.                           |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | mail, no   | No AMAP-Peer-Statement field.          | none        |
   | statement  |                                        |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | mail,      | A failure of check 1 (other than       | SHOULD, for |
   | demoted    | the both-fields drop below), 3,        | 5(b) and 6  |
   |            | 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 or 11.            | to 11       |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | drop: both | An AMAP-Peer-Statement and an          | none        |
   | fields     | AMAP-Peer-Control field in one         |             |
   |            | message (Section 12.6.8).              |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | drop:      | Check 2 (a known statement) or         | SHOULD, for |
   | duplicate  | check 12 (a known id).                 | check 12    |
   |            |                                        | only        |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | drop:      | to is not hosted here.                 | SHOULD      |
   | misrouted  |                                        |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | refuse:    | Section 12.6.6.                        | SHOULD      |
   | unresolved |                                        |             |
   | reply      |                                        |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | refuse: no | Section 12.6.6.                        | SHOULD      |
   | edge       |                                        |             |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+
   | refuse:    | A deployment admission policy          | SHOULD,     |
   | policy     | (Section 12.6.9).                      | with        |
   |            |                                        | policy_code |
   +------------+----------------------------------------+-------------+

            Table 4: Outcomes for a candidate from another host

   *Mail, demoted.* Demotion is a classification, not a delivery.  The
   candidate goes to ordinary mail admission and the deployment's lane
   policy; where that policy gives the pair no mail lane, it is not



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 59]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   delivered.  The demoted notice MUST NOT carry sender_exposure, the
   statement or the signature, and carries the mail-admission verdict
   the admitting component attached.  Mail admission MUST NOT treat an
   invalid statement as evidence of who sent the message.

   *Drop and refuse.* A dropped or refused candidate is neither placed
   nor handed to mail admission.  Every outcome other than peer and
   "mail, no statement" MUST be logged with its cause.  A refusal is not
   demoted, because the origin was verified and only an authorization or
   correlation claim failed; routing it as mail would be a silent
   transformation (Section 12.5).

   *Who is told.* A Control Notice (Section 12.6.8) MUST be sent only
   when every one of these holds; a configured k alone is never enough:

   *  checks 1 to 5(a) passed, so the statement is authenticated by a
      currently valid configured key and is well-formed enough to name.
      Before check 4 the sender is unauthenticated, and notifying the
      claimed sender would be backscatter; between checks 4 and 5(a),
      the statement cannot be named;

   *  the candidate was not a duplicate caught at check 2 (an exact
      retained statement: the first copy was already answered, and a
      replay on the path must not draw a second notice);

   *  the candidate is a statement, not a Control Notice: nothing is
      ever sent about a Control Notice (Section 12.6.8);

   *  the destination is the Runtime address configured for the key's
      owner, and never an address taken from the message.

   A "dropped, duplicate" notice (check 12) tells the sender that a
   record with that id already exists.  That record's disposition may
   have been placement or refusal: the notice proves a prior
   reservation, not that the task failed.  Whether and how the sending
   Agent learns of an outcome is governed by Section 12.6.8.

12.6.5.  The Replay Store, Windows and Recovery

   *Windows.* The receiver accepts ts when lower ≤ ts ≤ now + F, both
   bounds inclusive, where lower = max(H − P, floor):

   *  *F*, the allowance for clock skew, defaults to 300 seconds and
      MUST NOT exceed 900.







Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 60]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *P*, the past window, defaults to 3600 seconds, and MUST be at
      least 300 and at most 86400.  A message that arrives later than P
      is demoted, which is visible to the sender.  A longer P costs
      replay storage and a longer key retirement (Section 12.6.7).

   *  *H* is the latest receiver time ever observed, kept durably.  The
      lower bound uses H rather than the current clock, so that a clock
      that steps backwards cannot re-admit a statement whose record has
      been pruned.

   *  *floor* is set only by recovery and by window changes, both below.

   *Records.* Replay identity is scoped to the pair (configured Runtime,
   id), where the Runtime is the configured peer that owns the verifying
   key, so that rotating a key never resets it.  Each record holds the
   scope, the id and ts; the SHA-256 digest of the statement bytes; the
   notice_id minted at reservation; a state, which is reserved, decided
   or done; and, once decided, the _disposition_: placement, or a
   refusal or drop with its cause (and policy_code), and whether a
   Control Notice is still pending.

   *Recording.* The receiver records a candidate at check 12, after
   checks 1 to 11 have passed.  A candidate that fails any of them
   records nothing, so a mangled copy cannot suppress the intact one
   that follows.  Misrouted and refused candidates are recorded too, so
   that their replays are dropped quietly instead of being evaluated
   again each time.  Control Notices (Section 12.6.8) use the same
   store.

   *Reservation, decision and effect.* These are three durable steps, in
   order, each atomic:

   1.  *Reserve.* Check 12 creates the reserved record and mints a fresh
       notice_id.  The candidate stays in the intake location until the
       record is done.  A reservation is undecided, and authorizes
       nothing.

   2.  *Decide.* The receiver routes, correlates, permits and applies
       policy (Section 12.6.3), and persists the disposition on the
       record, which becomes decided.  A refusal or drop also marks its
       control notice as pending.

   3.  *Effect.* For a placement, the notice is written under the minted
       notice_id; for a refusal or drop, the Control Notice is durably
       queued.  Only then is the record done.  Placement is idempotent:
       a notice that is already present is not written again.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 61]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   A copy that arrives while another copy is reserved or decided matches
   it at check 2, and is dropped.  On restart, the receiver MUST finish
   every record that is not done, exactly once, by resuming its
   _recorded_ state, and MUST NOT infer a disposition from the absence
   of a notice:

   *  a reserved record is decided then, under the configuration in
      force at recovery (the receiver has no older one it can trust),
      and then takes effect;

   *  a decided placement is placed if the notice is absent, and is
      marked done without placing it again if the notice is present;

   *  a decided refusal or drop is not published: its pending control
      notice is queued, once, and the record is marked done.

   An implementation MUST survive a crash at each of these points: after
   reservation, after the decision, after a notice is placed, after a
   control notice is queued, and after a terminal refusal is recorded,
   including when the graph or policy changed while it was down.

   *Retention.* The receiver MUST retain each done record while H ≤ ts +
   P, and MAY retain it longer.  It MUST NOT prune a record that is not
   done.  A known statement replayed after its retention has lapsed
   fails freshness, so it is demoted and never placed.  Duplicate
   suppression is therefore effective only within retention: this
   profile does not promise exactly-once delivery, and an implementation
   MUST NOT claim it.

   *Resending.* A sending Runtime whose hand-off was ambiguous MAY
   resend the same id, signed again with a new ts.  If the first copy
   arrived and is retained, the resend is dropped at check 12, and the
   control notice tells the sender so; if the first copy did not arrive,
   the resend is placed.  A sending Runtime that resends MUST keep the
   same id, including across a resend that a person approved.

   This permission is idempotent only within retention.  Once the first
   copy's record has been pruned, a resend of the same id under a fresh
   ts finds no record, and is placed a second time.  A deployment that
   cannot accept that MUST forbid signing again in its own deployment
   profile, and resend only the original bytes, which check 2 drops or
   freshness demotes.  The permission is kept for portability, not as a
   recommendation.








Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 62]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Recovery.* The store and H MUST survive a restart.  If the receiver
   loses the store, or cannot show that a restored store is complete, it
   MUST restore this barrier: no statement that could already have been
   accepted under the lost coverage may be admitted again, including at
   the boundary, under a clock that stepped back, and under the largest
   F that was ever in effect.

   *  *With H intact*, the receiver sets floor to one second after
      max(C, H) + Fmax, persisted before admission resumes.  C is the
      moment from which it again holds complete evidence, H is the high-
      water clock at the loss, and Fmax is the largest F in effect at
      any point that could have admitted a statement still within the
      lost coverage.  Fmax is taken from the retained history of F if
      that history is provable, and is 900 otherwise.  Fmax MUST NOT be
      chosen from the wall-clock interval ending at C: after a clock
      rollback, that interval can miss a larger F that was in effect
      near H.  Retaining the largest F ever configured is safe.  Any
      statement accepted before the loss had ts ≤ H + F ≤ max(C, H) +
      Fmax, so none reaches the floor.  The floor is strictly above that
      bound: an inclusive floor would re-admit a statement accepted at
      exactly now + F, and C alone would re-admit one accepted before
      the clock stepped back.

   *  *With H lost as well*, no trustworthy bound exists, and the
      receiver MUST close peer admission: candidates reaching check 7
      are held in intake, and nothing is placed or demoted on a window
      the receiver cannot define.  Admission reopens only when the
      operator records a bound B that is at or after the largest
      receiver time before the loss.  The floor is then one second after
      B + Fmax, with Fmax determined as above: losing H does not by
      itself lose the history of F.  The held candidates are then
      evaluated in arrival order.  The current wall-clock time is not a
      bound.

   *Window changes.* Narrowing P or F takes effect at once.  Widening P
   MUST NOT re-admit anything: the receiver sets the floor to the lower
   bound in effect at the moment of the change, and the window then
   widens only as records accumulate.

12.6.6.  Correlation and Edges Between Hosts

   *The ledger.* A Runtime keeps a record for every peer message it
   issued to another host or placed.  Each record holds the id; the
   local Agent and the remote Agent; the direction (issued or placed);
   and an expiry, the configured reply window (Section 12.5).  The
   ledger is scoped to peer messages: a mail notice id never resolves.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 63]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Resolution.* A verified statement carrying in_reply_to resolves only
   if a record exists whose id equals in_reply_to, whose local Agent
   equals to, whose remote Agent equals from, and which has not expired.
   Possession of an id is not authority: an id presented by another
   Agent on the same host, or by any Agent on another host, does not
   resolve.

   *Permission.* A resolved reply to a record this Runtime issued is a
   reverse message, and is permitted without an edge (Section 12.5).  A
   resolved message against a record this Runtime placed is a follow-up
   in the same direction, and needs the edge from from to to.  A
   statement without in_reply_to needs the edge.

   *The receiver's own graph.* The edge MUST be checked against the
   receiver's own graph.  The sending Runtime checked its edge at
   submission (Section 12.4), but which peers may task an Agent is the
   receiving Runtime's decision.  If correlation fails, the outcome is
   "refuse: unresolved reply"; if permission fails, it is "refuse: no
   edge".  Neither is demoted.

   *At submission.* The sending Runtime MUST apply the same binding: a
   reply key resolves only if the submitting Agent is the record's local
   Agent.  It SHOULD also refuse at submission a message it already
   knows the receiver will refuse, such as one for a pair it knows has
   no edge or is held by policy, so that the Agent learns of it at once.
   The receiver remains the authority.

12.6.7.  Keys

   *Configuration.* The operator configures, at every receiver, each
   peer Runtime's domain set, its Runtime address (amap.router@<domain>
   or equivalent), and its key set.  Trust anchors are configured, not
   discovered: there is no DNS publication, directory or certificate
   chain.  A receiver MUST refuse to load a configuration in which:

   *  a key_id occurs twice, across all peers (the receiver selects a
      key by k alone);

   *  a not-before time is later than its not-after time;

   *  a public key is not a canonical encoding of a curve point; or

   *  a public key is of small order.

   A sending Runtime SHOULD make its key ids globally unique, for
   example by deriving them from a fingerprint of the public key.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 64]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   These are configuration-time checks, a gate separate from
   verification.  A bare Ed25519 implementation will construct and
   verify under a small-order or non-canonical key; the key loader, not
   the verifier, is what refuses one.  An implementation MUST
   demonstrate the refusal through its loader, and MUST NOT count
   passing the vectors marked for rejection at verification as covering
   it.

   *Rotation.* A receiver MUST support at least two concurrent keys per
   peer.  A rotation proceeds as follows:

   1.  Add the new key at every receiver.

   2.  Switch the sender to it.

   3.  If the sender stops using the old key at time T, receivers keep
       the old key valid until at least T + F + P, because a statement
       signed at T can carry a ts up to T + F, and arrive up to P after
       that.

   Validity is inclusive at both ends.  Revocation is removing a key or
   ending its validity.  Replay records are scoped to the Runtime rather
   than the key, so neither retiring nor revoking a key erases replay
   evidence (Section 12.6.5).

   *The signing key* is a Runtime credential (Section 3.1).  It MUST NOT
   be readable from any Agent Namespace or by the admitting component.
   It MUST NOT be used to sign anything except this profile's statements
   and Control Notices, which their kind members keep apart.

   *Verification policy.* Verification is Ed25519 as specified in
   [RFC8032], with the cofactorless equation [S]B = R + [k]A.  A
   verifier MUST reject a signature whose S is not less than L; a non-
   canonical encoding of R or A; and a key that failed the configuration
   checks above.  A point encoding MUST be decoded canonically before
   any other check is applied to it: the "negative zero" encoding of x =
   0 (y = p − 1 with the sign bit set) is non-canonical, and is rejected
   as such before a small-order check is reached.

   This document requires nothing about how Ed25519 is computed.  A
   vetted library, a system binary or any other implementation conforms
   if it produces these results.  The conformance suite holds the test
   vectors of Section 7.1 of [RFC8032] (TEST 1 to 3), and negative
   vectors marked for rejection either at verification or at
   configuration (Appendix J).  An implementation MUST pass both kinds
   through the implementation it ships.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 65]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


12.6.8.  Control Notices

   A receiving Runtime tells a configured sending Runtime what it did
   with a statement it did not place, using a signed _Control Notice_.
   The peer-control schema (Appendix F) pins it: version v 1, closed,
   with the members v, key_id, kind ("control"), id, from, to, ts,
   about, outcome, cause, and policy_code (with cause policy).

   *Form.* A Control Notice is carried in an AMAP-Peer-Control header
   field with the k, s and b grammar of Section 12.6.2, signed with the
   same per-Runtime key.  Its kind makes it impossible to read as a peer
   statement, and the reverse.  It carries no free text: the cause
   vocabulary is closed, and the receiving Runtime composes any words
   itself.  It travels as mail between Runtime addresses.

   *When.* A receiver SHOULD send one for every outcome Section 12.6.4
   marks, and MUST send one only when the eligibility conditions of
   Section 12.6.4 hold in full: never for a failure before check 5(b),
   never for a duplicate caught at check 2, never about a Control
   Notice, and never merely because a key was found.  There is one
   notice per record: the pending notice is part of the record's
   disposition (Section 12.6.5), MUST be queued durably before the
   record is done, and MUST be sent at most once, including across a
   crash.  A receiver MAY rate-limit Control Notices; any suppression
   MUST be logged.

   *policy_code* is defined by the deployment.  A receiving Runtime
   renders a description it defines locally.  An unknown token gets a
   generic description, and MUST NOT be interpreted.

   *Addressing.* from is the receiver's own Runtime address. to MUST be
   the Runtime address configured for the peer that owns the verifying
   key, and MUST NOT be an address taken from the message.  A control
   notice MUST NOT be sent to a Runtime that is not a configured peer.

   *Receiving one.* A Runtime applies checks 1 to 5 of Section 12.6.3,
   with AMAP-Peer-Control and the control schema in place of the
   statement's.  It then requires all of these: from is the Runtime
   address of the peer that owns the key; to is its own Runtime address;
   ts is fresh (Section 12.6.5); the notice's pair (Runtime, id) is new;
   and about names a ledger record that this Runtime issued to an Agent
   in the signer's domains.









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 66]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *What it does.* It SHOULD give the issuing Agent a failure notice
   authored by the Runtime in inbound/ (the delivery failure notice of
   Section 12.5), with no text from the Control Notice except the
   vocabulary values.  Where it does, the failure notice is owed from
   the moment the record is reserved, and the record is done only once
   the failure notice is durable; a crash in between is finished by
   recovery, once.

   *One per message.* An issued record receives at most one failure
   notice.  A later Control Notice about the same about, under a
   different id, is dropped.  A "dropped, duplicate" report means that a
   record for the message exists at the receiver, whose disposition may
   have been placement; it is not proof that the task failed.

   *Failures.* A Control Notice that fails any rule is dropped and
   logged: it MUST NOT be placed, handed to mail admission, or answered.
   A message carrying both fields is dropped.

12.6.9.  Optional: Sender Age, and Deployment Admission Policy

   A deployment MAY refuse authenticated peer messages for reasons of
   its own, such as a first-sight quarantine for a new sender, or a
   requirement that every delegation between hosts carry
   sender_exposure.  The refusal is "refuse: policy", with a policy_code
   defined by the deployment.  The policies themselves are the
   deployment's business, not this profile's.

   Measuring a sender's age at the receiver, from first sight, would
   make every Agent's first delegation to each host fail.  The optional
   signed member sender_since exists to avoid that:

   *  It is the time at which the sending Runtime first enrolled the
      sending Agent's identity, as that Runtime defines identity, taken
      from its durable registry.

   *  It is a Runtime assertion, covered by the signature, and MUST NOT
      be taken from text the sender supplied.

   *  It has the format of ts, and is not later than ts.  Skew is
      absorbed by the age itself: a receiver measures age as its own
      clock minus sender_since, so a few minutes of skew change nothing
      under a policy measured in hours.









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 67]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Continuity.* The sending Runtime MUST NOT reset it for a
      continuation of the same identity: a restart, a rebinding, a re-
      creation or a key rotation keeps the value.  A new enrollment of
      the identity starts a new value.  The sending Runtime decides
      which of the two a given event is, and MUST decide it the same way
      every time for that identity.

   *  *Consistency.* A receiver that enforces a sender-age policy MUST
      keep the last value it accepted for each pair (Runtime, from).  A
      later statement that asserts an _earlier_ value claims an older
      enrollment than the Runtime previously asserted; it is
      inconsistent, and the receiver refuses it with its own
      policy_code.  A later value is a new enrollment, and the age
      starts again.

   A receiver MAY enforce a minimum sender age from it.  Its absence
   means "not asserted", and a receiver MUST NOT read it as "new" or as
   "old enough".  A deployment that requires it refuses its absence with
   its own policy_code.

12.6.10.  The Intake Location

   The intake location is REQUIRED, as a structural property with no
   prescribed layout.  A message admitted from a shared transport that
   presents as a peer or control candidate MUST be held, until it is
   disposed of, in a location that is neither inbound/ nor peer/, that
   is writable by the admitting component and readable by the verifying
   component, and that is unreachable from any Agent Namespace.
   Candidates MUST be held as the candidate of Section 12.6.2: the
   verifier MUST NOT parse mail.  The verifier MUST apply the read-side
   discipline of Section 4.1 to candidates, since the admitting
   component is less trusted than the verifier.  The verifier disposes
   of each candidate exactly once: it places it in peer/, minting the
   notice_id at reservation (Section 12.6.5); or it hands it to mail
   admission, which, if it delivers, places it in inbound/ under a
   notice_id minted there; or it drops or refuses it, logging the cause.
   A candidate held while peer admission is closed (Section 12.6.5) is
   not yet disposed of, and stays in the intake location until admission
   reopens.

   How a Runtime divides its intake (one location or several, for
   example by candidate kind), and where it keeps the traffic it authors
   itself, are implementation choices; this section constrains only the
   properties above.







Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 68]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


12.7.  Sender Exposure

   The split between Runtime assertions and sender claims (Section 7.1)
   applies: disposition, verdict and sender_standing are Runtime
   assertions, while subject and body_text (and, on the mail tree, from)
   are sender claims.  An exposure record belongs on the assertion side.
   It records _delivery_, not _reading_: a Runtime can know that it
   delivered external mail to the sender's Namespace, but cannot know
   what the sender did with it.

   A Peer Notice asserting exposure, with the stamp in
   message.sender_exposure:

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "notice_id": "7b2a1c0d9e8f47a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8",
     "ts": "2026-09-03T12:05:00Z",
     "kind": "peer",
     "message": {
       "id": "7b2a1c0d9e8f47a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8",
       "from": "triage@fleet.example",
       "subject": "Customer asks for an export",
       "preview": "A customer mail this morning asks whether",
       "mailbox": "peer",
       "sender_exposure": {
         "asserted_by": "amap.router@fleet.example",
         "external_mail_delivered": true,
         "window_start": "2026-09-02T12:05:00Z",
         "window_end": "2026-09-03T12:05:00Z",
         "last_external_delivery_ts": "2026-09-03T08:41:10Z",
         "derived_from": ["1721457600000000001-4242"]
       }
     }
   }

              Figure 9: fixtures/valid/peer-exposure-true.json

   *  *Placement.* It is a member of message, beside sender_standing,
      provenance and verdict, so that the Runtime's assessments of the
      message are kept together.  The schema requires asserted_by (a
      bare addr-spec naming the asserting Runtime; between hosts, the
      signer), external_mail_delivered, window_start and window_end, and
      requires last_external_delivery_ts when the boolean is true.  Its
      absence when the boolean is false is stated here, not in the
      schema.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 69]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Shape.* A boolean over an explicit window, plus the most recent
      timestamp.  There is no count, because a count would assert a
      precision that a measure of delivery lacks. derived_from is
      optional, and present only where the Runtime observed the
      derivation itself (the sender's reply key named a notice in its
      mail tree).

   *  *Absence means "not assessed".* A consumer MUST NOT read the
      member's absence as "no exposure". false, asserted, is a stronger
      statement than the member omitted: it says that the Runtime
      assessed the window and delivered no external mail.  A Runtime
      that is the only writer of a sender's mail tree, and has written
      there only same-principal Agent mail and its own delivery failure
      notices, SHOULD assert false.  Notices the Runtime authors in the
      mail tree (the delivery failure notices of Section 12.5) are not
      external mail, and MUST NOT make the boolean true.  Moving
      window_start forward to the moment the Runtime's assessment began
      (for example, an instance's approval time after a reset) keeps the
