      window on the wire equal to the span assessed.

   *  *Not settable by the sender.* On one host, the Submit Request
      envelope is closed (Section 13.1), so a request carrying the
      member is rejected, which is stronger than stripping it.  Between
      hosts, it is taken only from the verified statement, and is
      removed on demotion (Section 12.6.4).  A Runtime MUST NOT accept
      it from any sender.

   *  *Use.* It MUST NOT drive routing or treatment (Section 12.3).  It
      is advisory, for audit, and covered by the signature.

   *Lineage declared by the sender is not included.* Such a member would
   ride on the Submit Request, whose envelope is closed, so adding it
   would be a major change; it would work only when the sender
   cooperates, which is the case where it is least needed; and a
   forgeable member invites readers to trust it.  Most of its value is
   recovered without one: when a sender's reply key names a notice in
   its _mail_ tree, the Runtime knows which external message the peer
   message derives from, and records that as its own observation
   (derived_from, and the audit log).

12.8.  Delivery Outcomes, Retention, Deletion and Presentation

   *  *Delivery outcomes are not a profile artifact.* A Connector that
      reports what it did with a notice (delivered, held, refused, and
      so on) writes the report under outbound/ext/<name>/, in a shape
      agreed out of band with its Runtime, under the stable Connector id
      that Section 4.1 requires.  Section 4.1 carries the one normative
      rule: an outcome is a claim by the receiving side, never proof of



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 70]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      delivery or of non-delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record
      is authoritative over it (Section 14.15).  If a second Connector
      needs outcomes, that is the point at which to define a shape for
      them in this profile.

   *  *Retention.* The record is the audit log, not the spool.  The
      Runtime logs every candidate it disposes of (id, from, to, tree,
      exposure, signature verdict, and any demotion or refusal cause) to
      the per-Agent audit/log.jsonl it owns, and to its own store of
      record.  Spool retention for peer/ follows the mail row of the
      deletion table (Section 4.2) unchanged.

   *  *Deletion rights.* The deletion table (Section 4.2) applies to
      peer/ artifacts exactly as to inbound ones: written by the
      Runtime, and deleted by the Runtime only.

   *  *Presentation.* A Connector presenting a peer body MUST meet the
      presentation obligations of Section 7.1, with one prohibition and
      two additions.  It MUST NOT convey that the sender is
      unauthenticated: on this tree, message.from is asserted by the
      Runtime from the restricted write path (Section 12.4), and saying
      otherwise contradicts the mechanism the tree exists to provide.
      It SHOULD convey that an authenticated request is still bounded by
      what the receiving Agent is authorized to do: a verified sender
      can ask for something the receiver may not perform, and a framing
      that reads as a grant invites the reader to treat verified
      identity as having settled that question.  It SHOULD convey that
      authenticated origin is not a warranty about content: peer content
      is authored by a peer and unscreened, and may paraphrase external
      mail (Section 12.7).  Authenticated _who_; unverified _what_.

      None of this is an enforcement mechanism.  Enforcement on this
      tree is the write-authority partition and the origin-follows-the-
      tree rule (Section 12.3); presentation is what a Connector states
      to a reader who can ignore it.  The reason to get it right is that
      the alternative asserts something false.

13.  Versioning and Conformance

13.1.  Versioning

   *The fail-closed rule.* contract_version is a major-version string.
   A consumer that reads a *higher major* than it speaks MUST *fail
   closed* — refuse to process the artifact — and MUST NOT silently mis-
   parse it.






Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 71]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Version-check ordering.* A consumer MUST implement the version check
   by reading contract_version *before* any schema validation, comparing
   majors as non-negative decimal integers.  An absent major, a lower
   major, or a higher major is a *version refusal*: fail closed, as a
   distinct, logged outcome, never folded into the malformed-document
   drop path of Section 7.1.

   Checking the version first is what makes fail-closed implementable at
   all.  A validator that runs schema checks first cannot distinguish
   "wrong version" from "malformed," and a strict schema would reject a
   future-major document for the wrong reason entirely.

   This ordering rule is about _inbound_ artifacts a Connector consumes,
   which have no mechanism in this protocol to carry a distinct outcome
   back to the Runtime.  It does not reach the _outbound_ direction: a
   Runtime version-refusing a Submit Request MAY carry that refusal on
   the ordinary request-rejection path — a top-level rejected Result
   with reason_code: "unsupported_contract_version" (Section 6.1) — and,
   per the conformance classes below, MUST do so for the version-absent
   request fixture.  That is still a distinct, legible outcome rather
   than a fold into the malformed-request case: reason_code is exactly
   this protocol's mechanism for saying _why_ a rejected fired, and a
   consumer MUST already tolerate a reason_code it does not otherwise
   interpret.  A Runtime has no equivalent document to write for a
   version-refused _Notice_ it never emits — hence the asymmetry:
   logged-only inbound, rejected outbound.

   *A version signal, not member rejection, is the boundary.* Rejecting
   a document because it carries an unrecognized member is not a version
   mechanism.  Under closed envelopes, a consumer that meets a new
   member rejects the _whole document_: inbound, that is silent loss of
   the message; outbound, it is an accidental schema error rather than a
   designed refusal.  And while the version string is unchanged, nothing
   can react to the new member.  A change that a consumer of the current
   wire major would reject or misread as a whole document therefore
   requires a new wire major, so that the consumer refuses it _by
   version_, legibly, and both sides upgrade deliberately.  Schema
   strictness and protocol version are separate axes, and this document
   does not use the first as the second.

   *Unknown-member tolerance is direction-aware.* The rule is stated per
   direction because the two directions have opposite threat models.

   *  *Runtime-authored artifacts — Deliver Notice, Inbound Message,
      Result, Peer Notice — are open.* A consumer MUST ignore members it
      does not recognize, at every level of the document, and MUST NOT
      reject, drop, or fail the artifact on their account.  Strictness
      in this direction defends nothing: the producer is trusted by



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 72]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      construction, and in the one posture where an attacker can author
      a Notice — a writable inbound tree — that attacker can author a
      fully schema-valid one, so strictness is not the defense there.
      Its failure mode is silent loss of mail.  Emitting an unknown
      member is still a *producer* non-conformance: a Runtime MUST NOT
      emit members this document does not define.  In the schemas,
      additionalProperties: false is absent from the deliver-notice,
      inbound-message, result and peer-notice schemas at every level —
      top level, message, Descriptor items, and attestation — while the
      clean-gating conditionals are orthogonal and remain.

   *  *The Submit Request envelope is closed*, additionalProperties:
      false at every level.  Closure does real security work there: it
      is what bars an outbound content_ref and any other smuggled
      member; the validator is the trusted Runtime; and a refusal is a
      _legible, per-request_ rejected Result, never a silent loss.  A
      Runtime MUST reject a request carrying unrecognized members.

   *  *Consequently:* adding an optional member to a Runtime-authored
      artifact is additive and needs no new wire major; adding any
      member to the Submit Request requires one.

   *  The Binding Record is closed, for the separate reason given in
      Section 9.1.  The signed Peer Statement and Control Notice are
      closed because they are signed bytes another Runtime acts on
      (Section 12.6.1); they carry their own version member, v.

   *Tolerance extends to values, not only members.* An optional,
   explicitly advisory enum on a Runtime-authored artifact —
   message.sender_standing and message.provenance (Section 7.1) — is
   scoped the same way.  A consumer MUST tolerate a value it does not
   recognize, treating it as opaque or as the member being absent, and
   MUST NOT reject, drop, or fail the artifact on that account; a
   Runtime MAY add a value to either vocabulary without a new wire
   major.  Without this, a Runtime adding a new sender_standing or
   provenance value would silently lose every Notice carrying it,
   against every Connector still validating the old enum — the member
   case again, at the value level.  In the schemas, the enum constraint
   is absent from these two members.

   This is *not* a universal loosening of every enum. kind, outcome —
   both the top-level Result outcome and the per-attachment outcome —
   and the inbound Descriptor's disposition remain *closed, enum-locked
   vocabularies*. kind and outcome gate which processing path a document
   takes at all, and disposition gates byte publication (Section 7.2),
   so a new value in any of them is a behavioral fork a consumer cannot
   safely treat as opaque.  Introducing one requires a new wire major.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 73]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *When the wire major changes, and when it does not.* The wire major
   exists to force a legible, fail-closed refusal where a _whole
   document_ that a counterpart already accepts would otherwise be
   silently misread or silently dropped.  A change whose only
   incompatibility already travels a designed, legible, per-artifact
   refusal path (a rejected Result for one request, or the drop of one
   Notice under Section 7.1) does not require one.  Changing the major
   for such a change would make every counterpart on the old major
   refuse _all_ traffic, including traffic the change does not affect,
   which is the failure the major exists to prevent.  Revisions of this
   document are not wire versions: a revision that requires no new wire
   major leaves contract_version unchanged.

   *Why the wire version is "2".* The wire version starts at "2", not
   "1", because the value "1" is already taken.  Before this document,
   implementations exchanged an earlier, incompatible shape under "1":
   it had no attachments, and its envelopes were closed.  Reusing "1"
   for this document's shapes would give one major two incompatible
   meanings, and would defeat the fail-closed rule above exactly where
   it is needed: a consumer of the old shape would accept a document it
   cannot process. "2" is also what current implementations emit and
   check.  Appendix L records the history.  The authors would be glad of
   the community's view on whether a reset is nonetheless worth its
   cost.

   *Change control.* A capability change starts with a change to this
   document, its schemas, and its fixtures, _before_ either side
   implements it.  Neither a Runtime nor a Connector may invent a wire
   member locally.  A change that breaks an existing fixture is taken
   deliberately by both sides, and requires a new wire major only under
   the rule above.

13.2.  Required versus optional

   contract_version is REQUIRED on the Submit Request, the Deliver
   Notice, the Inbound Message, the Result, the Peer Notice and the
   Fleet Roster.  It is OPTIONAL on the Binding Record (Section 9.1) and
   the Peer Directory, and the signed Peer Statement and Control Notice
   carry their own version member, v, instead.  The rest of this table
   reflects what implementations emit today; specified-but-unbuilt
   enrichment stays optional, and tightening any of it to required would
   be a future major bump.









Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 74]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026

   inbound/notices/processed/ is an OPTIONAL *directory convention*
   (Section 4.1), not a protocol artifact: it carries no schema, and no
   fixture exists or is needed for it.

   Emission of contract_version on the artifacts that require it is
   mandatory.  An implementation not yet emitting it has an
   implementation conformance gap, not a license from this document.

13.3.  Conformance

   *The fixtures are the other side.* fixtures/ holds golden artifacts,
   and a producer or consumer proves conformance by passing them with
   *no counterpart present* (Appendix J).  That is what makes
   independent implementation practical: neither side needs the other to
   exist in order to demonstrate conformance.

   Not every obligation in this document is wire-shaped.  A _behavioral_
   obligation — one about how an implementation acts against a
   filesystem, rather than about the shape of a document — lies outside
   the fixture gate by construction and is checked operationally
   instead.  Appendix J lists every obligation of this kind that a green
   run does not prove.

   This document defines two conformance classes.  An implementation MAY
   claim both.  Claiming either without the corresponding fixture run,
   and without the prescribed operational check for that class's
   behavioral obligations, is not conformance.

   *Runtime conformance class.* An implementation claiming Runtime
   conformance:




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 77]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  MUST produce Deliver Notice documents valid against the deliver-
      notice schema (Appendix C) and Result documents valid against the
      result schema (Appendix B); MAY produce Inbound Message documents,
      which when produced MUST be valid against the inbound-message
      schema (Appendix D); and MAY produce a Binding Record valid
      against the binding-record schema (Appendix E).

   *  MUST consume Submit Request documents: it MUST accept every valid
      request-* fixture and MUST reject every invalid request-* fixture.

   *  MUST demonstrate its producing side by confirming that its own
      emitted Notices, Results, and Inbound Messages satisfy the same
      schemas the suite's valid notice-*, result-*, and message-*
      fixtures satisfy — *including the three fixtures carrying
      unrecognized members*. A Runtime MUST NOT itself emit unrecognized
      members, but its _parser_, exercised by those fixtures, is what a
      Connector conformance run depends on it never having to special-
      case.  It MUST also confirm that any Binding Record it writes
      satisfies the valid identity-* shape.

   *  MUST uphold the filesystem and policy obligations of Sections 4
      through 8 that no document validator can observe.  Appendix J
      lists them explicitly as what a green fixture run does *not*
      prove, and they are obligations of the class regardless — write-
      side path discipline (the conjunctive parent-chain-pinning, no-
      follow-while-building, and non-following-final-component rule),
      ingest by copy, read-side open discipline, and single-writer/
      single-drainer chief among them.

   *Connector conformance class.* An implementation claiming Connector
   conformance:

   *  MUST produce Submit Request documents valid against the submit-
      request schema (Appendix A), and MUST NOT emit an outbound
      content_ref (Section 5.1).

   *  MUST consume Deliver Notice, Inbound Message, and Result
      documents: it MUST accept every valid notice-*, message-*, and
      result-* fixture — *including those carrying unrecognized members
      or unrecognized advisory-enum values* — and MUST reject, meaning
      drop rather than surface, every invalid notice-* fixture *except
      the version-refusal one*, which it MUST instead refuse via the
      distinct version-refusal path (Section 13.1): never folded into
      the drop path, and never surfaced to the Agent either.

      Section 7.1's drop rule is *two independent conditions, not a
      closure over schema validation*. "Fails schema validation for any
      reason other than an unrecognized member" (check 1) covers eleven



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 78]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      of the twelve other invalid notice-* fixtures — missing-required-
      member, wrong-kind, enum, pattern, and conditional violations
      alike.  The twelfth is schema-valid on its own, producing zero
      errors from the gate's schema validator, and is caught only by the
      content_ref index and prefix binding (check 2, Section 7.2), a
      named post-check the schema cannot express.  A Connector
      conformance claim requires running *both* checks; schema
      validation alone does not close this set.

      Accepting the clean-Descriptor fixture — a Descriptor asserted
      clean and carrying content_ref and sha256 — is part of this
      obligation, and acceptance means relaying the Notice, not fetching
      the bytes: a Connector that never dereferences content_ref
      satisfies it (Section 7.2).

   *  MUST return "not resolved" for a body whose Inbound Message is
      absent, and MUST NOT attempt any fallback fetch (Section 7.3).

   *  MUST tolerate a Binding Record that is absent, and MUST NOT crash
      or otherwise misbehave on one that is hostile or malformed
      (Section 9.1).

   *  MUST NOT require write access anywhere under inbound/,
      demonstrated by the operational check below rather than by a
      fixture (Section 4.1).

   *  MUST demonstrate its producing side by confirming that its own
      emitted requests satisfy the same schema the suite's valid
      request-* fixtures satisfy, and MUST uphold the write-ordering,
      atomicity, and read-discipline obligations of Section 4.1, which
      the fixtures cannot check.

   *Peer-origin sub-classes.* The peer-origin profile (Section 12) adds
   two sub-classes, each requiring the corresponding class above plus
   the profile's fixtures and operational checks.  Claiming either
   without both is not conformance.

   An implementation claiming *Runtime + peer-origin* conformance, in
   addition to the Runtime class:

   *  MUST produce Peer Notices valid against the peer-notice schema
      (Appendix F), and MUST confirm that its own emitted Peer Notices
      satisfy the same schema the valid peer-* fixtures satisfy;

   *  MUST refuse to emit into peer/ any document that would fail that
      schema, and MUST NOT emit a peer document into inbound/
      (Section 12.2);




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 79]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  MUST uphold the operational obligations of the profile: the write-
      authority partition, proven by the write probe, and verification
      placement (Section 12.3); a Runtime-asserted peer from
      (Section 12.4); in_reply_to only when resolved, and refusal rather
      than stripping (Section 12.5); the intake location, and hashing of
      bytes by the verifier itself (Section 12.6); and sender_exposure
      never settable by a sender (Section 12.7);

   *  if it verifies peer traffic from other hosts, MUST reach every
      step's expected outcome in the signed cases, and MUST pass the
      Ed25519 vectors through the implementation it ships (Appendix J).

   An implementation claiming *Connector + peer-origin* conformance, in
   addition to the Connector class:

   *  MUST accept every valid peer-* fixture and MUST reject every
      invalid peer-* fixture when read from peer/notices/, and MUST
      reject invalid/notice-kind-peer.json when read from inbound/
      notices/;

   *  MUST derive the origin class from the tree alone (Section 12.3),
      and MUST act on a peer message at most once, holding rather than
      fanning out when it cannot identify a single target
      (Section 12.4);

   *  MUST tolerate unknown members on a Peer Notice, whose envelope is
      open (Section 13.1).

   *Read-only inbound tolerance — the prescribed operational check.* Run
   the Connector against an inbound tree it cannot write — a genuinely
   read-only mount, not merely cleared permission bits, since a same-uid
   Agent can change a mode it owns — and confirm that it starts, relays
   every pending Notice, resolves bodies, and submits outbound requests,
   without requiring any write under inbound/ to succeed.

14.  Security Considerations

   This section gathers the threats this protocol's obligations exist to
   address.  It introduces no new mechanism: apart from the rule for
   special-use domain names (Section 14.16), which is stated only here,
   every requirement referenced here is stated normatively in Sections 4
   through 13.  The organizing principle throughout is the invariant of
   Section 3.2 — enforcement is Runtime-side, and no property depends on
   the Agent or its Connector behaving.







Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 80]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   The threat actor assumed throughout is a *fully compromised Agent*
   with write access to its own Namespace, running as a uid that owns
   the files it creates, able to act concurrently with the Runtime, and
   able to observe or predict the filenames the Runtime is about to use.

14.1.  Path authority and traversal

   An identifier drawn from a file's _contents_ MUST NOT name a write
   path (Section 4.1).  A Runtime that trusted a req_id member inside a
   request body to name the path its Result is written to would let the
   Agent, which controls that member, direct a Runtime-privileged write
   anywhere the Runtime can reach.  The obligation is that the Runtime
   derives identifiers from the _validated filename_, over a restricted
   character set, and re-derives every path from data it controls.

   The same reasoning is why inbound Sidecar directories and the body
   spool are keyed on the Runtime-minted notice identifier rather than
   the provider message.id: the provider identifier is external,
   arbitrary, and not character-set-safe, and using one as a path
   component would hand the choice of path to the sender.  The schemas
   pin notice_id and req_id to character sets that are safe as path
   components; message.id is deliberately unconstrained, because it is
   never used as one.

14.2.  Symlinks, descriptors, and open discipline

   A shared filesystem between a trusted and an untrusted party makes
   every path-based check racy.  The Agent can replace any component of
   a path it owns with a symlink, at any moment, including between a
   Runtime's check and the Runtime's subsequent act.

   Section 4.1 states the write-side discipline as three conjunctive
   requirements, and the conjunction is the point: each leg closes a gap
   the other two leave open.

   *  Pinning only the final component leaves the _parent_ swappable,
      and rename and directory-creation calls have no no-follow flag at
      all — so a bare "do not follow symlinks on writes" rule is not
      sufficient.

   *  Pinning the parent chain without refusing symlinks _while
      acquiring_ it means the pinned descriptor may point at whatever
      the Agent planted before the Runtime opened it — including across
      a Runtime restart, when the chain is re-opened.

   *  Pinning the whole chain correctly still says nothing about the
      final filename.  Every Runtime-written filename in the layout tree
      is predictable or observable to the Agent, so a pre-planted



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 81]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      symlink at that name receives the Runtime's write with the
      Runtime's privileges unless the final open refuses to follow it
      and, where the file is newly created, refuses to reuse an existing
      name at all (O_EXCL).

   The append-only audit log is the one write with no .tmp sibling to
   lean on, and it is called out separately for two reasons.  O_EXCL
   cannot apply to a file that legitimately already exists, so the
   final-component protection there is a no-follow, append-mode, *non-
   blocking* open plus an fstat through the resulting descriptor.  The
   non-blocking part is load-bearing rather than a performance nicety: a
   no-follow flag does not apply to a FIFO, because a FIFO is not a
   symlink, and opening a FIFO for writing blocks until a reader
   appears.  An Agent that plants a FIFO at that filename therefore
   stalls the Runtime's drain indefinitely — a denial of service that
   the exclusive-create branch happens to refuse for free, and that this
   branch must refuse explicitly.

   The read side mirrors all of it (Section 4.1): per-component no-
   follow opens or an equivalently pinned walk, a non-blocking open, an
   fstat through the open descriptor rather than a pre-open stat (which
   is itself a race), refusal of a multiply-linked file, and enforced
   size and count caps.  The caps are not optional hardening: the
   too_large Result value presumes one, and without them an Agent can
   present an unbounded Sidecar or an unbounded request and exhaust the
   Runtime.

14.3.  Time-of-check to time-of-use, and ingest by copy

   Even with every open performed correctly, validating a file _in
   place_ and then using it is a race: the Agent can rewrite the bytes
   between the check and the use, so the document that passed policy is
   not necessarily the document that gets composed and sent.  The
   obligation that closes this is ingest by copy (Section 4.1) — the
   Runtime copies the request and every Sidecar into Runtime-private
   Staging outside the Volume, and validates, evaluates policy on, and
   composes exclusively from that private copy, never re-reading an
   Agent-writable path after a decision that depends on its content.

   This is also what keeps the trust model honest.  Without it, the
   property "the request the Runtime approved is the request the Runtime
   sent" would rest on the Connector not rewriting a published file — an
   Agent-side obligation carrying a Runtime-side safety property, which
   the invariant of Section 3.2 forbids.  With it, that Connector
   obligation is pure well-formedness: a Runtime MAY treat an observed
   post-publish change as malformed, but nothing depends on the
   Connector honoring it.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 82]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


14.4.  Concurrency

   Every atomicity guarantee in this protocol — the .tmp-then-rename
   discipline, the commit sentinel, the derivation of req_id from the
   maximum of the pending, processed, and result sets — assumes a single
   writer and a single drainer per Namespace, and none of them provides
   mutual exclusion (Section 4.1).  Two concurrent drains can deliver
   the same request twice; two concurrent writers can collide on a
   req_id and clobber a published request, producing a verdict that
   names a request that no longer exists as written.  The exclusion
   mechanism lives outside this protocol, and an implementation that
   does not provide one is not conformant, because behavior under
   violation is unspecified rather than merely degraded.

14.5.  Attribution spoofing

   Attribution is the Namespace a file arrived in, never an identifier
   inside the file (Section 4.1).  A compromised Agent can write any
   agent_id it likes into a request; the member exists only as a cross-
   check, and a Runtime MUST reject a mismatch rather than believe it.
   Structural isolation is what actually enforces this: a Connector
   scoped to its own Namespace cannot name another Agent's.

   The Binding Record deserves the same skepticism from the other
   direction (Section 9.1).  It sits on an Agent-writable Volume, so its
   contents are untrusted data, it grants nothing, and it is never
   consulted for enforcement.

14.6.  Untrusted content

   Inbound mail is an injection vector aimed at the Agent's reasoning,
   and this protocol's posture is that _every sender-originated string_
   is untrusted content: bodies, subjects, previews, threading
   references, sender display names, and attachment Descriptors alike
   (Section 7.1).

   Two cases are worth restating because they are the ones most often
   assumed safe.

   *message.from is attacker-controlled display data.* Its display-name
   half is chosen freely by the sender, so a value such as
   "security@yourbank.example <attacker@evil.example>" is entirely legal
   and renders convincingly.  It MUST NOT be used for a trust decision
   or shown to a human or an Agent as verified identity.  Verified
   sender identity is only ever what the Runtime summarizes into
   sender_standing and verdict, or, on a Peer Notice, the message.from
   the Runtime asserts (Section 12.4).




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 83]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *An attachment filename is an injection payload.* A Descriptor is
   metadata about a file the Agent may never receive the bytes of, and a
   clean Disposition asserts something about _bytes_, never about the
   truthfulness of the strings describing them.  A quarantined file
   named to look like an instruction reaches the Agent's context intact
   even though its bytes were withheld. media_type is likewise a
   declaration, which is why policy is governed by the Runtime's own
   sniffing of the bytes rather than by the declared type.

   verdict, sender_standing, and provenance are advisory metadata for
   routing and presentation.  None of them is a license for an Agent to
   obey body content, and this document deliberately does not define
   what an Agent should do with a message — that is Connector and
   deployment policy.

14.7.  Recipient policy and header injection

   Recipient policy is the exfiltration boundary, and it is a Runtime
   decision (Section 5.1).  The Agent's draft.to and draft.cc are
   requests, not instructions.  Two obligations make the boundary
   mechanical rather than best-effort: the Runtime MUST evaluate policy
   over exactly the recipient set it will transmit to, and it MUST NOT
   transmit to any address not present in those members.  Without the
   first, policy can be evaluated over a parse of the recipients that
   differs from the one used for transmission; without the second, a
   Runtime-side addition (a bcc, an archive address) escapes the
   evaluated set.

   The narrow addr-spec profile exists to make the evaluation
   mechanical.  Display names, address lists inside a single element,
   quoted local parts, comments, IP literals, and folding whitespace are
   precisely the forms that make "does this address match the allowlist"
   a parsing problem with divergent answers — the classic confusion in
   which one parser sees the allowlisted address and the transmitting
   parser sees the attacker's.  The profile is deliberately narrower
   than [RFC5322] for that reason, and the cost is disclosed: some
   legitimate [RFC5322] addresses cannot be expressed under this
   document.













Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 84]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   Header injection is the second half.  Any Agent-authored string that
   reaches the composed message can attempt to introduce a header
   boundary with CR, LF, or NUL.  The schema patterns are the first line
   of defense, but a Runtime MUST also reject or strip those characters
   at composition time, because a document can reach composition by a
   path where schema validation was bypassed upstream.  The two fields
   most easily overlooked are the ones composed _directly into headers_
   rather than into a body or display context: reply_to_message_id,
   which becomes an In-Reply-To: header, and an attachment's media_type,
   which becomes a MIME part's Content-Type: [RFC2045].

14.8.  The outbound digest is not a trust boundary

   sha256 on an outbound attachment Descriptor is computed by the
   Connector over bytes the Connector wrote (Section 5.1).  The Agent
   controls both, so a matching digest proves only that the request is
   internally consistent.  It catches corruption and interrupted writes;
   it authenticates nothing.  A Runtime MUST NOT treat a digest match as
   evidence about the content's safety, and MUST apply its own policy —
   sniffing the bytes, applying type and size rules — to the staged copy
   regardless.

   The inbound direction is weaker still and is labelled as such:
   inbound size_bytes is provider-declared and advisory, not Runtime-
   verified (Section 7.2).

14.9.  Confirmation-oracle avoidance

   Inbound metadata is gated so that withholding bytes does not become
   an information channel. sha256 on an inbound Descriptor is emitted
   only where the Runtime asserts clean (Section 7.2).  Publishing a
   digest for a withheld attachment would let an Agent confirm whether a
   _guessed_ file was the one quarantined — a confirmation oracle —
   while providing no integrity value at all, since the Agent has no
   bytes to check it against.

   The same principle governs quarantined mail generally: it produces no
   Notice at all, rather than a Notice announcing that something was
   withheld.

14.10.  Byte-absence and artifact-absence as the access gate

   The access gate in this protocol is the absence of bytes, not a flag
   inside a document (Section 4.1).  A Runtime MUST NOT place non-clean
   bytes in an Agent's Namespace; content_ref is the grant, and it
   exists only where bytes were published.  An Agent that ignores every
   Disposition it is shown still cannot read what was never written.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 85]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   The same shape appears for bodies: a withheld or never-delivered
   message is simply not spooled, and a read against a missing artifact
   returns "not resolved," with no fallback fetch available to the
   Connector (Section 7.3).  Because retention may also remove an
   artifact (Section 4.2), "retired" and "never spooled" are
   indistinguishable from the Connector's side — which is a deliberate
   property, not an ambiguity to be resolved by a new signal.

   The content_ref binding rules (Section 7.2) close the corresponding
   path-confusion risk: a consumer derives the byte path from the
   enclosing notice_id and the array index rather than from the
   content_ref string, and refuses any reference that does not match the
   pinned pattern or points outside its own inbound tree.  Otherwise a
   Descriptor could name another Notice's Sidecar directory — including
   one belonging to a different delivery whose bytes the Agent was never
   granted.

14.11.  Fail-closed version handling, and the cost of tolerance

   A consumer reading a higher major than it speaks fails closed, and
   the version check runs _before_ schema validation so that "wrong
   version" and "malformed" remain distinguishable (Section 13.1).
   Folding the two together is how a protocol acquires silent,
   undiagnosable mail loss.

   The unknown-member tolerance rule is direction-aware precisely
   because tolerance has a security cost in one direction and a safety
   benefit in the other.  On Runtime-authored artifacts, strictness
   defends nothing — the producer is trusted, and an attacker able to
   author a Notice at all (a writable inbound tree) can author a schema-
   valid one — while its failure mode is silent mail loss.  On the
   Agent-authored Submit Request, closure is doing real work: it is what
   makes an outbound content_ref, or any other smuggled member, a hard
   rejection rather than a member the Runtime might one day interpret.
   A Runtime therefore MUST keep rejecting unrecognized members inbound
   from an Agent, and its rejection is legible — a rejected Result —
   rather than silent.

   The value-level tolerance is scoped to the two explicitly advisory
   vocabularies for the same reason: kind, outcome, and disposition gate
   processing paths and byte publication, and treating an unrecognized
   value in any of them as opaque would let a producer's new value
   silently select a consumer's default path.








Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 86]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


14.12.  Inbound integrity and the writability of the inbound tree

   A read-only inbound mount is the mechanism that makes a delivered
   Notice unforgeable (Section 4.1).  Permission bits alone do not
   achieve it: a same-uid Agent can change a mode it owns, so an inbound
   tree protected only by bits is writable by the attacker in practice.
   Deployments that leave inbound writable should understand what they
   are accepting — an Agent can then author a schema-valid Notice for
   mail that never arrived, or alter one that did.

   This is also why the tolerance rule does not weaken the inbound
   direction: in the writable-inbound posture, the attacker's forgery is
   schema-valid anyway, so schema strictness was never the control.  The
   control is the mount.

   Correspondingly, a Connector MUST NOT require write access under
   inbound/, and consumption tracking is Connector-private state kept
   elsewhere (Section 4.1).  A Connector that crashes on a read-only
   inbound tree is broken against any Runtime enforcing inbound
   integrity.

14.13.  Retention, deletion, and lost verdicts

   Deletion rights are named per artifact class (Section 4.2) because an
   unnamed right becomes either unbounded growth or an accidental data-
   loss path.  Two hazards are worth restating.

   *A Result deleted before it is read is a lost verdict.* No signal in
   this protocol tells a Runtime that a Connector has read one, so
   Runtime-side retention SHOULD be age-based and generous.

   *Deletion interacts with req_id monotonicity.* A Connector exercising
   its deletion rights in processed/ or results/ removes exactly the
   state from which the next req_id is derived, and MUST preserve
   monotonicity by other durable means.  Symmetrically, a Runtime MUST
   NOT treat processed/ as durable state — for deduplication, for
   instance — because the Connector may delete there.  The Runtime's own
   record of what it sent belongs outside this protocol entirely.

14.14.  What is wire-verifiable, and what is a Runtime obligation

   A green conformance run proves that documents have the right shape.
   It proves nothing about a filesystem.  The following are Runtime or
   Connector obligations that no document validator can observe, and a
   reviewer assessing an implementation must check them another way
   (Appendix J lists them too):





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 87]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  Sidecar file existence, and the binding between an ordinal and a
      directory entry on disk.

   *  Whether size_bytes and sha256 match the bytes actually on disk.

   *  Display sanitization of filename, and its never-a-path invariant.

   *  The keying of inbound Sidecar directories on the Runtime-minted
      notice identifier.

   *  The location of Runtime-private Staging, outside the mounted
      Volume.

   *  Write ordering and commit-sentinel atomicity.

   *  Caps, allowlists, and quotas.

   *  The absence of a spooled body for a quarantined or blocked
      message.

   *  A Connector's tolerance of a read-only inbound tree.

   *  Ingest by copy.

   *  Write-side path discipline, in all three of its conjunctive legs.

   *  Read-side open discipline.

   *  Single writer and single drainer per Namespace.

   *  Compose-time rejection or stripping of CR, LF, and NUL.

   Two of these deserve emphasis as trust-model statements rather than
   as testing notes.  First, disposition == "clean" is the _Runtime's
   assertion_, and this document deliberately does not specify the basis
   for it; a consumer that treats clean as a proof rather than as an
   assertion has misread the trust model.  Second, this protocol cannot
   make a Runtime trustworthy — it can only ensure that everything the
   Agent contributes is inert until a Runtime acts on it, and that
   whatever the Runtime asserts is legible and attributable to the
   Runtime.










Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 88]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


14.15.  The extension space, and outcomes as claims

   outbound/ext/<name>/ (Section 4.1) is Connector-owned and Agent-
   writable, and this document specifies no shape for anything under it.
   Its <name> is a stable, opaque Connector id (Section 4.1), so a
   Runtime's out-of-band agreement with a Connector survives that
   Connector's repository being renamed.  Nothing security-relevant may
   be built on it.  Its first use, a per-Notice outcome file, is written
   by the receiving Agent's own uid and is therefore forgeable by
   construction: a receiving Agent can claim a delivery that did not
   happen, deny one that did, or suppress a refusal.  An outcome is a
   statement by the receiving side about what it did with a Notice; a
   party MUST NOT treat an outcome as proof of delivery or of non-
   delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over
   it.  A Runtime that reads outcomes may let them change what a sender
   is told or what an operator sees; it MUST NOT let them change what
   its own record says happened.  There is deliberately no inbound
   extension space, because an inbound tree is a Runtime assertion about
   origin (Section 7.1) and a Connector cannot know what a vendor-named
   assertion means.

14.16.  Special-use domain names

   Deployments commonly give Agents addresses under names that are not
   part of the public DNS: special-use domain names listed in the
   registry established by [RFC6761] (such as .test, .local, .home.arpa
   and .onion), and names reserved for private use, such as .internal.
   A Runtime MUST NOT hand mail addressed to such a name to a mail
   system outside the deployment, whatever its recipient policy allows:
   doing so leaks fleet-internal addresses, and the mail they carry,
   onto the public Internet.  A deployment's own mail system that is
   authoritative for such a name may carry it, and then MUST NOT relay
   it onward.

14.17.  The Peer-Origin Profile

   The profile adds a tree that a consumer may treat as authenticated
   origin, so its security rests on who can write that tree and on what
   a verifying Runtime accepts from another host.

   *Forgery of the peer tree.* A component that parses mail from an open
   transport is the most exposed component in a Runtime.  If it could
   write peer/, any sender able to reach it could forge authenticated
   peer origin.  The write-authority partition and the placement of
   verification (Section 12.3) exist to prevent that, and are checked by
   a write probe rather than by configuration review.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 89]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Key compromise.* A Runtime's signing key speaks for every Agent in
   that Runtime's domains.  An attacker holding it can place peer
   messages, as any of those Agents, at every Runtime that configures
   the key, until the key is revoked; the key-domain check
   (Section 12.6.3) confines the damage to the compromised Runtime's own
   domains.  Keeping the key out of every Agent Namespace and out of the
   admitting component, using it for nothing else, and supporting
   rotation (Section 12.6.7) are the mitigations.  Because replay
   records are scoped to the Runtime rather than the key, rotation does
   not reopen a replay window.

   *Replay and clocks.* A statement is a bearer of authenticated origin
   for as long as it is fresh.  The replay store, the high-water clock H
   and the recovery floor (Section 12.6.5) bound how long that is,
   including across a clock that steps backwards and a store that is
   lost.  The profile does not promise exactly-once delivery, and says
   so; a deployment that needs it beyond the retention period has to
   forbid re-signing.

   *Parsing hostile input.* The verifier reads data an attacker chose.
   It verifies the signature over the exact bytes received before
   parsing anything, defines no canonicalization (so there is no second
   parse to disagree with the first), refuses duplicate JSON member
   names, and receives the message already reduced to a candidate
   (Section 12.6.2), so that it never parses MIME itself.  Oversize and
   invalid fields are carried as markers so that a malformed second
   field cannot be silently removed.

   *Backscatter and loops.* A Control Notice is sent only after the
   statement has been authenticated, only to the configured Runtime
   address of the key's owner, never about another Control Notice, and
   at most once per record (Section 12.6.8).  An unauthenticated message
   therefore cannot direct a Runtime to send mail to a third party, and
   two Runtimes cannot be made to answer each other indefinitely.

   *Authenticated is not trustworthy.* A verified peer is a same-
   principal Agent, which may itself have read hostile external mail and
   be relaying it.  The tree authenticates _who_, never _what_
   (Section 12.8). sender_exposure (Section 12.7) lets a Runtime say
   whether the sender was exposed to external mail, and absence of the
   stamp means that nothing was assessed.

   *Exposure in transit.* Between hosts, the statement travels in a
   header field.  Its subject, addresses and attachment names are
   encoded rather than encrypted, and are visible to every mail system
   on the path, as the rest of the message is.  The profile provides
   integrity and origin, not confidentiality; a deployment that needs
   confidentiality between hosts has to obtain it from the transport.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 90]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


15.  IANA Considerations

15.1.  Message Header Fields

   The peer-origin profile (Section 12) defines two header fields
   carried in mail between Runtimes.  IANA is requested to register them
   in the "Provisional Message Header Field Names" registry, following
   the procedure of [RFC3864]:

    +=====================+==========+=============+==================+
    | Header Field Name   | Protocol | Status      | Reference        |
    +=====================+==========+=============+==================+
    | AMAP-Peer-Statement | mail     | provisional | Section 12.6.2   |
    |                     |          |             | of this document |
    +---------------------+----------+-------------+------------------+
    | AMAP-Peer-Control   | mail     | provisional | Section 12.6.8   |
    |                     |          |             | of this document |
    +---------------------+----------+-------------+------------------+

                    Table 6: Header field registrations

   Change controller: IETF.

15.2.  Possible Future Registries

   This document creates no registry.  Several of its values are
   candidates for one, and the authors would welcome the community's
   view on whether IANA should govern them: the values of
   contract_version (Section 13.1), whose fail-closed semantics make an
   unambiguous assignment important; the open reason_code vocabulary of
   the Result (Section 6.1); and the closed outcome and cause
   vocabularies of the Control Notice (Section 12.6.8).

Appendix A.  Submit-Request Schema

   _(Normative.)_ The schema below is written in the JSON Schema 2020-12
   dialect [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12] and governs the artifact defined in
   Section 5.  This is the Agent-authored artifact, and its envelope is
   closed at every level: an unrecognized member is a hard rejection,
   surfaced as a rejected Result rather than as a silent drop
   (Section 13.1).

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
     "$id": "https://amap-spec/schemas/submit-request.schema.json",
     "title": "submit-request",
     "description": "agent -> runtime: an inert outbound request. AMMP\
       , section \"Outbound: Submit Request\". Agent-authored: this doc\
       ument's envelope stays CLOSED (additionalProperties:false) at ev\
       ery level per the asymmetry of section \"Versioning\" — an unrec\
       ognized member here is a designed, legible `rejected` refusal, n\
       ever a silent drop.",
     "type": "object",
     "required": ["contract_version", "req_id", "draft"],
     "additionalProperties": false,
     "properties": {
       "contract_version": { "const": "2" },
       "req_id": {
         "type": "string",
         "minLength": 1,
         "description": "monotonic per namespace; filename-safe (path a\
       uthority is the filename, not this field — the filename-authorit\
       y-for-paths obligation of section \"Obligations\").",
         "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*(?!\\n)$"
       },
       "agent_id": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "pattern": "^[^\\



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027                [Page 94]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


       u0000-\u001f\u007f]*(?!\\n)$" },
       "ts": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "pattern": "^[^\u0000-\
       \u001f\u007f]*(?!\\n)$" },
       "in_reply_to": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[^\u0000-\u001f\\
       u007f]*(?!\\n)$" },
       "draft": {
         "type": "object",

Appendix B.  Result Schema

   _(Normative.)_ JSON Schema 2020-12 [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12]; governs the
   artifact defined in Section 6.  Runtime-authored, and therefore open
   at every level: a consumer tolerates unrecognized members
   (Section 13.1).  The attachments[i].index == i binding stated in
   Section 6.1 is not expressible here and is enforced as a named post-
   check by the conformance gate (Appendix J).

Appendix F.  Peer-Origin Profile Schemas

   _(Normative.)_ JSON Schema 2020-12 [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12].  The first
   schema governs a Peer Notice, the artifact the peer-origin profile
   (Section 12) places under <agent-id>/peer/notices/ (Section 12.2).
   Its envelope is Runtime-authored and therefore open (Section 13.1).
   A document with kind: "peer" found under inbound/notices/ fails the
   deliver-notice schema (Appendix C), and a document with kind:
   "deliver" found under peer/notices/ fails this one; both are dropped
   under the rule of Section 7.1.

                 Figure 15: schemas/peer-notice.schema.json

   Between hosts, a peer message travels as mail carrying a signed Peer
   Statement in one AMAP-Peer-Statement header field (Section 12.6).
   The receiving Runtime verifies the statement's bytes before parsing
   them, then validates them against the schema below, which is closed
   at every level: these are signed bytes another Runtime acts on, not a
   Runtime-authored document a Connector reads.  The statement-*
   fixtures (Appendix J) exercise the schema, and the signed cases
   exercise the verification rules.

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
     "$id": "https://amap-spec/schemas/peer-statement.schema.json",
     "title": "peer-statement",
     "description": "runtime -> runtime: the signed statement that carr\
       ies a peer message between hosts. AMMP, section \"Peer Traffic B\
       etween Hosts\". The sending runtime signs the statement's exact \
       UTF-8 bytes with Ed25519 and ships both in one AMAP-Peer-Stateme\
       nt header field (section \"Carriage, and the Candidate the Verif\
       ier Sees\"); the receiving runtime verifies the signature over t\
       he received bytes before parsing, then validates against this sc\
       hema. CLOSED at every level, unlike the runtime-authored notices\
       : these are signed bytes another runtime acts on, a member the r\
       eceiver does not know is a member it cannot bind to what it publ\
       ishes, and the version member `v` is the only evolution path. A \



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 105]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


       statement that fails this schema fails verification, and the mes\
       sage is demoted to mail (sections \"Verification\" and \"Outcome\
       s\"). Numbers are lexical integers (no fraction or exponent) an\
       d strings contain no unpaired surrogate (section \"The Statement\
       \", checked at check 5(b) of section \"Verification\"); the sche\
       ma cannot express either, nor calendar validity, interval order\
       , the entropy of `id`, or any binding to the message: those are \
       the verification steps of section \"Verification\".",
     "type": "object",
     "additionalProperties": false,
     "required": [
       "v",
       "key_id",
       "kind",
       "id",
       "from",
       "to",
       "ts",
       "subject",
       "body_sha256",
       "attachments"
     ],
     "properties": {
       "v": {
         "type": "integer",
         "const": 1
       },
       "key_id": {
         "type": "string",
         "description": "names one key in the signing peer's configure\
       d key set; opaque, unique within that set, 1-64 characters.",
         "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}(?!\\n)$"
       },
       "kind": {
         "const": "peer"
       },
       "id": {
         "type": "string",
         "minLength": 1,
         "description": "the peer message id (section \"Correlation an\
       d Replies\"), bare. A sending runtime mints it under ^[A-Za-z0-9\
       _][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$ (hex, or base64url re-minted if it would star\
       t with '-'): the notice_id charset without '.', so its Message-I\

               Figure 16: schemas/peer-statement.schema.json

   A receiving Runtime reports what it did with a statement it did not
   place (refused, dropped or demoted) to the configured sending Runtime
   in a signed Control Notice, carried in one AMAP-Peer-Control header
   field with the same grammar and key (Section 12.6.8).  Its kind is
   "control", so neither document validates as the other; it is closed
   and carries no free text.

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

       e k/s/b grammar as AMAP-Peer-Statement, signed with the same per\
       -runtime key; `kind` is \"control\", so a control notice never v\
       alidates as a peer statement and is never placed for an agent. C\

       ailure notice of section \"Correlation and Replies\"). The schem\

Appendix G.  Peer-Directory Schema

   _(Normative.)_ JSON Schema 2020-12 [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12]; governs the
   optional peer directory defined in Section 10, which a Runtime MAY
   publish at <agent-id>/directory.json.  The document is Runtime-
   authored and therefore open (Section 13.1), and it is advisory: the
   schema pins its shape, never what it predicts.

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
     "$id": "https://amap-spec/schemas/directory.schema.json",
     "title": "directory",
     "description": "runtime -> connector: the router's most recent wor\
       d about which peers this agent may address, published per instan\
       ce at <agent-id>/directory.json. AMMP, section \"The Peer Direct\
       ory\". ADVISORY, NEVER AUTHORITATIVE: an address's presence is n\
       ot a prediction that a submit to it will be accepted, nor its ab\
       sence a prediction of refusal — authorisation is evaluated by th\
       e runtime at submit time and only the result (section \"Outbound\
       : Result\") reports what happened. A runtime MUST NOT read this \
       file back as authorisation; enforcement stays the runtime's own \
       graph check on every message. The file MAY be absent. Runtime-au\
       thored: envelope is OPEN at every level per the tolerance rule o\
       f section \"Versioning\" — a consumer MUST ignore members it doe\
       s not recognize; emitting an unrecognized member remains produce\
       r non-conformance.",
     "type": "object",
     "required": [
       "router",
       "written_at",
       "delegate_to",
       "mail_to"
     ],
     "properties": {
       "contract_version": {



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 115]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


         "const": "2"
       },
       "router": {
         "type": "string",
         "description": "the publishing runtime's own address, one bar\
       e addr-spec. Never appears in delegate_to or mail_to.",
         "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+(?\
       !\\n)$"
       },
       "written_at": {
         "type": "string",
         "minLength": 1,
         "description": "RFC 3339, the publishing runtime's clock. The \
       only staleness signal a consumer gets; an honest marker, not a f\
       reshness guarantee.",
         "pattern": "^[^\\u0000-\\u001f\\u007f]*(?!\\n)$"
       },
       "delegate_to": {
         "type": "array",
         "description": "sorted addresses this agent may task — the aut\
       horisation graph transposed for this instance. Always present; e\
       mpty when the lane is closed. Never this agent's own address, an\
       d never who may task THIS agent (an allowlist, withheld by const\
       ruction).",
         "items": {
           "type": "string",
           "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\
       (?!\\n)$"
         }
       },
       "mail_to": {
         "type": "array",
         "description": "sorted addresses on the mutual mail lane. Alwa\
       ys present; empty when the lane is closed, which is the normal c\
       ase for a delegation-only deployment.",
         "items": {
           "type": "string",
           "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\
       (?!\\n)$"
         }
       }
     }
   }

Appendix H.  Fleet-Roster Schema

   _(Normative.)_ JSON Schema 2020-12; governs the fleet roster defined
   in Section 11.  The document is Runtime-authored and therefore open
   (Section 13.1), and it pins shape only: whether a member exists says
   nothing about whether it may be addressed.

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
     "$id": "https://amap-spec/schemas/roster.schema.json",
     "title": "roster",
     "description": "runtime -> every agent: the fleet roster, the runt\
       ime's most recent word about which instances it has admitted, wr\
       itten once for the whole fleet to a location the deployment desi\
       gnates and exposes read-only to each agent it points at the rost\
       er. AMMP, section \"The Fleet Roster\". EXISTENCE IS NOT AUTHORI\
       SATION: a member's presence says the instance exists, never tha\
       t this agent may address it or that a submission to it will be a\
       ccepted; authorisation is evaluated by the runtime at submit tim\
       e and only the result reports what happened. NOT A SOURCE OF TH\
       E READER'S IDENTITY: the reader's own address may appear, and at\
       tribution stays the namespace a file arrived in. A runtime MUST \
       NOT read this file back. The file MAY be absent; absent or stal\
       e means unknown, never an empty fleet. Runtime-authored: envelop\
       e is OPEN at every level — a consumer MUST ignore members it doe\
       s not recognize; emitting an unrecognized member remains produce\
       r non-conformance.",
     "type": "object",
     "required": [
       "contract_version",
       "router",
       "written_at",
       "members"
     ],
     "properties": {
       "contract_version": {
         "const": "2"
       },
       "router": {
         "type": "string",
         "description": "the publishing runtime's own address, one bar\
       e addr-spec. Never appears in members.",
         "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+(?\
       !\\n)$"
       },
       "written_at": {

         "type": "string",
         "minLength": 1,
         "description": "RFC 3339, the publishing runtime's clock. The \
       only staleness signal a consumer gets; an honest marker, not a f\

         "pattern": "^[^\\u0000-\\u001f\\u007f]*(?!\\n)$"

Appendix I.  Golden Examples

   _(Normative.)_ The documents below are reproduced byte-verbatim from
   the conformance suite (Appendix J).  They are a small selection
   covering the core artifact types and three rejections; the suite
   itself is the authority.  One further example — a Binding Record — is
   shown inline at Section 9 instead of being repeated here.

I.1.  Valid Submit Request with attachments

   Sidecar blobs are named by array index (req-<id>.attachments/<i>); no
   content_ref may appear on a request and the schema rejects one
   (Section 5.1).

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "req_id": "00000010",
     "agent_id": "agent.research",
     "ts": "2026-07-21T04:10:00Z",
     "draft": {
       "to": ["owner@example.com"],
       "subject": "Report attached",
       "body_text": "See the attached report and notes.",
       "attachments": [
         { "filename": "report.pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf",
           "size_bytes": 48213,
           "sha256": "970e441b6c4ecd37abf2541e1276c680bdec8481cef9368ff\
       1d010fd6b784b07" },
         { "filename": "notes.txt", "media_type": "text/plain",
           "size_bytes": 128,
           "sha256": "087d07499f2c097ac5396af7a0f1ef5e7a977fa91c631ebd1\
       5eb61bb23ef20aa" }
       ]
     }
   }

             Figure 20: fixtures/valid/request-attachments.json

I.2.  Valid Deliver Notice with a clean attachment Descriptor

   content_ref's prefix equals the enclosing document's own notice_id
   and its trailing index equals the Descriptor's own array position
   (Section 7.2); a Connector that relays the Notice without ever
   dereferencing the reference is fully conformant.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 119]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "notice_id": "1721457600000000003-4242",
     "ts": "2026-07-21T04:06:00Z",
     "kind": "deliver",
     "message": {
       "id": "45",
       "from": "colleague@example.com",
       "subject": "Clean attachment (deferred-release wire shape)",
       "preview": "byte-access forward-valid example",
       "mailbox": "inbox",
       "attachments": [
         { "filename": "photo.jpg", "media_type": "image/jpeg",
           "size_bytes": 204800,
           "sha256": "04c22051bc3f76bc44b952d9fdd3e59214662e7b3fd8a84b8\
       9de09352aeb2264",
           "disposition": "clean",
           "content_ref": "1721457600000000003-4242.attachments/0" }
       ]
     }
   }

         Figure 21: fixtures/valid/notice-attachment-clean-ref.json

I.3.  Valid Inbound Message

   The body spool for a delivered message is keyed on the Runtime-minted
   notice_id, never on the provider message.id (Section 7.3).

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "notice_id": "1721457600000000000-4242",
     "id": "42",
     "date": "Mon, 20 Jul 2026 04:00:00 +0000",
     "from": "Alex Doe <owner@example.com>",
     "to": "agent@example.org",
     "subject": "status?",
     "body_text": "hey, how's the run going",
     "attachments": [
       { "filename": "report.pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf",
         "size_bytes": 48213, "disposition": "unscanned" }
     ]
   }

                Figure 22: fixtures/valid/message-clean.json




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 120]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


I.4.  Valid Result — a policy hold with per-attachment diagnostics

   attachments[i].index == i on a Result, contiguous and unique over
   0..n-1; per-attachment entries are diagnostic detail under one
   governing top-level outcome and do not license a partial send
   (Section 6.1).

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   {
     "contract_version": "2",
     "req_id": "00000010",
     "outcome": "queued_for_human",
     "detail": "no outbound screener wired; attachments fail-closed to \
       human review",
     "recipients": ["owner@example.com"],
     "message_id": null,
     "job_id": null,
     "attachments": [
       { "index": 0, "outcome": "dlp_held", "detail": "no verdict sourc\
       e" },
       { "index": 1, "outcome": "dlp_held", "detail": "no verdict sourc\
       e" }
     ]
   }

           Figure 23: fixtures/valid/result-attachments-held.json

I.5.  Invalid Deliver Notice — a content_ref that fails the binding

   The drop rule of Section 7.1 is two independent checks: this document
   is schema-valid and is caught only by the content_ref post-check
   (Section 7.2, Section 13.3).

   content_ref names a different notice's Sidecar directory and a non-
   matching index — it is neither <notice_id>.attachments/0 for its own
   array position 0, nor prefixed by this document's own notice_id.
   Schema validation alone reports zero errors; only the content_ref
   index/prefix post-check catches it.

   The conformance gate's own errors for this document:

   $.attachments[0].content_ref: 'OTHER-NOTICE.attachments/7' !=
     'n-index-mismatch.attachments/0'

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   {
     "contract_version": "2",

I.6.  Valid Deliver Notice carrying an unrecognized member

   The Runtime-authored envelope is OPEN: a consumer MUST ignore a
   member it does not recognize, at every level (Section 13.1).

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   { "contract_version": "2", "notice_id": "x", "ts": "t", "kind": "del\
       iver", "x_injected": "surprise",
     "message": { "id": "1", "from": "a@b", "subject": "s", "preview": \
       "p", "mailbox": "inbox",
                  "x_message_injected": "also surprise" } }

            Figure 25: fixtures/valid/notice-unknown-member.json

I.7.  Invalid Submit Request carrying an unrecognized member

   The Agent-authored envelope stays CLOSED at every level: an
   unrecognized member is a designed, legible rejected refusal, never a
   silent drop (Section 13.1).

   additionalProperties: false at the top level of the submit-request
   schema rejects any member this document does not define.

   The conformance gate's own errors for this document:

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   $: additional property 'x_injected' not allowed

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   { "contract_version": "2", "req_id": "00000021", "x_injected": "surp\
       rise",
     "draft": { "to": ["a@b"], "subject": "s", "body_text": "b" } }

            Figure 26: fixtures/invalid/request-extra-field.json

I.8.  Invalid Peer Notice — a deliver-kind document under the peer tree

   Origin class comes from the tree a notice arrived in, never from a
   self-declared field: a kind: "deliver" document found under peer/
   notices/ fails the peer-notice schema, the profile's cross-lock
   (Section 12.2).

   kind is const "peer" in the peer-notice schema; a document carrying
   "deliver" fails that const check.

   The conformance gate's own errors for this document:

   $.kind: 'deliver' != const 'peer'

   NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792

   { "contract_version": "2", "notice_id": "9f1c2b7e4d3a4f60b8e2c1d5a7f\
       39e04", "ts": "t", "kind": "deliver",
     "message": { "id": "9f1c2b7e4d3a4f60b8e2c1d5a7f39e04", "from": "pl\
       anner@fleet.example", "subject": "s", "preview": "p", "mailbox"\
       : "peer" } }

             Figure 27: fixtures/invalid/peer-kind-deliver.json

Appendix J.  Conformance Suite

   _(Normative for the classes of Section 13.3; the honesty statement
   below is part of the specification.)_

   The suite consists of golden artifacts under fixtures/valid/ and
   fixtures/invalid/, plus a validator, fixtures/validate.py.

   The suite contains *121 fixtures — 42 valid and 79 invalid*.
