   *Running it.* The validator is stdlib-only and takes no arguments:

   python3 fixtures/validate.py

   It exits 0 if and only if every fixture under valid/ passes and every
   fixture under invalid/ fails.  It requires no counterpart, no
   network, and no dependency: *the fixtures are the other side.*

   *Signed cases for the peer-origin profile.* The validator then runs
   fixtures/peer-signed/check_cases.py, which checks three further sets,
   all of which a Runtime + peer-origin implementation that verifies
   peer traffic from other hosts MUST pass (Section 13.3):

   *  rfc8032-vectors.json: the test vectors of Section 7.1 of [RFC8032]
      (TEST 1 to 3), and negative vectors for the verification policy of
      Section 12.6.7, each marked for rejection either at verification
      or at configuration, which are two separate gates;

   *  mime/: 10 raw messages, and the candidate the selection rule of
      Section 12.6.2 makes of each, reduced by a byte-exact splitter;

   *  cases/: 114 sequences of candidates and events (a crash at each
      point of Section 12.6.5, recovery, loss of the store with and
      without H, an operator bound, clock and window changes, and edge
      and key changes), each step with the outcome, cause, published
      members and Control Notice that the receiver configured in
      receiver.json or receiver-host-a.json MUST reach.  Single-step
      cases break exactly one rule; multi- cases pin the precedence of
      Section 12.6.3; seq- cases pin state across steps; config- cases
      are configurations a receiver MUST refuse to load.  The receiver



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 131]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      files set retention to its minimum, P, and the cases that probe
      the retention boundary assume it; a receiver that retains records
      longer, as Section 12.6.5 permits, maps those steps by its own
      retention.

   check_cases.py models only the state that Section 12.6.5 makes
   normative.  It is a self-check of the fixtures, not a Runtime, and
   its Ed25519 implementation, which is slow and not constant-time,
   exists for the gate alone.

   *How a fixture is mapped to a schema.* By filename prefix — request-
   to the submit-request schema, notice- to deliver-notice, result- to
   result, message- to inbound-message, identity- to binding-record, and
   peer- to peer-notice, statement- to peer-statement, control- to peer-
   control (Appendix F), directory- to peer-directory (Appendix G) and
   roster- to roster (Appendix H).

   *What the validator checks.* Schema validation in the JSON Schema
   2020-12 dialect [JSON-SCHEMA-2020-12], over the subset of keywords
   these schemas use (type, const, enum, minLength, pattern, minItems,
   minimum, items, required, properties, additionalProperties, allOf,
   and a single if/then pair) — plus two *named post-checks*, neither
   expressible in standard JSON Schema:

   *  the Result-side binding attachments[i].index == i, contiguous and
      unique over 0 through n-1 (Section 6.1);

   *  the content_ref index and prefix binding on Notice, Inbound
      Message, and peer-notice documents: every Descriptor carrying
      content_ref must equal <notice_id>.attachments/<i> for its own
      array position i, binding both the trailing index and the leading
      prefix (Section 7.2).

   A Connector conformance claim requires running *both* the schema
   validation and the second post-check, because exactly one invalid
   notice-* fixture — and its peer-* counterpart — is schema-valid on
   its own and is caught only by that post-check (Appendix I,
   Section 13.3).













Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 132]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *A note on pattern anchoring, and a portability cost.* Every schema
   pattern in this suite that ends in $ is written as (?!\n)$. The
   reason is that a bare $ matches before a single trailing newline in
   several widely used regex engines — Python's re, Java, and .NET among
   them — unlike the ECMA-262 dialect JSON Schema specifies.  Since
   every one of these patterns exists to forbid exactly the control
   characters a permissive $ would let through at the end of a string,
   the lookahead closes that gap in the schemas themselves rather than
   in any one validator.  Seven fixtures pin the trailing-newline case
   specifically, distinct from the CRLF fixtures, which embed \r\n and
   were already rejected even under a permissive engine.

   The cost is disclosed rather than discovered: *lookahead-less engines
   cannot compile these patterns at all.* RE2 (Go's regexp), Rust's
   regex crate, and POSIX ERE reject (?! outright, so the eight schemas
   carrying the guard (every schema except result and binding-record)
   fail to load rather than validating loosely.  Those engines already
   treat $ as strict end-of-string and never had the gap, so an
   implementer on one of them should strip the lookahead — not add a
   check outside the pattern, which would be both unnecessary and not
   what breaks.  The failure is loud (a compile error, never silent
   acceptance).

   *What a green run proves.* That every document shape this protocol
   defines is accepted or rejected as specified, by an implementation's
   own parser, with no counterpart present.

   *What a green run does NOT prove.* The following are filesystem and
   policy invariants that no document validator can observe.  They are
   obligations of the conformance classes regardless (Section 13.3), and
   are checked operationally:

   *  Sidecar file existence — an extra file, a missing file, or a
      directory present when the Descriptor array is empty or absent.

   *  size_bytes and sha256 actually matching the bytes on disk.

   *  filename display-sanitization, and the "never a path" invariant.

   *  The binding between an ordinal and a directory entry on disk.  The
      schema checks only the _Descriptor_ array's own index member, not
      that directory entry N exists.

   *  Inbound Sidecar directories keyed on the Runtime-minted notice
      identifier rather than the provider message.id.

   *  The location of Runtime-private Staging, outside the mounted
      Volume.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 133]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  Write ordering and commit-sentinel atomicity — Sidecars before
      req-<id>.json; .tmp plus rename.

   *  Caps and allowlists — type allowlists, size caps, Volume quotas.

   *  The absence of a spooled body for a quarantined or blocked message
      (enforcement by absence, Section 7.3).

   *  A Connector's tolerance of a read-only inbound/ tree.  The
      prescribed check is operational, not a fixture: run the Connector
      against an inbound tree it cannot write and confirm that it
      starts, relays every pending Notice, resolves bodies, and submits
      outbound requests, without requiring any inbound write to succeed
      (Section 13.3).

   *  Ingest by copy — validation, policy evaluation, and composition
      running over a Runtime-private snapshot taken before any of those
      steps, rather than re-reading an Agent-writable path
      (Section 4.1).

   *  Write-side path discipline, all three conjunctive legs: full
      parent-chain resolution through pinned directory descriptors from
      the Namespace root; each directory component opened
      O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY at the moment it is added to that chain;
      and the final component created O_EXCL and never followed, failing
      closed on EEXIST and ELOOP.  Any one leg alone is a known-
      insufficient partial mitigation (Section 4.1).

   *  Read-side open discipline — per-component no-symlink-follow opens,
      non-blocking opens, fstat-based regular-file verification through
      the open descriptor, and bounded reads and caps on every Agent-
      influenced path (Section 4.1).

   *  Single writer and single drainer per Namespace — an operational
      and deployment invariant, such as an OS-level lock held for the
      process lifetime (Section 4.1).

   *  Compose-time header-boundary stripping: even where the schemas'
      control-character patterns are bypassed upstream, the Runtime
      rejects or strips CR, LF, and NUL before composing the outbound
      message (Section 5.1).

   *  The peer-origin profile's operational obligations (Section 12),
      none of them visible to a document validator: the write-authority
      partition — no component that admits messages from a transport not
      restricted to authorised peer senders holds write authority over
      peer/, and the prescribed check is a write attempt from inside the
      admitting component that must fail; intake isolation for shared-



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 134]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      transport peer candidates, in a location that is neither inbound/
      nor peer/ and unreachable from any Agent Namespace; verification
      placement in a component holding peer write authority that hashes
      body and attachment bytes itself; sender_exposure never sender-
      settable; a Peer Notice carrying in_reply_to only when the placing
      Runtime resolved it from its own record, an unresolvable key being
      refused rather than stripped; and at-most-once action by the
      Connector, with an ambiguous target held rather than fanned out.
      Also invisible to the gate: the durability of the replay store, of
      H, of each record's disposition and of pending Control Notices
      across restarts; the closing of admission when H is lost; and the
      protection of the signing key (Section 12.6).

   Beyond these, the behavioral obligations of Sections 7 and 8 — the
   untrusted-content posture, the treatment of task_id as correlation
   rather than authorization, and the requirement that verified sender
   identity never be taken from a mail message.from — sit outside the
   fixture gate entirely.  They constrain what an implementation _does_
   with a valid document, which no document-level gate can see.

Appendix K.  A Deferred Seam-Visible "Handled" Signal (Non-Normative)

   *This appendix is non-normative and is not in force at this document
   version.* It records the reasoning behind a gap deliberately left
   open, not an addition to the protocol.  Nothing below is a directory,
   a member, or an artifact that a conforming implementation can rely
   on, and no requirement keyword appears anywhere in it.

   *The gap.* Making inbound consumption-tracking Connector-private
   (Section 4.1) closes the writability conflict but leaves a knowledge
   and capability split unbridged: only the Connector knows that a
   Notice has been relayed to its Agent, while on a read-only inbound
   tree only the Runtime can delete anything.  Neither side alone can
   turn "consumed" into "reclaimed."

   *A sketch, not a specification.* One shape that would bridge it is a
   Connector-written, zero-byte marker per acknowledged Notice, written
   into outbound/, where the Connector already has write access in every
   posture:

   outbound/acks/notice-<id>   # sketch only - not part of the protocol

             Figure 28: Sketch only — not part of this protocol

   A Runtime could then delete the acknowledged Notice and its spooled
   message, and finally the marker itself.  This is presented purely as
   a sketch: no directory and no wire member is introduced by this
   appendix.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 135]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *Why a Connector-forgeable signal would be acceptable here.* A
   garbage-collection signal is a resource decision rather than a
   security decision.  An Agent that falsely claims consumption loses
   only its own unread mail; one that never claims consumption only
   bloats its own inbox.  Neither crosses a trust boundary that matters,
   and neither touches any record of the exchange the Runtime keeps on
   its own side.  That is what distinguishes this case from every other
   "the Agent writes it, so it cannot be trusted" case in this document
   — but it is a distinction a future version would need to state
   explicitly rather than assume.

   *Why a high-water mark cannot substitute.* Section 8 requires task_id
   to be unguessable and never sequential, and nothing in this document
   orders notice identifiers, so no single "processed through N" cursor
   is expressible.  Any consumption signal has to be a _set_ of
   identifiers, or time-ordered — and time-ordering would require the
   consumer to process strictly in delivery order, which nothing today
   requires.

   *The lifecycle this would enable, and its boundaries.* A reliable "is
   this one done?" answer is the watermark a real retention lifecycle
   promotes against: cycling a working set, rolling handled traffic into
   period-compacted archives, then expiring or tiering to cold storage.
   Three boundaries would need to hold if this is ever specified.

   *  *The seam is not the record.* A Runtime that needs an exchange of
      record already keeps one outside this protocol, tamper-evident.
      Retention here is about an Agent's access to its own history, not
      about the durability of evidence; conflating the two produces an
      archive that satisfies neither.

   *  *An Agent-writable archive is never evidence.* A compacted archive
      living under outbound/, which is Agent-writable in every posture,
      can be rewritten by the Agent it belongs to.  Anything meant to be
      relied on has to be Runtime-written or kept outside this protocol
      entirely.

   *  *It must not grow the read surface.* The read available today is a
      point lookup from a notice identifier to a body.  "Search my
      archive" is a materially larger capability — decompression,
      indexing, query — for a deliberately dumb, credential-free relay
      to take on.  If archives are ever exposed to an Agent, that likely
      belongs behind a Runtime-served surface rather than the file-drop
      seam.

   *Why this is deferred rather than specified now.* A capability starts
   with a change to this document once a second implementation
   independently wants it, with members and fixtures proposed together.



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 136]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   Today exactly one reference Connector carries a private workaround
   for the underlying problem — a writability-probing fallback with
   three modes: move, ledger, and in-memory.  There is no second data
   point yet to generalize from, and specifying now would freeze one
   side's convention as the protocol's answer.

   *One honesty note for a future implementer.* The sketch's own
   garbage-collection step is not atomic: if a Runtime crashes between
   deleting the Notice artifacts and deleting the acknowledgment marker,
   the marker is orphaned, pointing at a Notice that no longer exists.
   Any real design needs idempotent collection, in which a missing
   target is not an error — recorded here so that it is not rediscovered
   from scratch.

Appendix L.  Historical Background

   This section is to be removed before publishing as an RFC.

   _(Informative.)_

   AMMP was specified and implemented before it was brought to the IETF.
   Its contract was versioned on its own scale, from 1.0.0 to 3.1.0,
   separately from the wire version that documents carry.  This appendix
   records that history, newest first, because implementations were
   built against each version, and because the reasons for several rules
   in this document are clearest as the story of what went wrong without
   them.  An entry that turned out to be wrong is left standing, with a
   correction attached, rather than quietly rewritten.

L.1.  draft-rapp-ammp-00 — brought to the IETF (contract 3.1.0)

   *  *One document.* The peer-origin profile's prose, previously a
      companion document in the repository, is now Section 12.  The
      contract's own version numbers no longer appear in the protocol
      sections: revisions of this document are draft revisions, and the
      wire version is contract_version (Section 13.1), which stays "2".
      The reasoning that explained earlier version changes moved into
      this appendix (Appendix L.2).













Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 137]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *The protocol is AMMP.* It was AMAP, the Agent Mailbox Access
      Protocol, and is renamed the Agent Mediated Messaging Protocol
      before its first submission: "mailbox access" named only its first
      channel, and the contract is a mediation seam for an Agent's
      correspondence, mail and peer traffic alike.  The abstract and the
      definitions of Agent and Runtime describe it that way, as a store-
      and-forward messaging runtime; email remains the only transport
      this document defines.  The acronym AMAP was also already in use
      by an expired 2003 individual draft.  Nothing on the wire changes:
      no document carries the protocol's name, and the header fields of
      Section 15.1 keep their names.

   *  *Editorial review for submission.* Terminology was alphabetized
      and Drop and Fail Closed became defined terms; requirements
      previously phrased as "never" are, where they are requirements,
      stated with [RFC2119] keywords; references to earlier revisions
      were removed from the protocol sections and the security
      considerations; the open questions the authors know of are listed
      in Section 1.6; and IANA considerations were added for the two
      header fields the profile defines.

   *  *The signed statement between hosts*, after reports from the first
      implementations of revision s5-r4, which now stands as the
      profile's text, without a revision label (an implementation names
      the draft revision it implements): the id grammar of the Peer
      Statement and Control Notice schemas is narrowed to ^[A-Za-
      z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$, the notice_id character set without "."
      (Section 12.6.1; see the correction to the 3.1.0 entry below); a
      point is decoded canonically before the small-order check
      (Section 12.6.7), and the gate's reference Ed25519 decoder was
      corrected to match, with two "negative zero" vectors added; the
      12288-octet limit is stated to apply to a field body as
      transmitted (Section 12.6.2); Fmax after the loss of H is taken
      from the retained history of F if provable, and is 900 otherwise
      (Section 12.6.5); and how a Runtime divides its intake is stated
      to be an implementation choice (Section 12.6.10).  Fixtures: two
      invalid statement fixtures (121 in all: 42 valid, 79 invalid);
      signed cases for a leading "-" and for the loss of the F history
      (114); and a MIME case for the size limit (10).

L.2.  How the versioning rules came about

   *The move from wire major "1" to "2".* When attachment support was
   added, every top-level schema and every nested object except verdict
   and attestation.claims was additionalProperties: false.  Under that
   regime, adding a member was not a safe additive change: a strict
   major-1 validator rejected the *whole document*, not just the new
   member.  Inbound, that was *silent total message loss* — an



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 138]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   attachment-bearing email vanished instead of degrading.  Outbound, it
   was an accidental schema error rather than a designed refusal.  And
   there was no signal to gate on while contract_version stayed "1".
   That is why attachments required a major change: a major-1 consumer
   receiving a "2" document failed closed _by version_, a legible and
   designed refusal, and both sides upgraded deliberately.

   *Two version axes.* From contract 3.0.0 the contract's own version
   and the wire major were allowed to diverge.  The wire major tracks
   whole-document acceptance compatibility; the contract version tracked
   the fuller set of obligations, including narrower, disclosed
   producer-side tightenings.  Contract 3.0.0 was a major contract
   change — it moved fixtures between the valid and invalid sets, and
   added Runtime obligations that a strictly compliant earlier
   implementation did not meet — while the wire major stayed "2".
   Neither of its two producer-side narrowings was the failure a wire
   major exists to prevent: the Submit Request tightening yields a per-
   request rejected Result, and the notice_id character-set tightening
   yields a per-Notice drop under check 1 of Section 7.1, a real cost,
   disclosed, but narrow and legible.  Changing the wire major to "3"
   would instead have forced every major-2 counterpart on both sides to
   refuse all traffic, including all the traffic the new tolerance rule
   protects.  Contract 3.1.0 was an additive minor change over 3.0.0,
   and the wire major stayed "2".

   *Corrections.* Two claims that shipped in earlier revisions of the
   contract's normative text were false, and were named rather than
   quietly replaced, because an implementer who read them may have built
   against them.

   1.  *The write-rule "strengthening" that was a regression.* An
       earlier revision described the exclusive-create and no-symlink-
       follow requirement on the final path component as having been
       "strengthened to" the pinned directory-descriptor walk — that is,
       replaced by it — and deleted the earlier clause outright.  That
       was a *weakening*: a parent chain pinned by descriptor is silent
       about the final .tmp filename itself, so dropping exclusive-
       create there let an Agent that pre-plants a symlink at a
       predictable .tmp name have the Runtime write through it.
       Section 4.1 states the rule conjunctively, with all three legs
       required together.

   2.  *The drop rule described as a closure over schema validation.* An
       earlier revision described the inbound drop rule as a pure
       closure over schema validation, and claimed that formulation was
       exact against the fixture set.  Both statements were false: the
       content_ref index and prefix binding is not expressible in the
       schema dialect used here, and a fixture exists that is schema-



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 139]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


       valid on its own and must nonetheless be dropped.  Section 7.1
       states two independent checks, and so does the Connector
       conformance class.

   A third correction concerns the change history itself: the contract
   version that introduced message.provenance was labelled an additive
   minor change, which was unsound against the strictly validating
   consumers of the time.  The 2.1.0 entry below records what actually
   happened.

   *Lessons from implementation.* Several rules in this document exist
   because an early implementation got them wrong: it trusted a req_id
   member inside a request body to name the path its Result was written
   to; it used the provider's message identifier as a path component; it
   minted guessable, sequential task_id values; and its schema coverage
   of control characters stopped at subject and filename, missing the
   two members composed directly into headers.  Each was a confirmed
   exploit path, and each is now a requirement (Section 4.1,
   Section 5.1, Section 8).

   *The peer-origin profile's presentation rule.* A prior revision of
   the profile said only that a Connector "MAY present peer bodies under
   the same untrusted-content framing it uses for mail".  That was a
   permission with no floor: it allowed the mail framing without saying
   what any framing had to preserve.  A Connector following it chose the
   cautious option, which on this lane is the wrong one, in the specific
   direction of telling an Agent not to act on work it was authorized to
   do.  Section 12.8 states what a presentation must and must not
   convey.

L.3.  3.1.0 — the protocol is AMAP; the outbound extension space; the
      peer-origin profile

   An additive *minor* bump; the wire major stays "2".  The entries
   below are as recorded at the time: the companion document they cite
   is now Section 12, and the items marked proposed were adopted in
   draft-rapp-ammp-00 (Appendix L.1).

   *  *The signed cross-host peer statement and control notice*
      (2026-10-09, proposed, not yet reviewed; companion-document
      section 5 revision s5-r4).  Two new schemas (Appendix F): the
      statement a sending Runtime signs with Ed25519 and carries in one
      AMAP-Peer-Statement header field, and the control notice a
      receiving Runtime returns about a statement it did not place, both
      CLOSED at every level; statement-* and control-* fixtures; and, in
      fixtures/peer-signed/, RFC 8032 vectors with negative cases, MIME
      selection cases, and signed sequences of candidates and events
      with the outcome a receiver MUST reach at each step.  The rules



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 140]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      are the companion document's (spec/peer-origin.md, section 5).
      Additive: nothing existing changes shape, and a deployment without
      cross-host peer traffic is unaffected.  The 30 new fixtures (8
      valid, 22 invalid) bring version 3.1.0 to 119 (42 valid, 77
      invalid).

      *Correction (draft-rapp-ammp-00).* The statement schema accepted
      an id or in_reply_to beginning with "-", which the notice_id
      character set forbids, so a receiver could verify a statement it
      could not then publish; one signed case minted such an id.  The
      grammar is narrowed (Appendix L.1), and the case was minted again.

   *  *The fleet roster* (2026-09-24).  A new, optional artifact
      (Section 11, schema in Appendix H): one Runtime-written file
      naming the instances the Runtime has admitted, so that an Agent on
      a deployment whose addresses carry an underivable suffix can learn
      which peers exist.  It answers existence, never authorisation, and
      states that separately from the Peer Directory.  Its readability
      obligation is split between the Runtime, which publishes only into
      a designated location and never creates it, and the deployment,
      which exposes that location.  Additive: a new schema and seven
      fixtures, and nothing existing changes shape.

   *  *The protocol is AMAP; the schema $id authority is amap-spec*
      (2026-09-15).  The protocol formerly called AMP ("Agent Mailbox
      Protocol") is renamed AMAP ("Agent Mailbox Access Protocol")
      because AMP collides with the IETF DTN working group's adopted
      draft-ietf-dtn-amp; the specification repository moves from agent-
      mailbox-protocol to amap-spec with it.  The six schema $id values
      move from https://agent-mailbox-protocol/schemas/… to
      https://amap-spec/schemas/…. Nothing on the wire changes shape: no
      document carries the protocol's name as a field, and $id is an
      identifier the gate never dereferences.  Implementations that
      mirror the Runtime's address spell its local part amap.router from
      this version.  This draft's filename is a separate decision and is
      unchanged here.  This version is marked DRAFT: its profile prose
      is a companion document (spec/peer-origin.md, itself DRAFT), and
      its schema and fixtures may still change before it is settled.

   *  *Outbound extension space.* outbound/ext/<name>/ is defined as a
      Connector-owned side channel a Runtime MAY read by out-of-band
      agreement, with no shape specified and nothing security-relevant
      permitted to depend on it (Section 4.1). <name> is pinned as a
      stable Connector id — chosen once, unchanged by any rename of the
      Connector's repository, package, or deployment, and opaque to the
      Runtime that reads it; the wording it replaced ("a Connector or
      deployment name") permitted a repository name to leak into a wire-
      visible path.  The reference Claude Code Connector chose claude-



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 141]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


      code as its id; ids are chosen by each Connector, and this
      document neither lists nor registers them.  One normative
      clarification sits beside it: an outcome written there is a claim
      by the receiving side, never proof of delivery or of non-delivery,
      and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it
      (Section 14.15).  There is deliberately no inbound extension
      space.

   *  *Peer-notice schema.* The peer-origin profile's artifact is pinned
      by peer-notice.schema.json (Appendix F): the deliver-notice layout
      with kind and mailbox fixed to peer, message.from a bare addr-
      spec, message identifiers in the notice-identifier character set,
      and the optional Runtime-asserted sender_exposure stamp with its
      required members.  The profile's prose is the companion document
      spec/peer-origin.md (v3.1.0 DRAFT).

   *  *The Peer Directory.* A Runtime may publish a per-instance
      projection of the authorisation graph, directory.json, at the
      Agent's Namespace root (Section 10, schema in Appendix G), so that
      a Connector can learn which peers it may address without the host
      rendering a snapshot onto an Agent-writable mount that goes stale
      whenever the fleet changes.  It is advisory and never
      authoritative, and a Runtime never reads it back as authorisation,
      which is what stops it decaying into an allowlist the Agent can
      see.  The Namespace root gains a Runtime-owned posture for
      Runtime-written files: the file sits beside the lanes rather than
      inside one, because it spans both.  Additive: a new optional
      artifact, a new schema and seven fixtures (4 valid, 3 invalid); no
      existing schema or fixture changes, and the wire contract_version
      stays "2".

      _Restored 2026-10-05._ This entry was in the versioning record
      this document was reconciled against and was lost in the
      reconciliation, along with its fixtures from the count below.

















Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 142]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Clarifications from implementation* (proposed, 2026-10-07).
      Questions from Runtime implementers reconciling against this
      document, each answered from the existing text and then stated: a
      Runtime knows the <agent-id> of every Namespace it serves and
      rejects a request from a Namespace it cannot name (Section 4.1);
      outbound/ext/<name>/'s id is a lowercase single path segment
      (Section 4.1); a Runtime may be built from several trusted
      components, and its obligations bind the composite (Section 3.5,
      informative); the Deletion rights table gains rows for outbound/
      ext/<name>/ and directory.json (Section 4.2); message.id is the
      mail store's identifier, not the Message-ID (Section 7); and a
      Runtime does not hand mail for special-use or private-use domain
      names to a mail system outside the deployment (Section 14.16).
      The companion peer-origin profile clarifies what a routable peer
      domain is.  No schema or fixture changes.

   *  *Fixtures: 75 total (27 valid, 48 invalid), up from 58.* 16 peer-*
      fixtures were added (6 valid, 10 invalid), covering a minimal
      notice, a reply, the exposure stamp asserted both ways, a clean
      attachment reference, an unknown-member case, and rejections for a
      deliver kind under the peer tree, a peer kind under the inbound
      tree, a display-name or CRLF from, encoded message identifiers, a
      missing asserted_by, a missing last-delivery timestamp when
      exposure is asserted true, an inbox mailbox, a content_ref index
      mismatch, and a trailing-newline identifier.  The validator maps
      the peer- prefix to the new schema and applies the content_ref
      post-check to it.  Three existing fixtures had example strings
      normalised to example.* identities (one free-text body, two
      addresses in injection examples); each stays valid or invalid for
      the same reason as before, and no schema changed.

      *Correction (2026-10-05).* The count above omits the seven
      directory-* fixtures (4 valid, 3 invalid) added with the Peer
      Directory.  With them and the fleet roster's seven, version 3.1.0
      has 89 fixtures (34 valid, 55 invalid).

      *Correction (draft-rapp-ammp-00).* The breakdown above does not
      sum: 58 + 16 is 74, and 37 + 10 is 47.  The record does not
      identify the seventeenth addition.  The totals from 89 onward are
      the ones verified against the suite as it ships (Appendix J).

L.4.  3.0.0 — direction-aware tolerance, and six closed safety holes

   A *major document bump*; the wire major stays "2".  Appendix L.2
   states why the two numbers diverge here, and why bumping the wire
   would have caused the exact harm this version exists to repair.





Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 143]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *Unknown-member tolerance, direction-aware.* The three Runtime-
      authored artifacts — deliver-notice, inbound-message, and result —
      became *open* at every level: additionalProperties: false was
      removed from the top level, from message, from Descriptor items,
      and from attestation, and a consumer must tolerate an unrecognized
      member.  Emitting one remains producer non-conformance.  The
      Agent-authored submit-request envelope stays *closed* at every
      level.  Consequence: adding an optional member to a Runtime-
      authored artifact is now genuinely additive; adding any member to
      the submit-request is a major change.

   *  *...and for values.* The enum constraint was removed from
      message.sender_standing and message.provenance, the two explicitly
      advisory vocabularies, and a consumer must tolerate an
      unrecognized value in either. kind, outcome (both levels), and
      disposition remain closed, enum-locked vocabularies.

   *  *Ingest by copy.* A Runtime must copy an Agent-authored request
      and its Sidecars into private staging before validating, must act
      only on that copy, and must not re-read an Agent-writable path
      after a decision depending on its content (Section 4.1).

   *  *Address syntax and header-injection discipline.* A new obligation
      in Section 5.1 plus schema patterns on draft.to/cc, draft.subject,
      attachment filename and media_type, draft.reply_to_message_id,
      in_reply_to, agent_id, and ts — including the two members composed
      directly into headers, which earlier schema coverage missed.

   *  *Path discipline, write- and read-side both.* The write-side rule
      became *conjunctive* (Section 4.1), and a new read-side rule
      applies the equivalent discipline to every Agent-influenceable
      read.  A notice_id character-set pattern was added to the deliver-
      notice and inbound-message schemas so that every legal notice_id
      is also a legal content_ref prefix. *Disclosed cost:* notice_id
      was previously unconstrained, so a Runtime minting identifiers
      outside the new character set — an ISO-8601 timestamp, standard
      base64, a URN, or anything else carrying punctuation outside it —
      now emits Notices and Inbound Messages that fail schema validation
      on a _pattern violation on a required member_, and a conforming
      Connector drops them. *Migration:* such a Runtime must re-mint
      identifiers under the new character set (unpadded base64url or
      lowercase hex, for instance) before any Connector it talks to
      upgrades, because the failure is otherwise silent on both sides.

   *  *Single writer, single drainer.* Section 4.1 now names the
      concurrency assumption that every atomicity, commit-sentinel, and
      req_id rule already depended on.




Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 144]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   *  *message.from named untrusted.* The untrusted-content sentence now
      covers explicitly the member most likely to be rendered to a human
      or used for a trust judgement (Section 7.1).

   *  *Document authority.* The contract, its schemas, and its fixtures
      were made normative; the rendering then generated from them was
      non-authoritative where they disagreed.  (This document is now the
      prose of record.)  The conformance-class text was moved into the
      contract itself so that the demotion deletes nothing, and a stray
      claim of a second, message-specific Sidecar directory was
      corrected to match the layout tree.

   *  *Corrections shipped with this version*, rather than a tidied
      history: (i) the write rule described in an earlier revision as
      "strengthened" had in fact been weakened — the exclusive-create
      requirement on the final component had been deleted rather than
      supplemented (Appendix L.2); (ii) the inbound drop rule described
      as a pure closure over schema validation was refuted by this
      version's own content_ref-binding fixture, and is now stated as
      two independent checks (Section 7.1, Section 13.3); (iii) the
      claim that this version's producer bytes are unchanged is
      explicitly _not_ made — two producer-side narrowings are disclosed
      above, each travelling a legible per-artifact refusal path; and
      (iv) the 2.1.0 entry below is corrected in place.

   *  *Fixtures: 58 total (21 valid, 37 invalid), up from 44.* The
      unknown-member notice fixture moved from the invalid set to the
      valid set and was extended with an unrecognized member inside
      message; valid unknown-member fixtures were added for result and
      inbound-message; the withheld-body invalid fixture was deleted,
      having become schema-valid under the relaxed envelope (its name
      always over-claimed what additionalProperties alone tested); the
      bad-provenance fixture moved to the valid set as an unrecognized-
      value case; an invalid extra-member submit-request fixture was
      added to pin the closed side of the asymmetry, previously untested
      at the top level; four invalid fixtures were added for the
      address-syntax and control-character rules; a traversal notice_id
      fixture was added; the content_ref index-mismatch fixture was
      added, and is the one invalid notice-* case that is schema-valid
      on its own; and six fixtures pin the trailing-newline anchoring
      case.

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


L.5.  2.3.0 — inbound byte access in force

   A *minor bump*, prose only: no schema rule and no fixture changed,
   and the wire major stayed "2".  It resolved an inconsistency carried
   since 2.0.0.  A fixture showing a clean Descriptor with content_ref
   and sha256 sat in the valid set as a deliberately forward-valid
   shape, while the prose forbade any Runtime from producing it — the
   gate blessed what the prose forbade.  This version sided with the
   fixtures: the release-scoped byte embargo was dropped, and the
   standing rule became the one stated in Section 7.2 — a Runtime may
   publish bytes and emit content_ref/sha256 only for a Descriptor it
   asserts clean, and a Runtime that cannot make that determination must
   not assert clean.  The substantive clarification is that disposition
   is the Runtime's _assertion_, its basis deliberately unspecified; the
   older prose presumed a scanner, which is what made byte access read
   as a deferred capability rather than as a policy decision whose wire
   shape major 2 already carried.  Nothing was tightened, and there is
   still no outbound content_ref.

L.6.  2.2.0 — deletion rights, read-only inbound

   A *permissive minor bump*: no wire member, no schema change, no
   fixture changed or added.  It (a) declared a read-only inbound tree a
   valid Runtime posture and made the inbound processed/ archive
   directory optional, (b) obliged a Connector not to require inbound
   write access, making consumption-recording Connector-private, and (c)
   named deletion rights per artifact class, along with the two
   constraints attached to them: a Connector must not delete or rewrite
   a published request, and a Connector exercising its new deletion
   rights must preserve req_id monotonicity by other durable means.  It
   also pinned three previously implicit reason_code rules: setting one
   on every Result became a keyworded SHOULD, and a consumer must
   tolerate an unrecognized code and must not infer outcome from it.

L.7.  2.1.0 — the body spool, and three optional Result members

   Recorded at the time as an *additive minor bump*: one new optional
   spooled artifact (the Inbound Message) and its schema, one new
   optional Notice member (provenance), and three new optional Result
   members (reason_code, attestation, ts).  No existing schema gained a
   required member, no existing fixture changed shape, and the wire
   major stayed "2".

   *Correction (recorded at 3.0.0).* That "additive minor" label was
   unsound as written.  Against a strictly validating 2.0.0 consumer —
   every schema at that version was closed at every level — a Notice
   carrying the new provenance member failed schema validation as a
   *whole document* and was silently dropped: precisely the failure mode



Rapp & Adams              Expires 24 April 2027               [Page 146]

Internet-Draft                    AMMP                      October 2026


   cited as the reason attachments had required a major bump,
   reintroduced as a minor.  Version 3.0.0 repairs the versioning model
   rather than relabelling this history, which is why this entry still
   records what shipped rather than what would have been correct.

L.8.  2.0.0 — attachments, and contract_version required

   A *major bump*, moving the wire major from "1" to "2".  It added
   attachment support in both directions — outbound Descriptors with
   required size_bytes and sha256 and their Sidecar bytes, inbound
   Descriptors with a disposition — and made contract_version REQUIRED
   on the submit-request, deliver-notice, and result artifacts, with no
   compatibility mode.  The reason the bump had to be major rather than
   minor is the reasoning in Section 13.1: under the then-universal
   closed envelopes, a new member caused a major-1 consumer to reject
   the _whole document_, which inbound is silent total message loss.  A
   version signal, rather than an unknown-member rejection, is what
   makes that refusal legible.

L.9.  Fixture identifier normalization

   Across these versions the fixture suite's identities were normalized
   to example.com and example.org placeholders, and deployment-specific
   identifiers were removed from fixture content.  This changed no shape
   and no expectation: every affected fixture validates exactly as
   before, and no identifier removed in that pass is reintroduced by
   this document.
